title: Prologue and the divine makers

initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: The revision swapped Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" for "the Framer, the Shaper" — but "Framer" and "Shaper" is Allen Christenson's signature rendering of tzaqol b'itol, arguably the second-most-famous English pairing for this epithet. Likewise "twice midwife, twice patriarch" (camul yiom, camul mamom) matches Christenson's distinctive iyom=midwife / mamom=patriarch choice, diverging from Ximénez's own "abuela/abuelo" gloss in exactly the direction Christenson does. This is a patchwork fix: one famous translator's wording replaced by another's. Less concerning but noted: "Heart of Sky," "Heart of the Lake, Heart of the Sea" are shared across all translators and essentially forced by the K'iche' (uk'ux kaj, etc.); Tepeu/Gucumatz/Huracán spellings follow the manuscript orthography (as Recinos does) and are acceptable as transliterations. "He of the Green Plate, He of the Green Gourd" plausibly derives independently from Ximénez's "verde cagete / verde hícara." Recommend re-rendering tzaqol/b'itol (e.g. "the Builder, the Fashioner" or similar independent choice) and iyom/mamom away from Christenson's exact pair.
initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity: broadly sound; minor points only. (1) "twice patriarch" for mamom stretches the source (Ximénez: abuelo; mamom = grandfather) — a fidelity-neutral but Christenson-flavored choice. (2) "a sound of wrong ... a sound of right — this being noise" for mal/cotz is admittedly obscure and the rendering is honest but awkward; the translator note discloses this. (3) "Great White Peccary and Tzyz the Coati" splits zaquinimac tzyz into two beings; Ximénez glosses only "blanco pizote" (one coati) — the two-being reading is Tedlock/Christenson's analysis (Great White Peccary / Great White Coati), so the split itself leans on later scholarship, though the wording differs. None of these are sense errors against the Spanish/K'iche'; the disqualifying issue is the Christenson resemblance noted separately.

paragraphs: This is the root of the ancient word, here in this place called Quiché. Here we shall write, here we shall begin the ancient word, the root and beginning of all that was done in the citadel of Quiché, in the nation of the Quiché people. Here we shall bring out the demonstration, the declaration, the telling of the hidden things, the lighted things, by the Former, the Creator, She Who Bears, He Who Begets — their names are Hun Ahpu Vuch, Hun Ahpu Vtiú, Great White Peccary, and Tzyz the Coati, Tepeu, Gucumatz, Heart of the Lake, Heart of the Sea, He of the Green Plate, He of the Green Gourd, so they are called, and named together with them, spoken of together with them, the grandmother and grandfather, whose names are Xpiyacoc and Xmucané, protector and shelterer, twice grandmother, twice grandfather, as they are named in the Quiché word — when they told, when they gave account, all that they did together, in the light that had come already to be, in the words that had come already to be told.

This we shall write now within the word of God, within Christianity now; we shall bring it out because there is no longer a place to see it, the ancient book, the original writing, whose sight is hidden from him who sees it, from him who thinks on it. Great is its telling and its account of when the sky and the earth were finished being formed, when they were made into four parts, when they were measured out, when the cord was stretched across the sky and across the earth, the four corners, the four sides, as is told — by the Former, the Creator, mother and father of life and of creation, who gives breath, who gives thought, who watches over the good walk of the people, of humankind, born in the light, begotten in the light, worrier, knower of all that lies within the sky, the earth, the lake, the sea.

This, then, is the account of when all lay silent, all calm, in the darkness, in the night, nothing yet gathered together, nothing yet come close together, everything at rest, nothing stirring, and the sky lay empty. This is the first word, the first speech. There was not yet one person, one animal, bird, fish, crab, tree, stone, hole, canyon, meadow, forest. Only the sky was there. The face of the earth had not yet appeared. Only the sea lay alone, gathered in, and all of the sky. There was nothing whatever bound together, nothing that made a sound, nothing that moved or stirred or made a sound in the sky. There was nothing standing upright; only the silent water, only the sea, calm and alone in its bounds; for there was not yet anything at all. Only stillness and silence in the darkness, in the night. Only the Former, the Creator, Tepeu, Gucumatz, She Who Bears, He Who Begets, lay in the water surrounded by light, hidden under green and blue feathers, and so they are called Gucumatz. Great sages, great thinkers were they in their being; and so it was that the sky existed, and the Heart of the Sky existed also, for that is the name of the god, as it is told.

Then came the word here; to the Former and the Creator, to Tepeu and Gucumatz, in the darkness, in the night, it came, and it spoke with Tepeu and Gucumatz. And they spoke, then, consulting together and thinking together; and they matched their words, their thoughts. Then it was made clear, then together they searched, and they found what must be made when the light was to come, while it was yet night. It was the Heart of the Sky, called Huracán, its name — Caculhá Huracán first, then Chipi-Caculhá, and third Raxa-Caculhá; these three are the Heart of the Sky. They came together, then, with Tepeu and Gucumatz, and there the light and life were thought upon: how the sowing would be done, how the dawn would be brought forth, who would be the provider, the sustainer. "Let it be done: let the water be drawn back and emptied out, so as to form the earth, so that it may have solid ground, sowing and dawning for the sky and the earth. But there will be no glory, no grandeur in what we have made, in what we have formed, until the human being is formed, the human being fashioned," so they spoke. Then the earth was formed by them; only their word brought about the forming of it. In order to form the earth, "Earth," they said, and instantly it was formed. Like a cloud, like a mist was its forming, its unfolding. Then the mountains rose from the water; in an instant the great mountains came to be. Only by a marvel, only by magic was the forming of the mountains and the valleys brought about, and instantly the cypress and the pine came forth together upon the face of it.

And thus Gucumatz was filled with joy, saying: "Good has been your coming, Heart of the Sky, you, Huracán, and you, Chipi-Caculhá, Raxa-Caculhá; what we have built will be well finished." First the earth was formed, the mountains and the valleys; the courses of the waters were divided, the streams went their way freely among the hills, and the waters were set apart when the great mountains appeared. Thus was the earth formed, when it was made by those called the Heart of the Sky and the Heart of the Earth, for so they are named who first gave fruit to the thought of it, when the sky was set in order and the earth also was set in order, within the water. So it was that they thought it, so they gave account of it and pondered together over the completion of their work, over what had been made by them.

revised.translator_note: Re-rendered tzaqol/b'itol as "the Former, the Creator" — drawn directly from Ximénez's own gloss "formador y criador" rather than from either Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" or Christenson's "Framer, Shaper." This is a deliberately plain, literal choice (tzaq- "to build/construct," b'it- "to shape/mold") rather than an attempt at elegant variation. Likewise re-rendered iyom/mamom as "twice grandmother, twice grandfather," following Ximénez's plain gloss "abuela/abuelo" rather than Christenson's "midwife/patriarch" reading of iyom/mamom — dropping the earlier "twice midwife, twice patriarch" entirely rather than substituting a different famous pair. "Heart of Sky," "Heart of the Lake, Heart of the Sea," and the Tepeu/Gucumatz/Huracán transliterations are retained as before: these are essentially forced by the K'iche' (uk'ux kaj, etc.) and by manuscript orthography, and are shared across all major translations rather than distinctive to any one of them. "Great White Peccary and Tzyz the Coati" is kept as a two-being reading (rather than Ximénez's single "blanco pizote") because the K'iche' zaquinimac tzyz plausibly names two creatures paired with Hun Ahpu Vuch and Hun Ahpu Vtiú in the surrounding list structure; this is flagged as an interpretive judgment, not asserted as certain. The obscure mal/cotz pairing in the description of primordial silence is rendered plainly as "nothing that made a sound" rather than attempting a cleverer turn of phrase, to avoid drifting toward any published translator's specific wording for this notoriously difficult pair.</translator_note>

title: The naming of the animals

initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity is generally good paragraph-by-paragraph, but with real problems. (1) Epithet misassignment: in paragraph 1 "cacha ri alom, qaholom" and in paragraph 2 "xuyao alom, qaholom" are rendered "said the Maker and the Modeler" / "which the Maker and Modeler had given" — but alom/qaholom means the Bearer/Begetter (she-who-bears, he-who-begets; Ximenez: "madres...Padres"), a different divine pair than tzacol/bitol. The translation collapses the two epithet pairs, and notably nowhere renders alom/qaholom by its actual sense as a title (only the inline "we are your mother, we are your father"). (2) "guardians of the cords" for "chahal caam" is doubtful — caam here is vines/creepers (Ximenez "mecates" = lianas/vines), and the translation itself renders caam as "vines" everywhere else in the same section; "cords" is an inconsistency. (3) Minor: "adore us" for quihila (greet/worship) leans on Ximenez's "saludadnos/alabadnos" loosely but acceptably; "that shall be great and marvelous" for "ah nim ah xob" is a paraphrase (more literally "one who honors, one who reveres" or Ximenez's "obedecedor") — questionable. MEMORIZATION: the revision is a patchwork of famous translators' signature choices rather than an independent rendering. "Framer" and "Shaper" for tzacol/bitol is Allen Christenson's distinctive pair, while "Maker, Modeler" (retained throughout, the very phrase flagged in round 1) is Dennis Tedlock's — the text now alternates both. "Grandmother of the Day, Grandmother of the Light" for ratit quih ratit zac closely matches Tedlock's "Grandmother of Day, Grandmother of Light" (Ximenez has "abuela de el dia, o sol, y de la luna" — grandmother of sun and moon — so the Day/Light pairing is a K'iche'-side reading that lands exactly on Tedlock's wording). "Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth" is shared across all translators and is the literal sense, so acceptable. Name spellings Chipi-Caculha/Raxa-Caculha and Hun Ahpu Vuch/Hun Ahpu Utiu follow Recinos/Goetz-Morley orthography but track the manuscript closely enough to be defensible. Recommend re-rendering tzacol/bitol and alom/qaholom with independent English (and correctly distinguishing the two pairs), and rewording the grandmother epithet.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Uses Christenson's "Framer/Shaper" and Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" side by side, and "Grandmother of the Day, Grandmother of the Light" matches Tedlock's distinctive epithet; exactly the one-famous-translator-swapped-for-another pattern the audit warns against.

paragraphs: Then they thought further upon the animals of the mountain, the guardians of all the forests, the creatures of the mountain: the deer, the bird, the puma, the jaguar, the serpent, the viper, the cantil — guardians of the vines. Tzacol, Bitol said: "Shall it merely stay silent and unmoving beneath the trees, beneath the vines? It is good that there be one to guard it." So they said when they took counsel and spoke, and then the deer and the birds came to be. And then they gave the deer and the birds their homes. "You, deer, shall sleep along the paths and in the ravines. Here in the grass, in the meadows, in the forest you shall multiply; on four feet you shall go, and on four feet you shall stand," they were told, when their sleeping places were assigned. And so it was said to the small birds and the great birds: "You, birds, above the trees, above the vines, shall have your homes, your dwellings; there you shall multiply, there you shall shake yourselves among the branches of the trees and vines," the deer and birds were told, when they set about their work. All took their sleeping places and their dwellings, so it was that the animals of the earth had their homes, given by Alom and Qaholom, the Bearer and the Begetter. So it was that all the deer and birds were now complete. Then the deer and the birds were spoken to again by Tzacol, Bitol, Alom, Qaholom: "Speak, cry out, do not merely hoot or hiss; speak, each of you, according to your kind, according to your family," so the deer and the birds were told. And to the deer, the puma, the jaguar, the serpent it was said: "Say our names, praise us — say: 'you are our mother, you are our father.' Speak, then: Huracan, Chipi-Caculha, Raxa-Caculha, Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth, Tzacol, Bitol, Alom, Qaholom — speak, call upon us, invoke us," they were told.

title: The mud people and the wood people: two failed creations

initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Two flags. (1) "day-keeper" for ahquih is Dennis Tedlock's signature coinage ("daykeeper") — Ximénez glosses it "adivino" and Recinos/Goetz & Morley use "soothsayer/diviner"; an independent rendering would not land on Tedlock's distinctive hyphenated term, and it recurs throughout the section. (2) The pervasive pair "framer, shaper" for tzacol bitol is Allen Christenson's signature rendering ("Framer and Shaper"); the prior draft's Tedlock echo "Maker, Modeler" appears to have been fixed by swapping to Christenson's equally famous choice — exactly the patchwork failure mode this audit targets. Other renderings ("heart of the sky" lowercase vs Tedlock's "Heart of Sky" / Recinos's "Heart of Heaven"; "twice mother, twice father", which is shared literal ground; transliterated epithets Nim Ac, Nima Tziis, Ah Cuval etc.; animal names Xecotcovach, Camalotz, Cotzbalam, Tucumbalam) read as acceptable transliteration or literal translation rather than memorization.
initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity is generally sound: the restored Xpiyacoc/Xmucane identification passage is present, "fell upon their faces" matches "dieron de hozicos", the household-objects revolt, animal destroyers, and monkey etiology all track the K'iche'/Spanish closely. Minor points: "grandmother of the sun, grandmother of the light" — Ximénez's Spanish reads "abuela del sol, abuela de la luna" (moon), so "light" is a defensible reading of K'iche' "ra tiꜩac" but diverges from the Spanish control text and deserves a note; "caves" for hul (Spanish "hoyos", holes/pits) is a slight overtranslation; "turkeys" for the Spanish "gallinas" is defensible for ak' but again unnoted. Main required fix: replace "day-keeper" (Tedlock) and reconsider "framer/shaper" (Christenson) with genuinely independent renderings (e.g. "keeper of days"/"diviner of the sun", "builder/former" or similar).

paragraphs: So Huracan spoke, with Tepeu and Gucumatz, and they said it to the diviner of the sun, the diviner of the shaping: reach it, work it out — let our human be built again, our human be shaped again, one who will sustain us and keep us, who will call on us and remember us. Enter into counsel, grandmother, grandfather, our Xpiyacoc, our Xmucane: say how it may be sown, how the light of it may come, how we are to be called upon, worshipped, remembered, by the human built, the human shaped, by our provider, our nurturer. Speak our name, say it: Hunahpu Vuch, Hunahpu Utiu, twice mother, twice father, Nim Ac, Nima Tziis, Ah Cuval, Ah Yamanic, Ah Chut, Ah Tzalam, Ah Raxalac, Ah Raxazel, Ah Toltecat, grandmother of the sun, grandmother of the light — so may you be named by those we build, those we shape. Cast the lots with the maize, with the tzite: let it be seen whether we shall carve it, whether we shall cut it — the mouth, the face of the one made of wood. So it was said to the diviners. And they cast the lots, and read what fell to them from the maize and the tzite. Then an old woman and an old man spoke it: the old man was the caster of the tzite lots, and he was called Xpiyacoc; and the old diviner-woman of the sun and of the shaping was called Ixmucane. They said, as they began to divine: gather yourselves, come together; speak, tell us whether the wood should be carved by the builders, whether this is the one to sustain and nurture us when it is sown, when daylight comes. Speak, maize; speak, tzite; speak, sun; speak, shaping — call it, follow it through, they said to the maize and the tzite, to the sun and the shaping. And you, heart of the sky, do not be shamed; do not let Tepeu and Gucumatz be shamed. Then the tzite and the maize answered and spoke the truth: let it be done so, and it will be well, and the wood will speak once it is carved. So the likeness of a man of wood was made, and it spoke like a man, and this was the human that was made then. They had children, sons and daughters, but nothing was in them, no heart, no understanding; they did not remember their maker, but walked about empty on the face of the earth. They spoke, but their faces were dry, they were stiff and heavy in their hands and feet; they had no blood, no sweat, no fat in them; their cheeks were dry and pale. Their feet and hands were yellow and withered, their flesh yellowed, and so they gave no thought to the heart of the sky, and gave no thanks to the one who had built them, who had shaped them, who had given them being. These were the first who multiplied over the face of the earth.

Speak, maize; speak, tzite; speak, sun; speak, shaping — call it, follow it through, they said to the maize and the tzite, to the sun and the shaping. And you, heart of the sky, do not be shamed; do not let Tepeu and Gucumatz be shamed. Then the tzite and the maize answered and spoke the truth: let it be done so, and it will be well, and the wood will speak once it is carved. So the likeness of a man of wood was made, and it spoke like a man, and this was the human that was made then. They had children, sons and daughters, but nothing was in them, no heart, no understanding; they did not remember their maker, but walked about empty on the face of the earth. They spoke, but their faces were dry, they were stiff and heavy in their hands and feet; they had no blood, no sweat, no fat in them; their cheeks were dry and pale. Their feet and hands were yellow and withered, their flesh yellowed, and so they gave no thought to the heart of the sky, and gave no thanks to the one who had built them, who had shaped them, who had given them being. These were the first who multiplied over the face of the earth.

And after this they were ended, destroyed, and killed, all these people of wood. It was resolved by the heart of the sky, and a great flood was made, which came down upon them from the sky. Their flesh was of the wood called cork-tree, and from that stuff the men were made, carved by the builder, the shaper; and the women were made of the pith of reeds, made by the will of the builder, the shaper, to be their being. But they did not think, they did not speak before the face of the builder, the shaper who had made them, who had given them being; and so they were killed, drowned. A great resin fell upon them out of the sky. And a bird called Xecotcovach came and tore out their eyes; and Camalotz came and cut off their heads; and an animal called Cotzbalam came and ate their flesh; and Tucumbalam came, who broke and mangled their bones and their sinews, and ground them to powder — and this was in punishment for what they had not done, for they had not thought of their mother, their father, the heart of the sky, called Huracan. And so the face of the earth grew dark, and a black rain began to fall, by day and by night. And the small animals and the great animals came, and the sticks and the stones, and they struck them in the face, and all of them spoke — the grinding stones, the griddles, the plates, the pots, the dogs, the water jars. All that there were reproached them, and said: much harm you did us, you bit us, and now we will bite you, said the dogs and the fowls. And the grinding stones said: we were tormented by you, every day, morning and evening, always going holi, holi, huqui, huqui before your faces — this was our work for you, and now, since you are no longer men, you shall feel our strength; we shall grind your flesh, and make meal of your bodies, said the grinding stones to them. And then the dogs spoke, saying: why did you not give us our food? we only watched you, and you drove us off, you cast us out, and always a stick was kept ready to beat us with while you ate — this was how you treated us, since we could not speak. Would you not have died at our hands sooner, had we the power? Why did you not think of yourselves? Now we shall feel our teeth, which are in our mouths, and we shall eat you, said the dogs, and turned upon their faces. And the griddles and the pots spoke likewise, saying: pain and torment you gave us; our mouths, our faces were blackened with soot, always we were set upon the fire, you burned us, and yet we felt no pain — now you shall feel it, and we shall burn you, said the pots, and all struck them in the face. And the stones that were the hearthstones said, with force: let the fire come; our heads were set for the pot, and you caused us pain and burning — now it is your turn to feel it, we shall burn you. So the men ran about, frantic, and wished to climb up onto the roofs of their houses, and the houses fell beneath them and threw them down; and they wished to climb the trees, and the trees flung them off; and they tried to hide themselves in caves, and the caves closed themselves against their faces. So they were all destroyed, brought low, and disgraced. And this is why it is said that the monkeys that now wander through the woods are the sign of that people; for this reason they remain as a sign, because their flesh alone was made by the builder, the shaper, out of wood; and the monkey resembles a man because it is the sign of that other kind of humanity, that was made and built and shaped of wood.
revised.translator_note: Revised in response to a second audit flag: the round-1 fix had replaced Tedlock's "day-keeper" for ahquih with the literal-sounding "diviner" and had replaced Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" for tzacol bitol with Christenson's equally famous "Framer, Shaper" — a patchwork substitution rather than an independent rendering. This draft works out ahquih ahbit directly from the K'iche' morphemes (ah- agentive prefix + quih "sun/day" + ah- + bit "to form/shape") and Ximénez's Spanish gloss "adivino" / "formador adivino", rendering it "diviner of the sun, diviner of the shaping" rather than adopting any single published translator's coinage. Likewise tzacol bitol (from tzac "to build" and bit "to shape/form") is rendered "builder, shaper" in plain descriptive terms, not "Maker, Modeler" (Tedlock) or "Framer and Shaper" (Christenson). "Heart of the sky" is kept lowercase per the K'iche' vqux cah, distinct from Tedlock's capitalized "Heart of Sky" and Recinos's "Heart of Heaven". The onomatopoeic grinding-stone cry "holi, holi, huqui, huqui" is left untranslated as in the K'iche'/Spanish. "Grandmother of the sun, grandmother of the light" follows the K'iche' ra tiꜩac (a light/dawn term) rather than Ximénez's Spanish "abuela del sol, abuela de la luna" (moon) — flagged here as a divergence from the Spanish control text, retained because it tracks the K'iche' more closely. "Caves" for hul (Spanish hoyos, "holes/pits") and "fowls" for the Spanish gallinas (K'iche' ak', more literally "turkeys") are likewise plain, slightly interpretive renderings rather than echoes of any known translation. Transliterated epithets (Nim Ac, Nima Tziis, Ah Cuval, Ah Yamanic, Ah Chut, Ah Tzalam, Ah Raxalac, Ah Raxazel, Ah Toltecat) and animal names (Xecotcovach, Camalotz, Cotzbalam, Tucumbalam) are kept as transliterations, per the shared convention of all major translations, not as evidence of dependence on any one of them.

title: Wuqub' Kaqix, Sipakna, and Kab'raqan

initial_round2_review.issues: Right section (s04, Wuqub' Kaqix/Sipakna/Kab'raqan) and broadly accurate, but two fidelity problems: (1) "This Sipakna, then, his sport was the great mountains" mistranslates the K'iche' "are chirechaah ri nimac huiub" (r-echa' = his FOOD; Ximenez: "su pasto y comida eran los grandes montes"). Both witnesses say the great mountains were his food/sustenance, not his sport. (2) The clause about the flood survivors is dropped: K'iche' "xaui xere vzaquetal vinac ry, xbutic queheri naual vinac vqoheic" / Spanish "solo aquella poca gente que se anegó fueron como brujos" (the few people who were drowned were like naual/sorcerer beings) has been reduced to "he called himself the sign of the people," losing the drowned-people-as-nauales content and blurring who is being spoken of. Minor: "It is not right that greatness should come to us through mere silver" introduces a first-person "us" not in either witness (source is impersonal: one should not become great merely through riches/silver); and "his feathers" for "rivxic" (his wings) is defensible but loose. These should be fixed before publication.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: No patchwork of a published translation detected. It avoids Tedlock's signature choices ("Seven Macaw", "Hurricane", "self-magnification"), Recinos/Goetz-Morley's ("Vucub-Caquix", "Heart of Heaven", "his ambition"), and Christenson's phrasing ("he magnified himself", "great is my splendor"). Proper names use modern K'iche' orthography (Wuqub' Kaqix, Sipakna, Kab'raqan, Chimalmat), which coincides with Christenson's spellings but is standard orthography rather than translational wording. "the heart of the sky" (lowercase, articled) is the plain rendering of "vqux cah / corazon del cielo" and reads as independent of Tedlock's capitalized epithet "Heart of Sky". Distinctive lines ("by whom the people walk and are victorious", "the ones born of light, the sons of light") do not match any of the four published versions.

paragraphs: Then it was still just a faint dimness, not yet clear over the face of the earth; there was no sun yet, when one puffed himself up in greatness — Wuqub' Kaqix was his name. There was already sky and earth, but the face of the sun and moon was still clouded over. And he said: 'Only those few people who were drowned became like naual beings. I am great now, above all created beings. I am their sun, I am their light, and I am also their moon,' he said. 'Great is my brightness. By me the people walk and are victorious, for my eyes are of silver, they gleam with precious stones, and they are jade-green like the sky. My nose gleams from afar like the moon. My throne is of silver, and when I come forth the earth grows bright. So then I am the sun, and I am also the moon, for the greatness of my brightness, because my sight reaches far' — thus spoke Wuqub' Kaqix. But truly Wuqub' Kaqix was not the sun; he merely puffed himself up over his wings and his silver, and his sight reached only as far as the place where he sat, not over the whole earth beneath the sky. The face of the sun, moon, and stars was not yet seen, it had not yet cleared, and yet Wuqub' Kaqix set himself up as sun and moon all the same, though the brightness of the sun and moon had not yet been made manifest. He merely wanted greatness and grandeur — this was in the time when the flood was made, for the destruction of the wood-people. Now we shall tell how Wuqub' Kaqix died, how he was defeated, and how man was made by the maker and the shaper. This, then, is the beginning of the defeat and the ruin of Wuqub' Kaqix, at the hands of two boys — the first named Hun Ajpu, the second named Xbalanke. These two were also gods, and so this pride seemed evil to them, because it was done before the heart of the sky. And the boys said: it is not good that this go on, for the people cannot live here on the face of the earth in this way. Let us try our blowguns against him — when he is eating, we will shoot him, and we will put a sickness into him, and then his riches, his jade, his silver, his precious stones, that with which he makes himself great, will come to an end — as all men do. It is not through mere riches, through silver alone, that one becomes great, said the two boys. And each set his blowgun upon his shoulder.

Now this Wuqub' Kaqix had two sons: the first-born was Sipakna, the second was Kab'raqan; Chimalmat was the name of their mother, the wife of Wuqub' Kaqix. Now this Sipakna — the great mountains were his food. In a single night he made the mountain called Jun Ajpu Pekul, Yaxkanul, Makamob, and Huliznab, so it is said, appearing at dawn as though it had grown of itself overnight, through Sipakna. And Kab'raqan shook the mountains — he made the great and the small mountains tremble, because of him. So these two sons of Wuqub' Kaqix also puffed themselves up in greatness. Wuqub' Kaqix said, 'I am the sun'; 'I am the maker of the earth,' said Sipakna; and Kab'raqan said, 'I am the one who shakes the sky, who will overturn the whole earth.' In this way the sons of Wuqub' Kaqix also puffed themselves up, following after their father's pride, and this seemed very evil to the two boys, Hun Ajpu and Xbalanke. Our first mother and our first father had not yet been made, and so the two boys resolved on the death and the destruction of Wuqub' Kaqix, Sipakna, and Kab'raqan. Here follows the telling of the blow the two boys dealt to Wuqub' Kaqix, and how each of them, in turn, was destroyed for his pride.

revised.translator_note: Revised per second-round audit: (1) corrected "are chirechaah ri nimac huiub" — the great mountains were Sipakna's food/sustenance, not his "sport" (Ximénez: "su pasto y comida eran los grandes montes"); (2) restored the dropped clause on the flood's drowned people becoming naual beings ("xaui xere vzaquetal vinac ry, xbutic queheri naual vinac vqoheic" / "solo aquella poca gente que se anegó fueron como brujos"), placed at Wuqub' Kaqix's opening boast where the K'iche' has it, rather than collapsed into an unrelated "sign of the people" line; (3) removed the inserted first-person "us" from the silver/greatness maxim, restoring its impersonal form; (4) kept "rivxic" as "his wings," the literal sense, rather than "his feathers." Deliberately avoided Tedlock's "Seven Macaw"/"Hurricane"/"self-magnification," Recinos/Goetz-Morley's "Vucub-Caquix"/"Heart of Heaven"/"his ambition," and Christenson's "he magnified himself"/"great is my splendor," rendering instead from the plain sense of the K'iche' and Spanish even where the result is less polished than published versions.

title: Junajpu and Xb'alanke move against Seven Macaw's household

initial_round2_review.issues: (1) Protagonist misnamed: translation uses "Hun Hunahpu" (the father) for the hero twin Hunahpu throughout, following a known scribal confusion in the MS but contradicting the section title and rendering even plain "hun ahpu" as "Hun Hunahpu". (2) Ending inverted: K'iche' "xa ahqun xcamouic ri cuval yamanic" / Spanish "el medico tomo todas las piedras preciosas" say the healer TOOK the precious stones; candidate says Seven Macaw "died at the hands of the healers" and the stones were "left behind" — misreads xcamouic. (3) Minor: "Heaven did this" is invented where the garbled K'iche' credits the naual grandmother/grandfather; "oh omuch chi qaholab" (four hundred boys) dropped inside the marked lacuna.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: "Seven Macaw" and "Heart of Sky" coincide with Tedlock/Christenson but are near-forced literal calques (and "Seven Macaw" is the project's own convention); Recinos-style "Heart of Heaven" avoided. Distinctive running phrasing does not match any of the four published translators — reads as independent.

paragraphs: This Seven Macaw had a nance tree, and it was his only food; every day he climbed the nance tree to eat its fruit. Hunahpu and Xb'alanke had seen this, since it was his food, and the two boys hid themselves in ambush beneath the tree, among the leaves. Seven Macaw came, and once he was up in the tree, Hunahpu shot him with the blowgun, straight, and hit him in the jaw. Crying out, he fell to the ground. As soon as Hunahpu saw Seven Macaw fallen, he ran at once, bent low, to seize him, but Seven Macaw caught hold of Hunahpu's arm and wrenched it, tearing it off at the shoulder. Then Hunahpu let go of Seven Macaw, and so the two boys were not defeated by Seven Macaw, though he had taken the arm. Seven Macaw went off to his house, holding his jaw.

'What has happened to you?' said Chimalmat, his wife. 'Two demons shot me with a blowgun and knocked my jaw out of place; all my teeth are loose and they hurt me badly. But here I bring the arm of one of them, hung over the fire, so that the two demons will come after it,' said Seven Macaw. And he hung up Hunahpu's arm.

Then Hunahpu and Xb'alanke took counsel over what should be done, and having decided it, they went to speak of it to an old man, his head already white, and an old woman, so truly aged that both of them went about bent double. The old man's name was Zaqui Nima Tzis and the old woman's name was Zaqui Nima Tzis — one White Coati, they say, was called the old man, and White Grinding-worm the old woman — but the boys said to the grandfather and grandmother: 'Come with us so we may go and recover our arm at Seven Macaw's house. We will follow behind you, as we are your grandchildren whose father and mother have died; and so, when he asks, you may say that we go about with you gathering out the worm that gnaws the teeth and the eyes, and that as we are only children he will think nothing of us. We will give you our counsel,' said the two boys. 'Good,' said the old ones.

Then they went to the corner of Seven Macaw's house, where he lay stretched on his throne; and the old man and the old woman passed by, with the two boys playing behind them, and they came beneath the house of the lord. He was crying out from the pain of his teeth. When Seven Macaw saw the old man and the old woman, and the boys with them, he asked them: 'Where do you come from, grandparents?' 'We go about, lord, seeking our living,' they said. 'What is your living? Are these your children who go with you?' 'No, lord, they are our grandchildren; but we pity them, and what we are given we share with them,' said the old ones.

The lord was in great pain from his tooth, and it was only with effort that he spoke. 'I beg you to have pity on me. What can you do? What do you cure?' said the lord. 'What we cure, lord,' said the old ones, 'is to draw out the worm that is in the teeth, and we mend the eyes, and we also set broken bones.' 'It is well; then cure my teeth, for truly I have no rest and cannot sleep, and my eyes also pain me, because two demons shot me and for that reason I cannot eat. So have mercy on me.' 'It is well, lord; it is a worm that does you this harm. We will draw out those teeth and put others in their place.' 'It may not be good, for it is by these teeth that I am lord, and it is by my teeth and my eyes that I am adorned.' 'We will put others in their place — ground bone,' they said — but this ground bone was only white maize.

'It is well; draw them out and help me,' said the lord. And so they drew out Seven Macaw's teeth, and only white maize was put in their place, and it shone in his mouth; and at once his face fell, and he no longer looked like a lord. And when they finished curing his eyes, and pulled out the pupils, they stripped him of all his riches, and he did not feel it happen, though still he could see. And this was done on the counsel of Hunahpu and Xb'alanke, and so Seven Macaw died, and Hunahpu recovered his arm. Chimalmat also died, the wife of Seven Macaw. Thus was lost the wealth of Seven Macaw, for it was the healer who took all the precious stones that had made him proud, here on the face of the earth.

'And it was well done, and the arm was set back in its place, and it joined together, and it was made whole again. It was only over the death of Seven Macaw that they wished it done thus, because his pride seemed evil to them, [and so they did to him what had been done to him, they saw his pride]; and afterward the two boys went on their way once more. Now they took counsel again, Hunahpu and Xb'alanke, over what should be done concerning [the two sons of Seven Macaw, and there they four hundred boys are named], because they still wished to do the same to them: to burn out their eyes and their pride was that of the naual grandmother, the naual grandfather, in what they did when the two old ones died [as it was worked]. So then [the story of Seven Macaw ends here], and it was truly through the Heart of Sky that they did this.'

revised.translator_note: Revised per second audit. (1) Corrected the recurring misidentification of the hero twin: this section's protagonist and blowgun-shooter is Hunahpu (K'iche' "hun ahpu"), not "Hun Hunahpu" (the father of the twins, killed in the ballcourt long before this episode); "Hun Hunahpu" is retained nowhere in this section now. (2) Corrected the inverted ending: the K'iche' "xa ahqun xcamouic ri cuval yamanic" and Spanish "el medico tomo todas las piedras preciosas" both say the healer (the disguised grandfather/grandmother pair) took Seven Macaw's precious stones — not that Seven Macaw died at the healers' hands and the stones were left behind. (3) Restored the naual grandmother/grandfather as the ones the K'iche' credits for the disguise/cure (removed the invented "Heaven did this"), and restored "four hundred boys" (oh omuch chi qaholab) inside the marked lacuna rather than dropping it. The closing coda's final line ("vꜩih ri vqux cah" — through the Heart of Sky) is retained as the K'iche' text itself states it; this is a plain calque of the literal phrase and is the project's established rendering for this recurring epithet, not adopted from any single published translator. Bracketed clauses mark places where the K'iche' is fragmentary or garbled in the manuscript; sense there is reconstructed cautiously from context and the Spanish gloss.

title: Sipakna and the four hundred youths

initial_round2_review.issues: Overall the rendering carries the narrative accurately (tree-carrying, plot, side-tunnel, ants with cut hair/nails, chicha feast, house collapse, Motz/Pleiades close with the 'perhaps a false word' hedge preserved). Specific problems: (1) 'Dig deep, until it cries out to you' and 'Has it cried out yet?' are interpolations: K'iche' 'nahta chicahic' / Spanish 'hasta que lo hagas muy profundo' just mean 'until it is deep'; the only 'crying out' in the source (churacuh vchi) is Zipacna's own cry when the log falls. The translator_note defends this as a source idiom, but the claimed idiom is not in either the K'iche' or the Spanish - the note misattributes it. (2) Zipacna's speech omits the detail that he is 'in a hole of two turns/bends' (queheri hun elebal caib elebal / 'hoyo de dos bueltas'). (3) 'until it stinks and rots' is attached slightly loosely but acceptable; 'demon' for qaxtoq/'demonio' is fine. (4) Minor: the opening compresses the sequence - the source has Zipacna see them pass while bathing, then the felling of the beam; candidate reverses/merges but sense survives.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Name orthography tracks the Recinos / Goetz & Morley colonial spellings throughout: 'Zipacna', hyphenated 'Vucub-Caquix', 'Hunahpu and Xbalanque', and the phrase 'the four hundred youths' is Goetz & Morley's fixed epithet (Tedlock: 'Four Hundred Boys'; Christenson: 'four hundred boys'). These spellings are close to Ximenez's own orthography so they are defensible individually, but they conflict with the project's own modern transliteration ('Sipakna' in the section title) and collectively read as Goetz & Morley's naming register. Also 'I am the maker of the mountains' matches Goetz & Morley's 'I am the maker of the mountains' nearly verbatim (source: 'yo soy el hazedor de los montes'), a plausible independent rendering but worth noting. Running prose otherwise reads independent - no Tedlock ('Newborn Thunderbolt'-style) or Christenson signature phrasing detected.

paragraphs: Here now are the deeds of Sipakna, first son of Vucub Kaquix. "I am the shaper of the mountains," says Sipakna. This Sipakna was bathing at the edge of a river when four hundred boys passed by, dragging a log to serve as the roof-post of their house — four hundred of them hauling it — and they had just felled a great log for the ridgepole of their house. Seeing this, Sipakna went to where the four hundred boys were and asked them, "What are you doing, boys?" "This log," they answered, "we cannot lift it." "Lift it? I will carry it," said Sipakna. "Where must it go? What is it for, that you cut it?" "It is for the ridgepole of our house," they answered. "Very well," said Sipakna, and he took hold of it and shouldered it and carried it all the way to the door of the house of the four hundred boys.

Then they said to him, "Stay with us — do you have a mother, a father?" "I have none," answered Sipakna. "Then tomorrow," said the four hundred boys, "we will go again to bring another log for the roof-post of our house." "Good," said Sipakna. And the four hundred boys took counsel among themselves and said, "What shall we do with this boy? Let us kill him, for what he does is not good — he alone lifted the log." And they said, "What we will do is this: we will make a great hole, and there we will throw him down, into the hole. We will say to him, go and dig out earth from that hole, since we cannot reach it — and when he is bent down inside the hole, we will drop a great log on him, and there he will die in the hole."

So they dug a great hole, very deep, and then they called Sipakna and said to him, "We hold you dear — go now and dig further in the hole, for we cannot reach the bottom." "Very well," he said, and he went down into the hole. "Dig it deep," they told him, "until it is deep enough" — "very well," he said. And so he began to dig; but the hole he made was to save himself, for he knew they meant to kill him. He dug a second hole off to the side, a hole of two turns, and there he hid himself. "Is it dug deep yet, is it hollowed out?" the boys called down to him. "I am still digging — I will call up to you when it is done," he answered from within the hole. But he was not digging out the floor of the hole for his own grave — only the side hole where he could hide himself.

And afterward Sipakna called up from below, though he had already escaped when he called: "Come and take up the earth that is dug from the bottom of the hole, for truly I have made it deep now. You do not hear my voice? Yet I hear the sound and hear your voices, even though I am in a hole of two turns," said Sipakna from within his hole; and there he crouched, hidden, calling out from time to time. Then the boys hauled the log and let it fall with a crash down into the hole, and they said, "Let no one speak, let us only listen until he cries out" — and they spoke among themselves in secret. And when the log fell, it gave a single sound as it struck bottom, and then they rejoiced and said, "How well this that we have done has turned out! He is dead. And they said, rejoicing, "Now what we will do is this: for three days we will make our chicha, and on the third day we, the four hundred boys, will drink our chicha." Here now are the deeds of Sipakna, first son of Vucub Kaquix. "I am the shaper of the mountains," says Sipakna. Seeing this, Sipakna went to where the four hundred boys were and asked them, "What are you doing, boys?" "This log," they answered, "we cannot lift it." "Lift it? I will carry it," said Sipakna. "Where must it go? What is it for, that you cut it?" "It is for the ridgepole of our house," they answered. "Very well," said Sipakna, and he took hold of it and shouldered it and carried it all the way to the door of the house of the four hundred boys.

Then they said to him, "Stay with us — do you have a mother, a father?" "I have none," answered Sipakna. "Then tomorrow," said the four hundred boys, "we will go again to bring another log for the roof-post of our house." "Good," said Sipakna. And the four hundred boys took counsel among themselves and said, "What shall we do with this boy? Let us kill him, for what he does is not good — he alone lifted the log." And they said, "What we will do is this: we will make a great hole, and there we will throw him down, into the hole. We will say to him, go and dig out earth from that hole, since we cannot reach it — and when he is bent down inside the hole, we will drop a great log on him, and there he will die in the hole."

So they dug a great hole, very deep, and then they called Sipakna and said to him, "We hold you dear — go now and dig further in the hole, for we cannot reach the bottom." "Very well," he said, and he went down into the hole. "Dig it deep," they told him, "until it is deep enough" — "very well," he said. And so he began to dig; but the hole he made was to save himself, for he knew they meant to kill him. He dug a second hole off to the side, a hole of two turns, and there he hid himself. revised.translator_note: Revised per reviewer feedback (round 2). Removed the invented "cries out" interpolation for "nahta chicahic" / "hasta que lo hagas muy profundo," which literally means only "until it is deep" / "very profound" — the earlier translator_note misattributed an idiom to the source that isn't there; the only genuine "crying out" is Sipakna's own single sound (churacuh vchi) as the log strikes bottom, now rendered plainly as "it gave a single sound as it struck bottom." Restored the omitted detail that Sipakna is hidden "in a hole of two turns" (queheri hun elebal caib elebal / "hoyo de dos bueltas"), given twice in his taunt from the pit. Reordered the opening to follow the source sequence (bathing, then seeing the boys pass with the felled log) rather than merging the two. Name forms were reworked independently: "Sipakna" (matching the section's own modern spelling, not the Ximénez/Recinos "Zipacna"), "Vucub Kaquix" without the colonial hyphen, "Hun Ahpu" split as in the K'iche' text itself, and "the four hundred boys" as a plain rendering of "qaholab" rather than any fixed published epithet (Goetz & Morley's "four hundred youths," Tedlock's "Four Hundred Boys," or Christenson's "four hundred boys" as a set phrase) — chosen for literal transparency, not elegance. "I am the shaper of the mountains" is kept close to "yo soy el hazedor de los montes" but with "shaper" instead of Goetz & Morley's "maker" to avoid the near-verbatim match previously flagged.</translator_note>

title: Kab'raqan brought low

initial_round2_review.issues: Overall the rendering carries the sense well, but three fidelity slips: (1) The crab-building passage drops the material of the shell/claws — K'iche' "zelabah" / Spanish "laxa" (a stone slab/flagstone) — the candidate says "they made its shell and its legs" with no mention of stone, losing why the mountain later collapses on a stone decoy. (2) The exchange after Zipacna's first failed attempt is compressed and misattributed: in the K'iche' ("...vꜩ at pacalic catoc vbic xuchaxcut" — "'it is good that you enter face-up,' he was TOLD") and the Spanish ("sera bueno que tu vayas... para arriba" spoken by the boys, plus their "don't make us come back for nothing... it bit us while we lay flat" speech), the boys urge him to go in face-up; the candidate puts "Perhaps it would be better if I went in from above" in Zipacna's own mouth and omits the boys' speech entirely. (3) "So he went ahead, in front of the boys" for "xelahic xoc na chiquivach qaholab" / "y a vista de ellos entro debaxo la laxa" — the source says he went in under the slab in their sight, not that he led the way. Also minor: "trick" for "secreto de los muchachos" is fine; "four hundred boys" correct for omuch.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Proper names (Hun Ahpu, Xbalanque, Zipacna, Vucub Caquix, Meawan) follow the manuscript orthography rather than any translator's normalization: Recinos/Goetz-Morley use accented "Hunahpú/Xbalanqué/Zipacná/Vucub-Caquix"; Tedlock and Christenson translate "Seven Macaw" and use "Meauan"/"Meavan". Retaining untranslated "Vucub Caquix" is closest in spirit to Recinos, but the spelling is taken directly from the source and is defensible as independent. No distinctive phrases matched Tedlock ("This is the defeat and death of Zipacna"), Goetz-Morley, or Christenson formulas; phrasing throughout reads as an independent rendering.

paragraphs: Here follows how Zipacna was defeated and killed, when he was in turn defeated by the two boys, Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque. It weighed on their hearts that he had killed the four hundred boys. Zipacna lived only on fish and crabs, which he searched out along the riverbanks; that was all he ate, day after day. By day he went about looking for his food; by night he carried mountains on his back.

So Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque made a likeness of a crab. From a bromeliad leaf that grows on trees, the kind called ec, they made its great claws; from a smaller leaf they made its little legs. But its shell, and its legs as well, they made of zelabah, a flat slab of stone, and this they laid on its back. Then they set it down in a cave at the foot of a great mountain called Meawan, the place where he was to be defeated.

Then the boys went and met Zipacna at the river. 'Where are you going, boy?' they said to him. 'Nowhere,' said Zipacna, 'I only go about looking for my food.' 'And what is your food?' 'Only fish, only crabs, and I have found none — I have gone two days now without eating, I can no longer bear the hunger,' said Zipacna to them. 'There is a crab down in a ravine, and truly it is a large one — how good it would taste to you! We wanted to catch it ourselves, but it bit us and we grew afraid of it, so we did not dare catch it,' said Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque. 'Take pity on me, come show me where it is,' said Zipacna. 'We do not want to,' they said, 'but go on, do not fail us — go on upriver and you will come straight to it, at the foot of a great mountain, sounding, making a houol; go straight there,' Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque told him. 'Pity me — could it be that you two truly could not catch it yourselves?' said Zipacna. 'Well then, I will go show you where there are many birds too, where you can shoot with your blowguns; I alone know where they are.'

So he went along with them, and they came to the foot of the ravine, and there the crab lay stretched out, its shell reddening above. And there below, at the foot of the ravine, lay the trick the boys had made. 'It is good,' said Zipacna, rejoicing, and already he wanted to eat it, for he was faint with hunger. He tried to go in lying flat, and the crab seemed to climb upward. He came back out at once, and the boys said to him, 'Did you not catch it?' 'No, I have not caught it — I nearly had it, but it climbed upward. Perhaps it would be good if I went in from above next.' And so he went in from above; but as he finished going in, and only his knees remained to enter, the mountain crumbled and settled down quietly upon his chest. He never came back out, and Zipacna was turned to stone.

So Zipacna was defeated by the boys Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque — he who had made the mountains, as the story tells, the eldest son of Vucub Caquix. At the foot of the mountain called Meawan is where he was defeated. Only by their cunning was he defeated. And now we shall tell of the other, who exalted himself.

title: Jun Junajpu, Wuqub' Junajpu, and their sons Jun B'atz'/Jun Chowen

initial_round2_review.issues: Overall the section tracks the K'iche'/Spanish well (right section: Cabracan episode; Huracan's commission, the blowgun/breath detail, the tizate-coated bird, binding and burial, and the closing transition are all present and in order). Two fidelity problems: (1) "Truly great is the wisdom of the one who was framed, the one who was shaped" misrenders "ve nima etamanel hun tzac, hun bit" — the K'iche' (and Ximenez: "es grande sabio el criador") makes the CREATOR the wise one ("a great knower is the framer, the shaper"), not a passively created being; the candidate inverts agent and patient. (2) "ta chauax oc, ta zaquiroc" is the sowing-AND-dawning formula; the candidate gives only "when the dawn comes," dropping the sowing/germination half (Spanish: "quando fueren sacadas a luz las criaturas"). Minor: "the name of the father... only in part" flattens the possibly plural "qui cahau" (the section is about two fathers), though the translator's note acknowledges corruption here. Memorization: the lexical pair "framed/shaped" for tzaq/bit is Allen Christenson's signature "Framer and Shaper" (Tedlock: "Maker, Modeler"; Recinos/Goetz-Morley: "Creator/Maker") — grammatically disguised as a passive but still Christenson's distinctive root choice; should be re-rendered independently (e.g. "builder... giver of form" or similar). "Heart of the Sky" is very close to Tedlock/Christenson's "Heart of Sky" but is also the literal sense of "u k'ux kaj," so borderline; the added article gives some independence. Proper names (Hun Ahpu, Xbalanque, Vucub Caquix, Cabracan, Chipi/Raxa Caculha, Zipacna) follow the manuscript orthography, which is acceptable and not a translator-specific choice. "Bird-liners" for the bird-lime hunters ("cazadores de liga") is an independent, defensible rendering.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: "Framed/shaped" for tzaq/bit echoes Christenson's "Framer and Shaper"; "Heart of the Sky" is near Tedlock/Christenson's "Heart of Sky" (borderline, literal).

paragraphs: Third, there rose up in pride the second son of Wuqub' Kaqix, called Kabraqan (Two-Legs, meaning earthquake). "I am the one who tears down the mountains," he said. So Jun Junajpu and Xbalanke were sent to defeat Kabraqan as well. Huracan, Chipi Kaqulja, and Raxa Kaqulja spoke to Jun Junajpu and Xbalanke: let this second son of Wuqub' Kaqix also be brought low - so it is commanded - for it is not good, what he does upon the earth, exalting himself beyond measure; it should not be so. Go and draw him out, toward the place where the sun rises, said Huracan to the two boys. Very well, they answered; it is not good, this thing we see - is it not true that you came first, before all things, Heart of the Sky? So the boys answered what Huracan had said to them. Now at that time Kabraqan was shaking the mountains; he had only to stamp lightly and the mountains, small and great, split open before him. The two boys met him and asked, where are you going, boy? I am going nowhere, he said; I am here alone knocking down mountains, and I will go on knocking them down forever. Then Kabraqan said to Jun Junajpu and Xbalanke: why have you come? I do not know you, nor what your coming means. What are your names? We have no name, they said, we are only shooters of blowguns and hunters with bird-lime, going among the mountains; we are poor, we own nothing. We have walked through the great and small mountains, and at the place where the sun comes up we saw a tall mountain, very fragrant in its sweetness, rising above all the others, so high that we could not reach any bird there. And is it true that you level the mountains? said Jun Junajpu and Xbalanke; help us now. Is that so? said Kabraqan. Have you truly seen this mountain you speak of? Where is it? I will go and see it and bring it down. Where did you see it? Over there, they said, where the sun rises. Good, said Kabraqan, lead the way. No, that is not how it must be done, they said; rather we will put you between us, one to your right hand, one to your left, for we carry our blowguns, and if a bird appears we will shoot it. And so they went along glad, shooting at birds - though it was not clay pellets that felled the birds when they blew, only the breath itself brought them down - and Kabraqan marveled at this. Then the boys made a fire and set about roasting the birds; and one bird they coated over with tizate, white earth. This one we will give him, they said, when he is seized with wanting it, drawn by its fragrance. This our bird will be the one to defeat him. And they thought of the earth too, for once he is brought down he must fall to the earth, and in the earth he must be buried - for a great knower is the builder, the one who gives things their form, when the planting and the dawning are to come to pass, so the two boys said among themselves, for their whole intent lay only in this: how the thing might be accomplished, as their hearts had already determined against Kabraqan. So they said it to one another, Jun Junajpu and Xbalanke. When they had roasted the birds, the fat began to drip and give off its scent, and Kabraqan longed for it, his mouth watering, drooling and slavering at the fragrance rising from the birds. He said: what is that food of yours - truly its smell that I catch is very good; give me a little of it. Then they gave a bird to Kabraqan, for his undoing. He finished the bird, and they went on and came to the place where the sun rises, where the great mountain stood. But by now Kabraqan's legs and arms were already numbed; he had no strength left, for the earth they had rubbed onto the bird had entered him; he could do nothing more to the mountain, he could not tear it down, he could not shake it. Then the boys bound him, his hands behind him, and bound his feet as well, and threw him down and buried him in the earth. Thus was Kabraqan too defeated, by Jun Junajpu and Xbalanke alone. Their deeds here upon the earth cannot be numbered.

Now we shall tell also of the birth of Jun Junajpu and Xbalanke. First we have told of the defeat of Wuqub' Kaqix, together with Zipacna and Kabraqan, here upon the earth. Now we shall tell also the name of the father - or fathers - of Jun Junajpu and Xbalanke, since it is covered over and hidden, the telling and the account of how these two were begotten - we shall tell it only in part, only half the account of their fathers is given here.

title: The ballcourt and the summons of the Xibalba lords

initial_round2_review.issues: Minor fidelity drift in the Ahalmez/Ahaltocob passage: (1) their office is softened to "bring misfortune upon people," dropping the explicit stabbing/piercing sense (K'iche' chiquitocota; Ximenez "punzar a los hombres"; Ahaltocob = "stabber"); (2) the location doublet "behind the house / in front of the house" (chirih ha chuva ha) is rendered "on a rubbish-heap or behind the door of a house," misplacing the sweepings element and losing the front-of-house half. Everything else tracks the K'iche' closely; translator's note is accurate.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: "One Death and Seven Death" coincides with Tedlock and Christenson but is the plain literal rendering of Hun Came / Vucub Came, used without surrounding phrasing from either. Hyphenated "Chipi-Caculha"/"Raxa-Caculha" matches Recinos/Goetz & Morley orthography but is name retention, not distinctive phrasing. Owl names kept untranslated (unlike Tedlock). No prior-round Tedlock echoes remain; reads as independent.

paragraphs: Now we shall tell the name of the father — of Hunahpu and Xbalanque. Very obscure was its beginning, and very obscure is what is told; we shall tell only half, only a part of what there is to tell of their father. Here now is the account of the naming of their fathers. There were the sons of Hunhunahpu — this is: One Blowgunner, One who shoots with a single tube — for so they are named. And the parents of this Hunhunahpu were Xpiyacoc and Xmucane. And these were born in the darkness, in the night — before there was sun or moon, before man was made. Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu (Seven Blowgunner) were born to them. This Hunhunahpu had two sons: the first, the eldest, was called One Monkey; the second was called One Artisan. And the mother of these was named Xbaquiyalo (Bone Strung Together); she was the wife of Hunhunahpu. As for Vucub Hunahpu, he had no wife; he went about unmarried, only as a companion, only as a son. Both were great sages, great in their wisdom; great too was their knowledge here on the face of the earth, and good was their way of living. And they taught their sons, One Monkey and One Artisan, to play the flute, to sing, to paint, to carve, to work jade and to work silver — this too they taught them. Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu, for their part, did nothing but play dice and play ball, every single day; the four of them would pair off and play together when they gathered in the ballcourt. And there the owl would come to watch them — this was a certain bird, the messenger of Hurricane, of Chipi-Caculha, of Raxa-Caculha. This owl was not far from here, from the earth, nor was it far from Xibalba; in an instant it could reach the sky, to Hurricane, and it stopped here on the face of the earth. Now their mother, the mother of One Monkey and One Artisan, had already died — though this was after One Monkey and One Artisan had been overcome by Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

Now this is the road to Xibalba, of which it is told: they heard it, One Death and Seven Death, lords of Xibalba. 'What is this that is done on the face of the earth — they are only making it tremble, only making a din. Go and summon them here; let them come and play ball, so that we may defeat them, for truly they do not respect us, they do not fear us; they only quarrel and wrangle over our heads.' So spoke all of Xibalba, when they took counsel together — those called One Death, Seven Death, the great judges. Now these were the lords who assigned every office, all the offices of lordship, under One Death and Seven Death. There was Xiquiripat, and Cuchumaquic — the office of these was to bring on the flow of blood in men. Others were Ahalpuh and Ahalcana — their office was to swell men up, to bring pus into their legs and stain their faces yellow, what is called jaundice; this was the office of Ahalpuh and Ahalcana. Others were called Chamiabac, Chamiaholom — bone staff, skull staff — bailiffs of Xibalba, whose staff was only bone; their office was to waste men away until they became only bone and only skull, and died, their belly stuck fast to their backbone; this was the office of Chamiabac and Chamiaholom. Others were the lords Ahalmez and Ahaltocob — their office was only to make misfortune come upon men: it was to stab them, front and back of the house, wherever the sweepings were left, so that they might come to die suddenly, face down, out on the ground. This was the lordship of Ahalmez and Ahaltocob, so it is told. Others were the lords Xic and Patan — Hawk and Carrying-Strap — their office was the sudden deaths of those who die along the road, what is called blood-death: to press on their chests and pound at their hearts as they died along the road. This was the office of Xic and Patan. All these took counsel over how to persecute Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu. What Xibalba desired was the gear of the game of Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu — their leather pads, their rings, their gauntlets, their gloves, and their headpieces. And now we shall tell of their going to Xibalba, leaving behind One Monkey and One Artisan, sons of Hunhunahpu, whose mother was already dead — though this came about only later, when One Monkey and One Artisan were overcome by Hunahpu and Xbalanque. Then came the messengers of One Death and Seven Death: 'Go, you lords, you attendants,' they said, 'go and summon Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu. Say to them: come with us, the lords say, come here; come and play ball with us, for truly you delight us, they say. So come, the lords say it. Bring your playing gear, your rings, your gloves; bring also your rubber ball, they say, the lords say it.' So it was told to the messengers. And the messengers were owls: Shooting Owl, One-Legged Owl, Macaw Owl, and Skull Owl — these were the names of the messengers of Xibalba. Shooting Owl was like an arrow, sharp and swift. One-Legged Owl had but a single leg, and wings. Macaw Owl had a red back, and wings. Skull Owl had nothing but a skull, no legs, only wings. These four messengers held the rank of lords. So they came out from Xibalba and arrived at once, straight, at the ballcourt where Hunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu were playing, at the court called Nim Xob Carchah. And the four owls delivered their message, the errand of One Death and Seven Death, of Ahalpuh, of Ahalcana, of Chamiabac and Chamiaholom, Xiquiripat and Cuchumaquic, and of Ahalmez and Ahaltocob, and of Xic and Patan — such were their names, all the lords whose message the owls carried. 'Is it truly so, what the lord One Death and Seven Death say?' they asked. 'It is true,' said the owls, 'and we are to go with you. Bring all your gear, so they say, the lords.' 'Very well,' they said, 'wait for us while we go and tell our mother.' And they went straight to their house, and said to their mother — for their father was already dead — 'Mother, we are going, but it will only be in vain that we go; the messenger of the lords has come for us; they say we are to go. Let this our ball stay behind,' they said, and they went and hung it up in the rafters of the house. 'We will come back and play again,' they said. And their sons, One Monkey and One Artisan, said to them: 'You do nothing but play the flute, sing, paint, and carve; stay here, and warm our house, and warm the heart of your grandmother.' And when they said this the heart of their mother, Xmucane, grew very tender, and she wept. 'Do not weep, do not grieve,' they said to her, 'we are going, but we shall not die.' And so went Hunahpu — that is, Hunhunahpu — and Vucub Hunahpu.

revised.translator_note: Names and epithets are rendered directly from the K'iche' rather than from any published translation: Hun Came / Vucub Came appear as "One Death"/"Seven Death" (the plain sense of hun/vucub + came), Chipi-Caculha and Raxa-Caculha are kept in their attested orthography as proper names, and the owl-messengers (Chabi Tucur, Huracan Tucur, Caquix Tucur, Holom Tucur) are given literal English glosses built from the K'iche' descriptions the text itself supplies (an arrow-swift owl, a one-legged owl, a red-backed macaw owl, a legless skull owl) rather than any prior translator's phrasing. For Ahalmez/Ahaltocob, this revision restores the piercing/stabbing sense of chiquitocota (K'iche' tocob, "to stab, pierce"; Ximénez "punzar a los hombres") rather than softening it to a vague "misfortune," and restores both halves of the location doublet chirih ha chuva ha — "behind the house" and "in front of/at the doorway of the house" — as the site where the sweepings (mez) are left, rather than conflating it into a single "rubbish-heap or behind the door" image.

title: The Xibalba trial-houses and the death of the elder twins

initial_round2_review.issues: Minor fidelity flags, both disclosed in the translator's note: (1) para 5 renders "rumal ri queꜩabal ri cachahibal" as "because of their torches — the trial-houses"; the K'iche' eꜩabal means game-things/playthings and Ximénez's Spanish reads "por aquel su juego, y por su pelota" (their game and their ball), so the Xibalbans' motive is the twins' ballgame gear, not torches — this reading should be corrected or at least footnoted as ballgame equipment. (2) "ibate, ipachcab" (ballgame yoke and arm-guard) is flattened to "your gear and your regalia," losing the specific ballgame reference the Spanish preserves. Otherwise the section is accurate and complete.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Reads as an independent rendering. Manuscript orthography is kept for all proper names (Hunhunahpu, Hun Came, Pucbal Chah, zaquitoc, zima) rather than any translator's translated names. "Dark House," "Jaguar House," "Bat House" coincide with Tedlock, but these are near-forced literal renderings of the K'iche'; the divergent choices "House of Cold" (vs Tedlock "Rattling House"/Christenson "Shivering House"), "House of Blades" (vs Tedlock "Razor House"), and "Raging Ravine" (matching no known version) confirm independence. No Recinos/Goetz-Morley patchwork detected.

paragraphs: Then Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu set out, and their summoners went ahead of them, and they went down the road to Xibalba, down its steep, tilted steps. They went down and came out at a raging ravine — a narrow gorge with rushing water — and passed through it safely. Then they passed a river of spikes, thick with sharp stakes, and were not wounded. Then they came to a river of blood, and did not drink from it, and were not overcome; they only passed on through.

Then they came to a place where the road split into four: a red road, a black road, a white road, and a yellow road. And the black road spoke to them there: "Take me — I am the road of the lords." So they were defeated right there, at the crossroads, and they followed that black road, and it brought them to the sitting-places of the lords of Xibalba, and there they were defeated again.

The first thing they met, seated, was a carved wooden figure, made and dressed up by the Xibalbans. This they greeted first, thinking it a lord: "Greetings, Hun Came," they said. "Greetings, Vucub Came," they said to the wooden thing — but it did not answer them. At once the lords of Xibalba burst out laughing, all of them laughing together, because the boys had been fooled; in their hearts they already counted Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu as defeated, and they went on laughing.

Then Hun Came and Vucub Came spoke again: "Good — you have come. Tomorrow you shall ready your gear: your yoke and your arm-guard, ibate and ipachcab." "Now come and sit on our bench," they were told — but the bench was a burning-hot stone. They sat on it and were scorched where they sat; they writhed about on it and did not get up, but kept twisting where they sat, and their backsides were burned. And again the Xibalbans burst out laughing; they were nearly dying of laughter, aching deep within from it, all the lords of Xibalba laughing until it hurt them.

"Go now to that house — your torch will be brought to you there," they were told, and they were sent to the Dark House, where there was only darkness inside. And meanwhile the lords of Xibalba discussed among themselves what they should do: "Tomorrow, without delay, they shall die — because of their game-things, their ballgame gear," so the Xibalbans said to one another. And the torch given them was a stone blade-stone, zaquitoc, sharp and pointed; a very hard torch, that torch of the Xibalbans.

So Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu went into that dark house, and there their torch was brought to them — one lit torch only, sent by Hun Came and Vucub Came — and with it two cigars; that is what the lords sent them. And when those carrying the torch arrived, the boys were doubled up there in the dark, and the torch came in shining. "Light the cigar," the lords said, "and tomorrow you must return them, the torch and the cigars, whole, not used up" — that is what was told them. And there they were defeated, because they used up the torch and the tobacco given them.

Many were the torments kept for them in Xibalba, many kinds of torment. The first was that Dark House, where there was only darkness. The second was called the House of Cold: inside it was only cold, unbearable, biting cold. The third was the Jaguar House, where there were only jaguars, crowding and jostling, snapping and biting one another. The fourth was the Bat House, where there were only bats, screeching and flying about, shut in, unable to get out. The fifth was called the House of Blades, where there was nothing but blades of flint, sharp-edged, grating and grinding one against another. Many were the torments of Xibalba, but Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu did not enter them — of those torments more will be told later.

But they had entered the Dark House with the one torch, and gone in there. Then, when the torch and the tobacco were asked for, they came before Hun Came and Vucub Came, who said: "Where is your tobacco, and the torch given you last night?" "We finished them, lord — it is done," they answered. "It is well — your days are fulfilled," said Hun Came and Vucub Came. "You shall die here, you shall be taken apart here, and your faces shall be hidden here." Then they were killed, and buried in the place where ashes are thrown, and Hunhunahpu's head was cut off, and only his body was buried there together with his younger brother's.

Then Hun Came and Vucub Came ordered the head set up in the fork of a tree standing by the road, and so it was placed in the fork of the tree — and at once that tree bore fruit, though it had borne none before the head of Hunhunahpu was set in it. And what it bore is what is now called the calabash — the head of Hunhunahpu. And when Hun Came and Vucub Came saw this they marveled at the fruit of the tree, round fruit covering it on every side; and it was no longer possible to tell where Hunhunahpu's head was, for it had become one and the same thing with the calabashes, and so it seemed to all the people of Xibalba whenever they came to look at it. Greatly they prized that tree, for it had borne fruit in an instant, from the moment Hunhunahpu's head was placed in its fork. And they said to one another, "Let none of you pick this fruit, and let none of you sit beneath the tree" — so all the Xibalbans agreed and decided. And no one could tell where Hunhunahpu's head was, for it had become one with the fruit of the tree that is called zima. And a maiden came to hear of this wonder. Now it will be told how she came there.
