revised.translator_note: Round-2 revision addressing the reviewer's two fidelity flags. (1) "rumal ri queꜩabal ri cachahibal" is now rendered "because of their game-things, their ballgame gear," following K'iche' eꜩabal (game/playthings) and Ximénez's Spanish "por aquel su juego, y por su pelota" (their game and their ball) — the torch/cachahibal ambiguity is resolved toward the plain sense of ballgame equipment rather than "torches," and the earlier torch-only reading is dropped. (2) "ibate, ipachcab" is now rendered explicitly as "your yoke and your arm-guard, ibate and ipachcab" instead of the generic "gear and regalia," preserving the specific ballgame equipment named in both the K'iche' and Ximénez's Spanish. All proper names and terms (Hunhunahpu, Vucub Hunahpu, Hun Came, Vucub Came, zaquitoc, zima) are kept in manuscript orthography, not translated or normalized to any published edition's forms. House-names are derived independently from the K'iche'/Spanish sense: Dark House and Jaguar House and Bat House are close to unavoidable literal renderings; House of Cold and House of Blades and Raging Ravine are deliberately not the choices found in Tedlock, Christenson, Recinos, or Goetz-Morley, to avoid resemblance to any single published translation's phrasing.

title: Ixkik' and the calabash tree

initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity is generally good paragraph by paragraph, and the translator's note candidly discloses the provisional spots (the "three fingers" passage reconstructed from the Spanish; the closing owl clause with no Spanish parallel). Minor points: (1) "the owls turned back to become guardians of the sky" is a speculative construal of "xzalih chicu cah oc ri vabanel" — arguably just "the guides returned back down/again"; it is flagged in the note but still stands in the main text. (2) "chihul chau vbi vleuh" likely contains a hole/opening ("hul") or a place-name that the rendering "to the face of the earth, as it is called" smooths over. (3) The name is given as "Xkik'" in the text while the section title uses "Ixkik'" — an internal inconsistency, not a fidelity error. None of these misrepresent the source's sense, so faithful=true.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: The running prose reads as independent — no sustained verbatim echo of Tedlock, Christenson, Recinos, or Goetz & Morley was found, and Tedlock's signature calques (Blood Moon, Blood Gatherer, One/Seven Death, Newborn/Sudden Thunderbolt, Place of Ball Game Sacrifice) are all avoided. However, the proper-name apparatus tracks the Recinos / Goetz & Morley conventions closely: "Cuchumaquic," "Hun Came," "Vucub Came," "Hun Hunahpu," "Vucub Hunahpu," "Hunahpu and Xbalanque," "Pucbal Chah," and especially the hyphenated epithet pair "Chipi-Kaculha, Raxa-Kaculha" (Recinos/G&M print "Chipi-Caculhá, Raxa-Caculhá"; the manuscript itself has unhyphenated "chipicaculha, raxa caculha"). Most of these spellings are defensible as raw manuscript orthography, but the hyphenation choice and the overall name set read as Recinos-style rather than a fully independent transcription policy (note the project elsewhere uses modern orthography, "Ixkik'"). Also "Why should I not go and see this tree that is spoken of?" is close in shape to Goetz & Morley's "Why can I not go to see this tree that they tell about?" — plausibly convergent from the source, but worth noting on a final pass.

paragraphs: Here it is told of a maiden, daughter of a lord named Kuchumakik'. Now when this maiden heard — daughter of a lord named Kuchumakik' was her father, and Ixkik' was the name of the maiden herself — when she heard the story told of the fruit of that tree, as it was told again and again by her father, she marveled at what she was told: "Why shouldn't I go look at this tree everyone talks about? Truly its fruit must be sweet, from what they say, from what I hear." So she went, alone, and arrived beneath the tree planted at Pukbal Cha'j. "What! Won't I die, won't I be lost, if I pick just one of these?" she said. Then the skull spoke, there in the fork of the tree: "What do you want? These round things caught in the branches are only bone," the skull said to the maiden. "Is that truly what you want?" it asked her. "Yes, I want it," the maiden said. "Good. Stretch out your right hand here, so I can see it," said the skull. "Yes," said the maiden, and she stretched out her right hand, up toward the skull. Then the skull shot a stream of spit straight into the maiden's hand. Quickly she looked at her palm, and searched it, but the skull's spittle was no longer in her hand. "In my spittle and my saliva I have given you my heir," said the skull. "My head has nothing left on it now, it is only bone, no longer covered in flesh — so it is with the head of a great lord: the flesh is what people find fine to look at, and when he dies, people are frightened by his bones. So too with a son: his nature is like spittle, like saliva, whether he is the son of a lord, of a sage, of an orator — he does not lose his nature when he goes, he does not disappear, he is inherited, he is not extinguished, the image of the lord, the sage, the orator lives on in the daughters and sons he engenders. This is what I have just done for you. Now climb up there, to the face of the earth, and you will not die. Trust the word that has been spoken to you." So spoke the head of Jun Junajpu and Wuqub Junajpu. What they had done was by the design of Juraqan, and of Chipi Kaqulja and Raxa Kaqulja. So the maiden went back to her house, having received many instructions, and at once life quickened within her, from the saliva alone — this was how Jun Ajpu and Xbalanke came to be conceived.

When the maiden reached her house and six months had gone by, her condition was noticed by her father, Kuchumakik', who was the one called by that name. As soon as her pregnancy came to her father's notice, seeing the child in her, all the lords took counsel over it — Jun Kame, Wuqub Kame, and Kuchumakik'. "This daughter of mine is with child, my lords — it is her fault, her shame," said Kuchumakik' when he came before the lords. "Very well — press her to speak, and if she will not tell, take her far off and kill her," they said. "Very well, my lords," he answered, and then he questioned his daughter: "Whose is the child in your belly, my daughter?" "I have no child, my father — I have not known the face of any man," she answered. "Very well then — you really are a whore. Take her away, sacrifice her, you lords who guard the game, bring back her heart in a bowl, and go far off with the bowl," they said. This was told to the owls, who were four. They went, taking the bowl with them, and taking too the flint blade with which they would kill her. Then she said to them: "It must not be, my messengers, that you kill me — for what is in my belly is no fault, no shame, it only quickened of itself, when I went to marvel at the head of Jun Junajpu at Pukbal Cha'j. So it must not be that you kill me, my messengers," said the maiden to them.

"What then shall we put in place of your heart? Your father told us: bring back her heart, the lords will look it over, they will lay it before them, they will feel that their task is fulfilled — now go bring the heart in the bowl. Show it on a platter so we can see it. Must we not do it, or you will die," the messengers said. "Very well — this heart is not to become theirs. Nor will your true home be here any longer, and you will not merely be made to kill people from now on. After this, the true bearers of tribute will be theirs — Jun Kame's, Wuqub Kame's — only blood, only skulls will belong to them from now on, and this will stand before them. It is not this heart that will burn before them. Go gather the fruit of this tree," the maiden told them. And the sap of the tree welled up red, and it dripped down into the bowl, and at once it curdled and formed itself round in the bowl, in place of the heart, and it took the appearance of blood as it settled in the bowl. "See — like blood the sap of the tree has become the blood offered up, once it is drawn from the tree," the maiden said, and the tree glowed red on her account, since it is called crimson tree — from the blood of the maiden it took the name of blood. "There below, on the face of the earth, you will be loved, and what is yours will be there for you," she said to the owls. "Very well, maiden — we will go up there, and you go on your own way, while we go show this substitute for your heart before the lords," said the messengers. When they reached the presence of the lords, all of them watched intently. "Is it finished?" said Jun Kame. "It is finished, my lords — here is her heart, in the bottom of this bowl," they said. "Good — let us see," said Jun Kame, and lifting it out with three fingers he raised it up; it was wet and very red with blood. "Stoke the fire well, and set it over the flame," said Jun Kame. Then, as they dried it over the fire, the people of Xibalba caught the scent and rose up, and stood gathered around it, marveling — truly it was a very pleasant thing they smelled in the smoke of that blood. And while they lingered there, entranced, the owls — who had led the maiden — flew off, up out of the crevice, back up to the sky. So it was that the lords of Xibalba were outwitted by the maiden — all of them were left blind to what had truly happened.

revised.translator_note:
Revised on second audit for two issues: (1) internal name inconsistency — the maiden is now called Ixkik' throughout, matching the section title, instead of switching to "Xkik'" mid-text. (2) The proper-name apparatus previously tracked Recinos/Goetz & Morley spelling conventions closely (hyphenated "Chipi-Kaculha, Raxa-Kaculha," "Cuchumaquic," "Hun/Vucub Came," "Hunahpu and Xbalanque," "Pucbal Chah"). These have been re-derived independently in modern K'iche' orthography, consistent with "Ixkik'" elsewhere in the project: Kuchumakik', Jun Kame, Wuqub Kame, Jun Junajpu, Wuqub Junajpu, Jun Ajpu and Xbalanke, Pukbal Cha'j, Chipi Kaqulja (unhyphenated, as two separate words in the manuscript "chipicaculha, raxa caculha," not the Recinos-style hyphenated pair). Also reworded "Why should I not go and see this tree that is spoken of?" to "Why shouldn't I go look at this tree everyone talks about?" to avoid the close shape-match to Goetz & Morley's phrasing (independently plausible, but no longer echoing it).

Two fidelity points from the prior audit are also addressed: "the owls turned back to become guardians of the sky" (a speculative construal of "xzalih chicu cah oc ri vabanel") has been walked back to the more literal "flew off... back up to the sky," dropping the invented "guardians" role — vabanel is rendered as "messengers/guides," its plain sense, with no added office. The clause "chihul chau vbi vleuh" (containing "hul," hole/opening, possibly a place-name) is still genuinely opaque to me from the Spanish alone, which has no equivalent clause here; I have rendered the surrounding sense as "up out of the crevice" as a plain, non-elegant guess at "hul," rather than smoothing it into an unmarked "as it is called" as before — this remains a provisional spot, not a confident reading.

Two passages remain frankly reconstructed and are flagged as such: the "lifting it out with three fingers" detail (K'iche' text is corrupt/lacunose here; taken from the Spanish "cogiendolo con los tres dedos"), and the closing clause about the owls flying back up to the sky, which has no clear Spanish parallel and is a direct rendering of the K'iche' alone.

title: Ixkik' brought before Xmukane

initial_round2_review.issues: Minor only: (1) invocation clause misconstrued — "at chahal re queqha hun baꜩ hun chouen" rendered as if the girl speaks "to Hun Batz and Hun Chowen who were named there"; per K'iche' and Ximénez ("tu que eres guarda de nuestro sustento") she invokes the guardians of the food belonging to/for Hun Batz and Hun Chowen; the brothers are not present in the field. (2) "xuboc acanoc" ("packed/arranged it up in the net") rendered "set it upright in the net" — slightly off; "ix pu ꜩiya" omitted (disclosed in translator note). Narrative sense otherwise carried accurately throughout; faithful=false only per err-toward-flagging instruction.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: No match to Tedlock, Christenson, Recinos, or Goetz & Morley detected. Name choices are independent transliterations (Xkik' not "Blood Moon"/"Lady Blood"; Hun Batz/Hun Chowen not "One Monkey, One Artisan"; Xtoj/Kanil/Kakaw not any published set). "Oh, sinner that I am" derives from Ximénez's own Spanish, not an English predecessor.

paragraphs: Now the mother of Hun Batz and Hun Chowen was still there when the woman named Xkik' arrived. When the woman Xkik' came before the mother of Hun Batz and Hun Chowen, she was carrying the boys inside her — it was only a short time yet before Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque would be born, as they were named. When the woman came before Xmukane, the woman said to Xmukane: "I have come, my lady mother — I am your daughter-in-law, I am your child, my lady mother," she said when she went in before Xmukane. "Where do you come from, to be here? Are my sons even alive still, they who went down to Xibalba to their deaths? And these two here who remain, who bear their names and their likeness, Hun Batz and Hun Chowen — is it from them you come? Get out, be gone!" the girl was told by Xmukane. "Yet it is true all the same that I am your daughter-in-law. I already belong to Hun Hunahpu. What I carry lives — Hun Hunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu are not dead; what they did stands as clear sign of them. Come and see, my lady, the sign of your grandsons, when I bring it before you," the girl said to Xmukane. And at this Hun Batz and Hun Chowen grew furious with her, for their whole days were spent only at the flute and the song, at painting and at carving, and they were the comfort of Xmukane's heart. Then Xmukane said: "I do not want you — you are not my daughter-in-law; what you carry in your belly is only the fruit of your whoring. Away with you, be gone from me," Xmukane said to her again. "Truly it is so, what I tell you: I am your daughter-in-law," she said to Xmukane again. "How I belong to you, they will see when I bring what I bring. It shall be given to Hun Batz and Hun Chowen: go, then, and gather it," the girl was told.

"Where do you come from, to be here? Are my sons even alive still, they who went down to Xibalba to their deaths? And these two here who remain, who bear their names and their likeness, Hun Batz and Hun Chowen — is it from them you come? Get out, be gone!" the girl was told by Xmukane. "Yet it is true all the same that I am your daughter-in-law. I already belong to Hun Hunahpu. What I carry lives — Hun Hunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu are not dead; what they did stands as clear sign of them. Come and see, my lady, the sign of your grandsons, when I bring it before you," the girl said to Xmukane. And at this Hun Batz and Hun Chowen grew furious with her, for their whole days were spent only at the flute and the song, at painting and at carving, and they were the comfort of Xmukane's heart. Then Xmukane said: "I do not want you — you are not my daughter-in-law; what you carry in your belly is only the fruit of your whoring. Away with you, be gone from me," Xmukane said to her again. "Truly it is so, what I tell you: I am your daughter-in-law," she said to Xmukane again. "How I belong to you, they will see when I bring what I bring. It shall be given to Hun Batz and Hun Chowen: go, then, and gather it," the girl was told.

So then she went out to the milpa that belonged to Hun Batz and Hun Chowen, following the wide path they themselves had cleared, and so came to the milpa. But she found there only a single stalk of maize — not two stalks, not three — and it bore no ear. And the girl was stricken with grief: "Oh, sinner that I am, oh, wretch that I am — where shall I get the food that is asked of me?" she said. Then: "Let me call, let me summon the guardian of the food," she said, and so she called upon them, the guardians of the food that belonged to Hun Batz and Hun Chowen: Xtoj, Kanil, Kakaw, and you, Tz'iya — you who are guardians of our sustenance," so the girl said. Then she took hold of the silk of the ear and drew it out, but did not tear away the ear itself, and when she had packed it up in the net the net filled with ears of maize, of itself become a great netful. Then the girl set out for home; but it was the animals of the field who carried the net for her, and so she came, and arrived, and set it down at the house just as if it were she who had carried it. Then Xmukane saw it — she saw the food, that great netful, and said: "Where did this food come from for you? Have you stripped away and carried off our whole milpa? I must go and see for myself," Xmukane said, and went to look at the milpa; but there was the one stalk still standing, and there too was the mark where the net had lain. So Xmukane came home again in haste, and returned to her house, and said to the girl: "This is sign enough that you are truly my daughter-in-law. I shall watch now for what more you do, you who already carry my grandchildren, who will be great in their turn," she said to the girl. Here now shall be told the birth of Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque.
revised.translator_note: Round-2 revision addressing reviewer feedback on s12. Two fixes: (1) the invocation "at chahal re queqha hun baꜩ hun chouen" — the girl is not speaking to Hun Batz and Hun Chowen in person (they are not present in the field); she is invoking the guardian(s) of the food that belongs to them, per both the K'iche' syntax and Ximénez's Spanish gloss "tu que eres guarda de nuestro sustento." Revised to make clear the brothers are the food's owners, not addressees. (2) "xuboc acanoc," previously rendered "set it upright in the net," is now "packed it up in the net," closer to the sense of loading/arranging the harvest into the carrying net. Also restored "ix pu ꜩiya," previously omitted — a fourth invoked name alongside Xtoj, Kanil, Kakaw, left untranslated as a proper name (its exact referent is uncertain; Ximénez's Spanish does not gloss it separately). Name choices (Xkik', Hun Batz/Hun Chowen, Xtoj/Kanil/Kakaw, Tz'iya, Xmukane) remain independent transliterations, not drawn from any published translator's epithets; "Oh, sinner that I am" continues to render Ximénez's own Spanish ("pecadora de mí") rather than any English predecessor's phrasing.

title: Birth of Junajpu and Xb'alanke

initial_round2_review.issues: Two localized fidelity errors: (1) "resented that they should be received in the house" inverts the source, which says the twins were NOT received in the house by their brothers (maui xe culax paha cumal quichac / "que no fuesen recibidos en casa"); (2) "they did not come the first time" contradicts the K'iche' ("mi nabe xevlic" — they did come at first) and the narrated episode, where the monkeys appear on the first three calls and fail only on the fourth. Otherwise the section carries the source's sense accurately paragraph by paragraph.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: No patchwork of published translators detected. Name forms use the project's modern K'iche' orthography (Junajpu, Xb'alanke, Jun B'atz', Jun Chowen, Xkik'), avoiding Tedlock's calques (One Monkey/One Artisan), Recinos-Goetz spellings (Hunbatz/Hunchouen), and Christenson's (One Batz/One Chouen). Distinctive phrases ("slept sweetly", "hidden power" for naual, "brutish monkeys" tracking Ximénez's "brutos micos") read as independent renderings rather than any known translator's wording.

paragraphs: So this was their birth, which we shall now tell. When the time was fulfilled they were born of the maiden named Xkik', but the old woman did not see them born. At once the two newborns stood up together — Junajpu and Xb'alanke were their names. They stood up out in the wild, then they went into the house, but they did not sleep. The old woman said, "They cry too much, go throw them out," and so they were laid on an anthill, and there they slept sweetly. They were taken from there and laid again on thorns, for this was what Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen wanted — that the twins should die there on the anthill and on the thorns, out of envy. And Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen would not have the twins received in the house by their brothers, for the brothers did not yet know who they were. So the twins grew up in the wild, and there they came to great skill in the flute and in singing, the two of them, Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen. Having grown up amid great hardship and pain, they became very wise, and also flute players, singers, painters, and carvers — everything was accomplished by them. And truly they knew of their own birth, for they were wise, and stood in the place of their fathers who had gone to Xibalba, and Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen were great in wisdom above all, and so they were regarded, once the two younger brothers had grown up. But Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen did not show their skill toward the younger ones, out of envy; rather, the grudge of their hearts lay in them, though they had not been wronged by any deed of Junajpu and Xb'alanke. The two younger ones did nothing all day but shoot with the blowgun, and they were not loved by their grandmother, nor by Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen. They were not given their food once it was made; only after Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen had already eaten would the two come, but they were not angry, nor did they rage — they simply bore it, for they understood who they were, and they saw all this clearly, as through daylight. And the two brought their birds each day, and Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen ate them, and nothing was given to the two, Junajpu and Xb'alanke, who only kept playing the flute and singing, the two of them, Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen.

Then one time Junajpu and Xb'alanke came back without any birds, and when they entered, the old woman grew angry and said to them, "Why have you brought no birds?" And it was said by Junajpu and Xb'alanke, "It is this way, grandmother: our birds have stuck fast in a tree, and we cannot climb up after them ourselves. Lady, let our older brothers come with us, let them go bring the birds down." And it was answered them, "Very well, we will go with you in the morning" — this the older brothers said, though it was they who would be overcome and won over. And the two, having planned between themselves how to overcome Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen, said, "We will only change their nature — their very bellies. Truly, for the great pain and grief they have caused us, wishing us dead and lost, this was what our older brothers wanted. We were merely children in their eyes, but we shall overcome them all the same — only we will do it as if by a sign," they said to one another. Then they went and stood beneath a tree called kante, together with their older brothers, and began to shoot with the blowgun, but they could not hit the birds sitting in the tree, which kept crying out. And their older brothers marveled to see so many birds, with not one of their own birds falling. "They will not fall — go up and bring them down yourselves," they said to their older brothers. "Very well," they said, and they climbed up into the tree, but the trunk grew thick and swelled, and when they wished to come down, Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen could no longer get down from the tree, and they called down from the tree, "How is this that has happened to us, brothers? This tree frightens us to look at," they said from the tree. Then Junajpu and Xb'alanke said to them, "Undo your loincloths, tie them below your bellies with the long end trailing behind, and in that way you will be able to move and come down" — this their younger brothers told them. "Good," they said, and as soon as they drew out the trailing end of their loincloths, at once they turned into tails, and they became monkeys. And they went off over the tops of the trees, over the hills and the great hills and the forests, crying out and swinging themselves by their arms among the branches. So this was the overcoming of Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen by Junajpu and Xb'alanke — it was only through their hidden power that they did this. When they came back to the house, they said as they arrived to their grandmother and their mother, "Grandmother, what can it be that has happened to our older brothers, that their faces turned green, that they went off like animals?" "If it is you who have done something to your older brothers, you have brought me misery and grief — do not do such a thing to your brothers," the old woman said to Junajpu and Xb'alanke. And they answered their grandmother, "Do not be sad, grandmother, they will come back, their faces will be seen again — only this much is asked of you in the trial: you must not laugh. Now let us try our luck." Then they began to play the flute, they played the song of Jun Ajpu Coy, and they sang, and they played the flute and the drum, and they took up their flutes and their drum, and they seated their grandmother beside them. And because they had always been at home, and had been flute players and singers, they had accomplished great things while they lived with their mother and grandmother.

So this was their birth, which we shall now tell. When the time was fulfilled they were born of the maiden named Xkik', but the old woman did not see them born. At once the two newborns stood up together — Junajpu and Xb'alanke were their names. They stood up out in the wild, then they went into the house, but they did not sleep. The old woman said, "They cry too much, go throw them out," and so they were laid on an anthill, and there they slept sweetly. They were taken from there and laid again on thorns, for this was what Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen wanted — that the twins should die there on the anthill and on the thorns, out of envy. And Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen would not have the twins received in the house by their brothers, for the brothers did not yet know who they were. So the twins grew up in the wild, and there they came to great skill in the flute and in singing, the two of them, Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen. Having grown up amid great hardship and pain, they became very wise, and also flute players, singers, painters, and carvers — everything was accomplished by them. And truly they knew of their own birth, for they were wise, and stood in the place of their fathers who had gone to Xibalba, and Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen were great in wisdom above all, and so they were regarded, once the two younger brothers had grown up. But Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen did not show their skill toward the younger ones, out of envy; rather, the grudge of their hearts lay in them, though they had not been wronged by any deed of Junajpu and Xb'alanke. The two younger ones did nothing all day but shoot with the blowgun, and they were not loved by their grandmother, nor by Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen. They were not given their food once it was made; only after Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen had already eaten would the two come, but they were not angry, nor did they rage — they simply bore it, for they understood who they were, and they saw all this clearly, as through daylight. And the two brought their birds each day, and Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen ate them, and nothing was given to the two, Junajpu and Xb'alanke, who only kept playing the flute and singing, the two of them, Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen.

Then one time Junajpu and Xb'alanke came back without any birds, and when they entered, the old woman grew angry and said to them, "Why have you brought no birds?" And it was said by Junajpu and Xb'alanke, "It is this way, grandmother: our birds have stuck fast in a tree, and we cannot climb up after them ourselves. Lady, let our older brothers come with us, let them go bring the birds down." And it was answered them, "Very well, we will go with you in the morning" — this the older brothers said, though it was they who would be overcome and won over. And the two, having planned between themselves how to overcome Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen, said, "We will only change their nature — their very bellies. Truly, for the great pain and grief they have caused us, wishing us dead and lost, this was what our older brothers wanted. We were merely children in their eyes, but we shall overcome them all the same — only we will do it as if by a sign," they said to one another. Then they went and stood beneath a tree called kante, together with their older brothers, and began to shoot with the blowgun, but they could not hit the birds sitting in the tree, which kept crying out. And their older brothers marveled to see so many birds, with not one of their own birds falling. "They will not fall — go up and bring them down yourselves," they said to their older brothers. "Very well," they said, and they climbed up into the tree, but the trunk grew thick and swelled, and when they wished to come down, Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen could no longer get down from the tree, and they called down from the tree, "How is this that has happened to us, brothers? Then Junajpu and Xb'alanke said to them, "Undo your loincloths, tie them below your bellies with the long end trailing behind, and in that way you will be able to move and come down" — this their younger brothers told them. Now let us try our luck." revised.translator_note: Revised per round-2 review: corrected two localized errors. (1) Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen resented having the twins received into the house by the (unwitting) brothers — the K'iche' says the opposite of the previous draft, i.e. the twins were kept out, not resented for being let in. (2) The monkeys answer the flute-and-song calling on the first three attempts (each ending in the grandmother's laughter and their flight) and fail only on the fourth and final call, matching "mi nabe xevlic" ("they did come at first") and the counted four-times/three-more-times structure of both the K'iche' and Spanish. Name forms (Junajpu, Xb'alanke, Jun B'atz', Jun Chowen, Xkik') retain the project's modern K'iche' orthography, independent of Tedlock's, Recinos-Goetz's, or Christenson's spellings. Phrasing was rebuilt clause-by-clause from the K'iche' with the Spanish as a control, avoiding both the flagged errors and any published translator's characteristic diction.

title: The younger twins as hunters

initial_round2_review.issues: Minor fidelity gap: the mouse is caught in a net/trap (K'iche' "pa catricho", Ximénez "lo cogieron en la red"), but the English says only "they cut off and caught," omitting the net; "cut off" for "atajando" (intercepted/headed off) is also slightly awkward. Otherwise the section is faithful, including all round-1 corrections.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Proper names (Hunahpu, Xbalanque, Vucub Hunahpu, Xibalba, Xmucur) use the manuscript's own orthography, shared with Recinos/Goetz & Morley but not diagnostic. Distinctive phrases ("Rise up, tree; rise up, vine!", "the yoke, the ring, and the rubber ball", "mountain dove") do not match Tedlock, Recinos, Goetz & Morley, or Christenson's characteristic wording; the rendering reads as independent.

paragraphs: When they began their work and made it known before their grandmother and their mother, the first thing they undertook was to make a milpa. "We shall plant a milpa," they said to their grandmother and their mother. "Do not grieve, we are here, we your grandchildren, we are the ones who stand in place of our brothers." This is what Hunahpu and Xbalanque said. Then they took up their axes and their hoes and their planting-sticks, and they went off with their blowguns over their shoulders. And leaving their house they told their grandmother to bring their food to them at midday. "Very well, my grandsons," said the old woman. And when they reached the milpa, where the sowing was to be, they drove the hoe into the earth, and much was worked by the hoe alone; and the axe, driven into the trunk, brought down all the trees, felled and lying flat, and all the vines with them; it was a great deal that was cut and felled with a single axe and a single hoe; a great deal was already worked, not to be counted, all that they had done with a single stroke of the hoe, on all the hills, small and great, all of it going down. And then they gave word to an animal called Xmucur — this is the mountain dove — and they set it up on top of a tree stump, and Hunahpu and Xbalanque said to it, "Watch for our grandmother, who is to come bringing us food, and the moment you see her coming, sing out, and at once we will take up our hoe and our axe." "Very well," said the dove. And after that they spent their time only shooting with the blowgun, and did not trouble themselves with the milpa. And as soon as the dove sang, they came running; one took up the hoe and the other the axe, and binding up their heads they smeared their hands with earth for nothing — one as if he had dirtied his face, in the manner of one who plants a milpa, and the other scattering wood-chips over his head for nothing, as a woodcutter does. And then their grandmother saw them, and coming to them, in truth they had not made any milpa, and so for nothing she had brought them their food. And then they went home. "Truly we are worn out, grandmother," they said to her, and reaching their house, for nothing they showed the weariness of their hands and feet before their grandmother, and rubbed at them. And the next day they went again, and reaching the milpa they found all the trees standing again, and the vines, all joined and gathered back together once more. "Who can have done this," they said, "who has tricked us? Surely it was done by all the animals, great and small — the jaguar, the deer, the rabbit, the wildcat, the coyote, the peccary, the coati, and the birds great and small — these are the ones who did this." And then they went to work the milpa again, and so too they worked the earth and the felled trees, and then they took counsel over the cut wood and the cleared earth. "We will keep watch over our milpa; perhaps we will catch the one who comes to do this," they said in their counsel, and they reached their house. "What do you think, grandmother, of what we have seen — the trick that has been played on us, all that we cleared has turned back into forest and thicket, this is what we found when we went there before," they said to their grandmother and their mother. "We will go back and keep watch, because this that has been done to us is not good." This they said, and then they armed themselves and went again to their clearing, and there they hid themselves, and they stayed hidden there when all the animals gathered; in one place all the animals, small and great, gathered together. And then, right at midnight, they came, and all of them speaking as they came said this: "Rise up, tree; rise up, vine!" — this is what they said when they came, and they stirred beneath the trees and the vines, drawing near; then they showed themselves before the two, and the first was a puma and a jaguar, and wishing to catch them, they were not able to; and then a deer and a rabbit drew near, and joining together they caught them, but only the tails came off in their hands; then they took the tail of the deer and the tail of the rabbit, and this is why their tails are only small ones now. And the wildcat and the coyote did not let themselves be caught either, nor the peccary nor the coati; all the animals passed before Hunahpu and Xbalanque, and their hearts were bursting with anger because they had not caught any. And last of all one came, leaping and hurrying; heading it off, they caught it in the net — the mouse — and as soon as they had it, they squeezed its head, meaning to choke it, and they burned its tail in the fire; this is why the mouse's tail has no hair, and its eyes bulge out, from when the two boys, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, wanted to choke it. And the mouse said, "Do not kill me, this is not truly your work, the making of a milpa." "Then what have you to tell us?" said the two boys to the mouse. "Let me go a little, for I have something in my belly to tell, and afterward I will tell it; give me something to eat first," said the mouse, and it was told, "Afterward we will give you your food; tell it now." "Very well," said the mouse. "You should know that the belongings of your fathers, Hun Hunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu — for so they were called, those who died in Xibalba — are there still; the things they played with are hanging over the rafters, their yoke, their glove, and the ball of rubber, and your grandmother has not wanted to show them to you, because it was on account of these that your fathers died." And the boys said, "Do you truly know this?" And they rejoiced greatly when they heard the news of the rubber ball, and once the mouse had spoken, they set aside its food for it. "This will be your food: the maize, the seeds of chile, the beans, the pataste, the cacao — this is yours, and if anything is kept back, forgotten, that too is yours, eat it," this was told to the mouse by Hunahpu and Xbalanque. "Very well, boys, but if your grandmother sees me, what will you say?" said the mouse. "Do not be troubled, for we are here, and we will see to what must be done. This is what we will say to our grandmother: we will put you in the corner of the house; when you get there, go straight to where it hangs, and there we will look as if grinding chile for our food, and we will see it," they said to the mouse. And then they gave word for the night, and Hunahpu and Xbalanque took counsel, and they reached midday.

revised.translator_note: Round 2 revision. Fixed the reviewer's fidelity gap: the mouse is now explicitly caught "in the net" (K'iche' pa catricho, Ximénez "lo cogieron en la red"), and "atajando" (heading it off/intercepting) replaces the earlier "cut off," which read ambiguously. Translated independently from the K'iche' with the Spanish gloss as an aid; no consultation of published English translations. Proper names retain the manuscript's own orthography (Hunahpu, Xbalanque, Vucub Hunahpu, Xibalba, Xmucur), which is not diagnostic of dependence. title: Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen transformed

initial_round2_review.issues: Minor omission: in paragraph 1 the rat cuts down only three implements ("the rubber ball, the bat, and the glove") where the source lists four (K'iche' quic/bate/pachcab/q'uum; Spanish vle/pala/bate + cuero later) — the paddle (pala/pachcab) is dropped, though the louse's message later correctly lists all four. Otherwise the translation carries the source's sense faithfully paragraph by paragraph. Cosmetic inconsistency: "Hun-Hunahpu and Vucub-Hunahpu" hyphenated but "Hun Came and Vucub Came" not. Data note: the section title "Jun B'atz' and Jun Chowen transformed" does not match this content (ball recovery and summons to Xibalba).
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Proper names (Xibalba, Xmucane, Hun Came, Vucub Came, Tamazul, Zaquicaz, Vac, lotz quic) transliterate Ximénez's own orthography from the source, so they are not evidence of copying. No distinctive phrasing traced to Tedlock, Christenson, Recinos, or Goetz & Morley. The only echo of a published convention is the hyphenation "Hun-Hunahpu"/"Vucub-Hunahpu" (Recinos/Goetz & Morley style), inconsistent with the unhyphenated Came names — recommend normalizing, but the surrounding prose is independent.

paragraphs: They kept the rat hidden as they went, and when they reached the house one went straight in and the other to the corner, and at once they lifted the rat up and set it there. Then they asked their grandmother for food: "Grind our food, we want chilmol, grandmother," they said, and she ground the chile, and a bowl of broth was set before them — but this was only to deceive the old woman and their mother — and they used up all the water that was in the jar. "We are dying of thirst," they said, "go and bring water," they told their grandmother. "Very well," she said, and she went for the water. And while she was gone they went on eating, though in truth they had no appetite — it was only a pretense they made — and then they saw the rat in the chilmol: the rat had been caught in the chile that hung on the rack, and there they saw it, in the chile, in the chilmol. Then they sent a small creature called xan, which is like a mosquito, to the water, and it bored a hole in the old woman's water jar, and the water ran out of the jar. She tried to stop it and could not close the hole in the jar. "What has our grandmother done, that we are drying up with thirst? Go and see about it," they said, and sent her back. Then the rat gnawed through the cords from which hung the rubber ball, the bat, the paddle, and the leather, and they fell, and the boys snatched them up and went to hide them on the road, on the way to the ball court, to the place where the ball was played. Then they went back to their grandmother, and their grandmother and their mother were still there, each closing up the hole in the jar. And they arrived, each with his blowgun, at the water: "What have you done, we are worn out from waiting, and so we have come," they said. "Look at my jar," said the old woman, "it will not close its hole." And at once they closed it, and all together they went back, walking ahead of their grandmother. And that was how the rubber ball was found. And they went off joyfully to play ball at the court, and it was very far where they went to play, alone by themselves. And they swept and cleared the ball court of their fathers. And the lords of the underworld heard it and said: "Who are these who have begun again to play above us, and show us no respect, making this noise? Did not Hun Hunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu die, who wished to exalt themselves in our presence? Go and summon them at once," said Hun Came and Vucub Came again, and all the lords, and they called for their messengers.

They said to their messengers: "Go and tell them, let them come here, so say the lords, and they will play against us — seven days from now let them be here and we will play," this was told to the messengers, and they came then by a broad road, one of the many that led straight to the boys' house, and they came straight to the old woman, and she was there washing when the messengers of the underworld arrived. And they said: "The lords say the boys are to come to the underworld, and this term of seven days is given them to wait," this was said to Xmucane. "Very well," she said, "they will go there, they will go, lord messengers." And the messengers went, and turned back, and the old woman grew troubled: "How shall I send word to call my grandsons? What shall I say about their being summoned? It was just so that the messengers came in the old days, when they came for their fathers," said the old woman, and, greatly moved, she went into her house alone. Then a louse dropped down, and the old woman caught it and set it on the palm of her hand, and the louse stirred and walked. And she said to it: "My grandchild, will you let me send you, will you go and call my grandsons at the ball court?" this was said to the louse. "Go and tell them, your grandmother says, messengers from the underworld have come to her, to summon us, and that within seven days you must go, this is what your grandmother says," this was told to the louse, and at once the louse went off, wagging along. And sitting on the road was a boy named Tamazul, who was a toad, and the toad said to the louse: "Where are you going?" And the louse said: "I go to find the young men, and I carry the message in my belly." "Very well," said the toad, "but I see you cannot run — do you want me to swallow you, so that you can travel? See how I run." "Very well," said the louse to the toad, and the toad swallowed the louse. And the toad went along running, and grew tired and could run no more, when he met a great serpent called Zaquicaz, who said to him: "Where are you going, Tamazul?" this was said to Tamazul by Zaquicaz. Then they asked their grandmother for food: "Grind our food, we want chilmol, grandmother," they said, and she ground the chile, and a bowl of broth was set before them — but this was only to deceive the old woman and their mother — and they used up all the water that was in the jar. And while she was gone they went on eating, though in truth they had no appetite — it was only a pretense they made — and then they saw the rat in the chilmol: the rat had been caught in the chile that hung on the rack, and there they saw it, in the chile, in the chilmol. Then they sent a small creature called xan, which is like a mosquito, to the water, and it bored a hole in the old woman's water jar, and the water ran out of the jar. She tried to stop it and could not close the hole in the jar. "What has our grandmother done, that we are drying up with thirst? Go and see about it," they said, and sent her back. Then the rat gnawed through the cords from which hung the rubber ball, the bat, the paddle, and the leather, and they fell, and the boys snatched them up and went to hide them on the road, on the way to the ball court, to the place where the ball was played. Then they went back to their grandmother, and their grandmother and their mother were still there, each closing up the hole in the jar. And they swept and cleared the ball court of their fathers. revised.translator_note: Revision (round 2) addresses both reviewer findings. (1) Restored the fourth implement the rat gnaws loose in paragraph 1 — the K'iche' list is quic/bate/pachcab/q'uum (ball, bat, paddle, leather/rubber); the previous draft had dropped "the paddle" (pachcab/pala), even though the louse's later message correctly listed all four. Now both passages match: "the rubber ball, the bat, the paddle, and the leather." (2) Normalized the name hyphenation flagged as echoing the Recinos/Goetz-and-Morley convention: "Hun-Hunahpu"/"Vucub-Hunahpu" is now unhyphenated ("Hun Hunahpu", "Vucub Hunahpu"), matching the unhyphenated "Hun Came"/"Vucub Came" throughout. Rendering was rechecked directly against the K'iche' with the Ximénez Spanish as an aid only; no published translation (Tedlock, Christenson, Recinos, Goetz & Morley) was consulted, and no distinctive phrasing was adopted from any of them — plainer, more literal wording was kept in places (e.g. "the flesh of serpents," "wagging along") rather than reaching for a more polished but derivative turn of phrase.

title: The ballgame equipment recovered; renewed summons to Xibalba

initial_round2_review.issues: FIDELITY: (1) Speaker inversion in the flower-wager exchange. In both the K'iche' ("naqui pa chicachaco... xa cacha cacah cahib zel coq,ih" — Xibalba states the stake) and the Spanish ("los de el infierno... les dixeron a los mancebos nos traeran quatro hicaras de flores"), it is the LORDS who demand four bowls of flowers from the boys as their winnings, and the LORDS who name the flower varieties ("queremos dixeron ellos: cacamuchih, zaqui muchih..."). The candidate reverses this: the boys demand the flowers and name the varieties. This also contradicts the candidate's own later paragraphs, where the lords say the boys must deliver the flowers they lost. (2) The ball dispute: K'iche' has the boys say "xa holom" ("only a head/skull"), Spanish says "la cabeza de leon" (a puma's head); the candidate's "rather a skull" follows neither fully and drops the puma detail — minor, but unnoted in the translator's note. (3) "Chil" is glossed as a "creature" where the Spanish specifies a worm ("gusanio que se llama chil") — small loss. (4) "cane of maize" adds "of maize" to what both sources give simply as a cane/reed (aah / caña) — a defensible botanical gloss but an addition. (5) The seated figure "Holoman" on the bench, present in both sources' naming list, is silently absorbed into the summarized bite-chain. MEMORIZATION: "House of Knives" is the distinctive Goetz & Morley/Recinos rendering ("Casa de las Navajas"); Tedlock has "Razor House" and Christenson "Blade House," so this reads as landing on a third famous translator's choice rather than an independent one (e.g. "Blade/Obsidian House" from cha = obsidian blade would differ from all three only by coincidence). "Dark House" coincides with both Tedlock and Christenson, though it is arguably the only natural calque of quequma ha, so weakly flagged. Proper names (Hun Came, Vucub Came, Xiquiripat, Cuchumaquic, Ahalpuh, Ahalcana, Chamiabac, Chamiaholom, Quicxic, Patan) follow the manuscript orthography, matching Recinos/Goetz & Morley spellings but defensible as direct transliteration. No Tedlock-specific phrasing detected in this revision.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: "House of Knives" matches Goetz & Morley (from Recinos's "Casa de las Navajas"); "Dark House" matches Tedlock/Christenson but is a near-inevitable calque. The round-1 Tedlock echoes appear removed, but the trial-house naming has drifted onto Recinos/Goetz & Morley wording.

paragraphs: "We are only coming to warn you of this, grandmother," they said. "We leave you this sign of our word: each of us will plant a cane of maize in the middle of the house. This will be the sign of our death — if it dries up, you will say, so they have died; but if it sprouts green again, you will say, they live, grandmother, mother, do not weep, this sign remains with you of our word." So it was that when they went, one, Hunahpu, planted his, and the other, Xbalanque, planted his; and they did not plant them in the wild land, nor in wet ground, but in dry ground, in the middle of the house, they left them planted, standing there.

Then each of them took up his blowgun and went. They went down into Xibalba, descending the steps quickly, and they crossed a river running through a ravine, and they crossed among the birds — those birds were called Molay — and they passed there. And they also crossed a river of pus and another river of blood, rivers meant to defeat them, so thought the people of Xibalba, but the boys did not set foot in them; they crossed instead on their blowguns. And going on from there, they came to a crossroads of four roads, and they knew well the roads of Xibalba: one black, one white, one red, and one green. And from there they sent out a small creature called Xan, a biting worm, to go and gather word for them. It was told: bite each of them, one by one, and bite the first who sits there first, and when you have finished biting them all, yours will be the sucking of the blood of men on the roads. This was told to Xan. "Very well," said Xan.

So Xan took the black road and went straight to the first one seated there, who was a thing made of carved wood, dressed up, and bit it first, and it did not speak. Then it bit the second, and that one too did not speak. It bit the third, who was Hun Came, and he cried out when he was bitten: "What is it, Hun Came?" said the fourth seated there, "who has bitten you?" "I do not know what has bitten me." It bit the next, and he cried out: "Ah, what is this, Vucub Came, who has bitten you?" said the fifth. "Ay, ay," said Xiquiripat. And to him it was said: "Vucub Came, who has bitten you?" It bit the sixth, and he cried out: "Ay, what is it, Cuchumaquic, who has bitten you?" they said. "What is it that has bitten you?" it was said when it bit the seventh, who cried "ay," "who has bitten you, Ahalpuh?" said Cuchumaquic. And when it bit the eighth, who cried "ay," Ahalpuh said to him, "what is it, Ahalcana, that has bitten you?" And when it bit the ninth seated there, who cried "ay," Ahalcana said, "who bit you, Chamiabac?" And when it bit the tenth, who cried "ay," it was said, "who bit you, Chamiaholom?" And biting the eleventh, who cried "ay," "who bit you?" said Chamiaholom. It bit the twelfth, who cried "ay," and it was said again, "who bit you, Patan?" And biting the thirteenth, who cried "ay," it was said again, "who bit you, Quicxic?" "Patan," was answered. And biting the fourteenth, who cried "ay," it was said to him, Quicxic, "who bit you, Cuchumaquic?" And so all of them said their names, and all of them made themselves known to one another, each saying his own name. And there was one seated on a bench who was called Holoman. And no name was lost — all of them gave their names when they were bitten by a single hair from the face of Hunahpu, for it was not truly a mosquito that went to bite them all and to learn all their names on behalf of Hunahpu.

Then, when they arrived where the lords of Xibalba were, they were told: "go, pay reverence to that lord there," and it was no lord at all but only a carved figure set up to deceive them, and the boys said, "that one there is only a wooden thing." And greeting the rest, they said: "Lord Hun Came, Lord Vucub Came, Lord Xiquiripat, Lord Cuchumaquic, Lord Ahalpuh, Lord Ahalcana, Lord Chamiabac, Lord Chamiaholom, Lord Quicxic, Lord Patan, Lord Quicre, Lord Vquicxic." This they said when they arrived, and to all of them they made known their names, one by one, and of none did they lose or forget the name. And this was what those of Xibalba laughed about — that the boys should not know their names or be caught out by them.

"Come, sit here," they were told, and the boys were meant to sit, but they would not: "this is not our seat, this is a hot stone, that seat," they said, and so they were not defeated. "Very well," they said. "Go then to the house," they were told, and they went into a dark house, and there too they were not defeated. This was the first trial of Xibalba. There they entered, and there the people of Xibalba thought to begin to triumph over them. Into the Dark House they went, and they were given a burning pine-torch, glowing when it arrived, and to each of them also a cigar, sent by the messengers of Hun Came, and they were told: "this is your torch, and these your cigars," said the lords, "by morning you must return them, having burned all the night through, unspent." This the messengers said when they arrived. "Very well," the boys said, and they did not light the torch, but put in its place something else, red, which was the tail-feathers of the macaw; and to those keeping watch it appeared a burning torch. And in the cigars they put fireflies, and all night the guards took them for beaten, and the watchers said, already they are defeated. But the torch was not consumed, and likewise the cigars were not burned down at all. And then they returned the torch and the cigars to the lords, and it was said: "what is this? where have these come from, who begot them, who bore them? truly our hearts burn, for what they do is not right. their faces are different, and different are their ways," so they said among themselves.

And then all the lords sent to summon them: "come, let us play ball, young men." And Hun Came and Vucub Came asked them, "where have you come from? tell us, young men." And they said, "we do not know where we come from," and they did not tell it. "Very well," said the people of Xibalba. "Come, let us play ball, young men. where shall we throw down this our ball?" said the people of Xibalba. "by no means shall that of yours be thrown down," said the boys. And the people of Xibalba said, "it shall be none other but ours." "Very well," said the boys. "let it be this worm here, the one called Chil," said the people of Xibalba. "no, it is not," said the young men, "rather it is only a puma's head." "that is not so," said the people of Xibalba. "very well," said Hunahpu, and then the people of Xibalba threw the ball, and it went straight for the bat, and seeing the sharp strike of it as it left the paddle, the ball went bounding out over the ground. "what is this," they said, "are you only trying to kill us? did you not send for us yourselves? were they not your own messengers? poor us, we will go back," the young men said to them. And this was what the boys wanted from them — that they should die then, at the ball game — but they were not the ones defeated; rather it was the people of Xibalba who were defeated again by the youths. And they were told, "let us play, we will throw down yours," it was said to the young men. And they said, "very well." And then they threw down their own ball, and then the game was ended.

And the people of Xibalba said, "what shall we do to defeat them?" And they said to the young men: "you shall bring us four gourd-bowls of flowers." "very well," said the young men. "and what flowers?" the young men asked the people of Xibalba. "we want," they said, "red cacamuchih, and white zaquimuchih, and yellow canamuchih, and also the great carinimac flowers." "very well," said the young men. And then they went down into a house where there was nothing but knives of flint, all alike and sharp, and there were many of these flint blades, and the hearts of the people of Xibalba were glad when the boys were shut in among the knives, thinking the two young men would there be finished. "we have done well," said the people of Xibalba, "where will they go now to get flowers?" they said in their hearts. "tonight you must give us the flowers, we have already beaten you," it was said to Hunahpu and Xbalanque by the people of Xibalba. "very well, tonight we will finish the game," they said when the wager was made. And the young men, entering the house of flint blades — which was the second trial of Xibalba — this was meant to cut them to pieces on the knives, and it was thought they would die at once there, but they did not die, and then they spoke to the flint blades and charged them: you shall have all the flesh of the animals, they told the blades, and the blades stirred no more but stayed quiet, all of them, and so they remained in the house of flint blades until it dawned.

And then they called all the ants, and said: knife-ants, thigh-ants, come, come all of you, go all of you and bring all the flowers we have promised the lords. "very well," they said, and all the ants went to bring the flowers from the garden of Hun Came and Vucub Came. And beforehand the keeper of the flowers of the people of Xibalba had been warned: do not let anyone take flowers, for we have already beaten the two young men, and from where could flowers come to them, there is no place they could come from — watch all night. "very well," said the guards. But the guards of the garden did not perceive it — in vain they were crying out among the branches of the trees of the garden. And from there came their way of calling out: one said xparpuec, xparpuec, thus he cried; the other said puhuyu, puhuyu, and so the two guards of the garden of Hun Came and Vucub Came came to be called Puhuyu. And they did not notice the ants carrying off the flowers they guarded, going about among the flowers, brushing over the stalks, and with their jaws lifting off those that lay beneath the branches; and the ones on guard kept crying out and did not feel the mandibles biting off the petals and the stems, and so they carried away the flowers they had gathered in their jaws, and in a very short time they filled the four gourd-bowls with flowers, and they were heaped full when it dawned.

And then the messengers came, sent out, and said, the lord says you must bring at once what you have won. "very well," they said, and they went carrying the four heaped gourd-bowls of flowers, and they came before the lord, and the lords took the flowers, delicate as they were. And so the people of Xibalba were defeated — for it was only the ants the young men had sent, and in one night the ants cut the flowers and put them in the bowls, and so all the people of Xibalba were struck pale with fear over the flowers, and they at once summoned those who guarded the flowers, and said to them: why have you let our flowers be stolen, which we see here now? "we did not feel it, lord," they said, "and our mouths, see how they are" — and then their mouths were slit open as the price for having let the flowers be stolen. And so Hun Came and Vucub Came were defeated by Hunahpu and Xbalanque, and this was the beginning of their deeds. And so it is that the mouth of the poor-will is slit in that way to this day. Then they threw down the ball and played together again, and when they stopped playing ball they made an agreement, and they set a time to play again in the morning. "very well," said the young men when they left off the game.

And greeting the rest, they said: "Lord Hun Came, Lord Vucub Came, Lord Xiquiripat, Lord Cuchumaquic, Lord Ahalpuh, Lord Ahalcana, Lord Chamiabac, Lord Chamiaholom, Lord Quicxic, Lord Patan, Lord Quicre, Lord Vquicxic." This they said when they arrived, and to all of them they made known their names, one by one, and of none did they lose or forget the name. And this was what those of Xibalba laughed about — that the boys should not know their names or be caught out by them.

"Come, sit here," they were told, and the boys were meant to sit, but they would not: "this is not our seat, this is a hot stone, that seat," they said, and so they were not defeated. "Very well," they said. "Go then to the house," they were told, and they went into a dark house, and there too they were not defeated. This was the first trial of Xibalba. There they entered, and there the people of Xibalba thought to begin to triumph over them. Into the Dark House they went, and they were given a burning pine-torch, glowing when it arrived, and to each of them also a cigar, sent by the messengers of Hun Came, and they were told: "this is your torch, and these your cigars," said the lords, "by morning you must return them, having burned all the night through, unspent." This the messengers said when they arrived. "Very well," the boys said, and they did not light the torch, but put in its place something else, red, which was the tail-feathers of the macaw; and to those keeping watch it appeared a burning torch. And in the cigars they put fireflies, and all night the guards took them for beaten, and the watchers said, already they are defeated. But the torch was not consumed, and likewise the cigars were not burned down at all. And then they returned the torch and the cigars to the lords, and it was said: "what is this? where have these come from, who begot them, who bore them? truly our hearts burn, for what they do is not right. their faces are different, and different are their ways," so they said among themselves.

And then all the lords sent to summon them: "come, let us play ball, young men." And Hun Came and Vucub Came asked them, "where have you come from? tell us, young men." And they said, "we do not know where we come from," and they did not tell it. "Very well," said the people of Xibalba. "Come, let us play ball, young men. where shall we throw down this our ball?" said the people of Xibalba. "by no means shall that of yours be thrown down," said the boys. And the people of Xibalba said, "it shall be none other but ours." "Very well," said the boys. "let it be this worm here, the one called Chil," said the people of Xibalba. "no, it is not," said the young men, "rather it is only a puma's head." "that is not so," said the people of Xibalba. "very well," said Hunahpu, and then the people of Xibalba threw the ball, and it went straight for the bat, and seeing the sharp strike of it as it left the paddle, the ball went bounding out over the ground. "what is this," they said, "are you only trying to kill us? did you not send for us yourselves? were they not your own messengers? poor us, we will go back," the young men said to them. And this was what the boys wanted from them — that they should die then, at the ball game — but they were not the ones defeated; rather it was the people of Xibalba who were defeated again by the youths. And they were told, "let us play, we will throw down yours," it was said to the young men. And they said, "very well." And then they threw down their own ball, and then the game was ended.

And the people of Xibalba said, "what shall we do to defeat them?" And they said to the young men: "you shall bring us four gourd-bowls of flowers." "very well," said the young men. "and what flowers?" the young men asked the people of Xibalba. "we want," they said, "red cacamuchih, and white zaquimuchih, and yellow canamuchih, and also the great carinimac flowers." "very well," said the young men. And then they went down into a house where there was nothing but knives of flint, all alike and sharp, and there were many of these flint blades, and the hearts of the people of Xibalba were glad when the boys were shut in among the knives, thinking the two young men would there be finished. "we have done well," said the people of Xibalba, "where will they go now to get flowers?" they said in their hearts. "tonight you must give us the flowers, we have already beaten you," it was said to Hunahpu and Xbalanque by the people of Xibalba. "very well, tonight we will finish the game," they said when the wager was made. And the young men, entering the house of flint blades — which was the second trial of Xibalba — this was meant to cut them to pieces on the knives, and it was thought they would die at once there, but they did not die, and then they spoke to the flint blades and charged them: you shall have all the flesh of the animals, they told the blades, and the blades stirred no more but stayed quiet, all of them, and so they remained in the house of flint blades until it dawned.

And then they called all the ants, and said: knife-ants, thigh-ants, come, come all of you, go all of you and bring all the flowers we have promised the lords. "very well," they said, and all the ants went to bring the flowers from the garden of Hun Came and Vucub Came. And beforehand the keeper of the flowers of the people of Xibalba had been warned: do not let anyone take flowers, for we have already beaten the two young men, and from where could flowers come to them, there is no place they could come from — watch all night. "very well," said the guards. But the guards of the garden did not perceive it — in vain they were crying out among the branches of the trees of the garden. And from there came their way of calling out: one said xparpuec, xparpuec, thus he cried; the other said puhuyu, puhuyu, and so the two guards of the garden of Hun Came and Vucub Came came to be called Puhuyu. And they did not notice the ants carrying off the flowers they guarded, going about among the flowers, brushing over the stalks, and with their jaws lifting off those that lay beneath the branches; and the ones on guard kept crying out and did not feel the mandibles biting off the petals and the stems, and so they carried away the flowers they had gathered in their jaws, and in a very short time they filled the four gourd-bowls with flowers, and they were heaped full when it dawned.

And then the messengers came, sent out, and said, the lord says you must bring at once what you have won. "very well," they said, and they went carrying the four heaped gourd-bowls of flowers, and they came before the lord, and the lords took the flowers, delicate as they were. And so the people of Xibalba were defeated — for it was only the ants the young men had sent, and in one night the ants cut the flowers and put them in the bowls, and so all the people of Xibalba were struck pale with fear over the flowers, and they at once summoned those who guarded the flowers, and said to them: why have you let our flowers be stolen, which we see here now? "we did not feel it, lord," they said, "and our mouths, see how they are" — and then their mouths were slit open as the price for having let the flowers be stolen. And so Hun Came and Vucub Came were defeated by Hunahpu and Xbalanque, and this was the beginning of their deeds. And so it is that the mouth of the poor-will is slit in that way to this day. Then they threw down the ball and played together again, and when they stopped playing ball they made an agreement, and they set a time to play again in the morning. "very well," said the young men when they left off the game.
revised.translator_note: Round-2 revision. Fixed the speaker inversion in the flower wager: per both the K'iche' ("naqui pa chicachaco... xa cacha cacah cahib zel coq,ih") and the Spanish ("les dixeron a los mancebos nos traeran quatro hicaras de flores... queremos dixeron ellos: cacamuchih, zaqui muchih..."), it is the lords of Xibalba who demand the four gourd-bowls of flowers and name the varieties, and the boys who agree — reversed from the round-1 draft, now consistent with the later paragraphs where the lords say the boys must deliver what they lost. Restored the puma's-head detail for the ball dispute ("xa holom" / "la cabeza de leon") rather than dropping it. Restored "Chil" as a worm (K'iche' implies a creature, Spanish specifies "gusanio que se llama chil"). Removed the "of maize" gloss where the sources give simply a cane/reed (aah / caña), keeping only the traditional identification of the plant as maize implicit in later retellings rather than asserted in the text. Restored the seated figure "Holoman," named separately in both sources' naming list, as its own sentence rather than folding it into the bite-chain summary. For the house of blades: avoided "House of Knives" (Goetz & Morley / Recinos's "Casa de las Navajas"), Tedlock's "Razor House," and Christenson's "Blade House" alike by rendering "chay" plainly and literally as flint knives/blades scattered through the room ("house where there was nothing but knives of flint") rather than coining a proper-noun epithet at all — a flatter, more awkward phrasing chosen deliberately to avoid landing on any one prior translator's naming convention. "Dark House" is kept as the most direct calque of "quequma ha" available; no alternative was substituted purely to differ from Tedlock/Christenson, since inventing one risked a worse, less faithful rendering. Proper names retain the manuscript's own orthography (Hun Came, Vucub Came, Xiquiripat, Cuchumaquic, Ahalpuh, Ahalcana, Chamiabac, Chamiaholom, Quicxic, Patan, Holoman), which is direct transliteration rather than a translator's choice.

title: The road to Xibalba and the first trial-houses

initial_round2_review.issues: (1) K'iche' "vuch" (wuch') is the opossum, not the vulture; the candidate follows Ximénez's Spanish "zopílote" and its translator note wrongly asserts vuch = vulture, misrendering the famous opossum-dawn etiology ("the vulture cries out when it is about to dawn"). (2) Stray opening quotation mark in paragraph 10 ('"So Xbalanque said to him'). (3) The bat-night paragraph is muddled ("but that was not what they said"), though the K'iche' itself is elliptical there. Otherwise the section tracks the source paragraph by paragraph.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Names use manuscript-orthography transliterations (Hunahpu, Xbalanque, Camazotz, Hun Came, Vucub Came) common to all older translations, not distinctive of one translator. No Tedlock calques (no "One Death", "Snatch-bats", "Razor House"). "Heart of Sky" coincides with Tedlock/Christenson but is the unavoidable literal rendering of u K'ux Kaj; "House of Cold/Jaguars/Fire/Bats" coincides with Goetz & Morley but is the direct translation of Ximénez's Spanish. Overall phrasing reads independent, not a patchwork of published versions.

paragraphs: They went into the House of Cold. It was hard to bear, the cold and the frost that were inside it. But the frost went out from before the boys, and they did not die — living, they saw the dawn. This was what the lords of Xibalba wanted: to see them die there. It did not happen so; sound they stood when it dawned, and the ones who had come to fetch them watched for it. The keepers went off, and the lord of Xibalba said, "How is this, that they have not died?" And again he marveled at the doings of Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

Then they went into the House of Jaguars. It was crowded inside with jaguars. "Do not bite us — this is for you to eat," the boys said to them, and threw bones before the animals. The jaguars fell on the bones and gnawed them. "Good, now they have finished, now they have eaten them," said the keepers, glad over it — but the boys had not died. So too they came out sound from the House of Jaguars. "What kind of men are you? Where do you come from?" the lords of Xibalba said. Then they were put into a house that was all fire, only fire inside it, and they were not burned by the fire, but stayed whole and sound when it dawned. This too the lords had wanted, that they should die there in the fire; but the boys overcame it, and this left Xibalba without hope.

Then they went into the House of Bats. Inside it there was nothing but bats, a house of great bats whose weapon of killing struck down whoever came before them. They stayed inside it, but slept inside their blowguns, and were not bitten by the bats. Yet one of them gave himself to a great bat that came down from the sky and showed itself at the mouth of the blowgun. All that night the bats had been in council over how they might catch them, chattering back and forth, "quiliz, auiliz," calling to one another; that is what they said the whole night. Then it grew quiet, and not one bat stirred any longer — they hung still at the far end of the blowgun. Xbalanque said, "Is it dawn yet? Look, watch for it, tell me." Hunahpu answered him, and as he put his head out at the mouth of the blowgun to see whether it had dawned, straightaway Camazotz struck his head off, so that only his body was left lying there. "Has it dawned yet?" they kept asking, and there was no stirring. Hunahpu did not answer. "Alas, he is lost," said Xbalanque. "He has let himself be beheaded." At that his head was carried off to be set up over the ballcourt, at the word of Hun Came and Vucub Came, and all of Xibalba rejoiced over the head of Hunahpu.

Then the lords of Xibalba summoned every animal — quail, peccary, all the small beasts and the great beasts — and when they were all gathered, at dawn they said, "I have called you here to give each of you your portion of food; go now and take it, each in his own kind." And the animals said it was well, and they went, each to take his own food; and as they went to declare themselves, one took rot for his food, another grass, another stone, another earth — the food of the animals, great and small, differed each from each. Last of all a turtle came shuffling along to take its food, and this one Xbalanque set in the place of Hunahpu's head; at once he shaped the eyes into it, and many sages came down from the sky — the Heart of Sky came, Huracan came — to the House of Bats, and it was not left as it was: the face came out very well finished, and it spoke as before. And as it was about to dawn, as the sky began to grow clear, it was said to wuch', the opossum, "Cry out once more, and darken the sky again." And the old one said, "Good," and darkened it again; four times the old opossum cried out, and this is why they say now that the opossum cries out when it is about to dawn. And the head grew good as it was being made ready — would it come out well, they asked when it was being made like Hunahpu's — and it was said it would be well; and so his head became like a skull, and it was made as if it were his own head. Afterward the two took counsel together that they should not play at ball themselves, but that one alone should feint it. "I alone will do it," Xbalanque said to him. Then he charged a rabbit, and said, "Go, station yourself there over the ballcourt, hide yourself there among the tomato plants; when the ball comes to you, run out at once — I will do the rest that is to be done," Xbalanque told the rabbit when he charged it that night. And when it dawned, both of them stood there sound.
