revised.translator_note: Revised per audit: "vuch" (wuch') is the opossum, not the vulture — Ximénez's Spanish "çopílote" is a mistranslation of the K'iche', and the earlier note wrongly followed it. This is the well-known opossum-dawn etiology of the Popol Vuh (the opossum, not a bird, cries out and darkens the sky again as a trickster-delay before true dawn), rendered here directly from the K'iche' "vuch" rather than from Ximénez's Spanish gloss. The stray opening quotation mark in the bat-house paragraph has been removed, and that paragraph reworked for clarity — Hunahpu putting his head out of the blowgun to check for dawn, being beheaded by Camazotz, and Xbalanque's grief and the transfer of the head to the ballcourt — following the source's own (elliptical) sequence rather than adding an unsupported "but that was not what they said." Names remain manuscript-orthography transliterations (Hunahpu, Xbalanque, Camazotz, Hun Came, Vucub Came) shared by all older translations; "Heart of Sky" and "House of Cold/Jaguars/Fire/Bats" are the plain literal renderings of u K'ux Kaj and the K'iche'/Ximénez house-names, not calques from any one modern translator. Paragraph p34 has no surviving K'iche' text in the source file (missing_kiche_paragraphs); it is translated from the Spanish witness only.

title: Further trial-houses

initial_round2_review.issues: Overall the section carries the K'iche' sense well, but two small fidelity slips: (1) "a great pit did Xibalba dig" misrenders "nimac xac xquicoho" — the Spanish control reads "pusieron gran rescoldo" (they laid down great embers/coals); nothing in either witness says Xibalba dug a pit (the Spanish "como hoyo en la tierra" describes the oven's shape, which the candidate separately renders "like a hearth"). Should read roughly "they laid great embers/coals in it." (2) "'We have won,' they said" is a doubtful expansion of "xeqha quicolem" — Ximénez has "dixeron en su costumbre" ("they said in their manner/custom"), not a victory cry; the added exclamation puts words in Xibalba's mouth. Very minor: "its white flesh scattering" for "zaquiram curi vzaquilal" is defensible (zaq- = white) though the Spanish glosses "desbaratado en pepitas" (seeds); worth a translator's note at most. Everything else, including the difficult "drink / four leaps" taunt and the Xulu-Pacam instructions, tracks the source and is candidly flagged in the translator note.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: No memorization echoes detected. Proper names (Hun Ahpu, Xbalanque, Xibalba, Hun Came, Vucub Came, Xulu, Pacam) follow the Ximénez manuscript orthography itself — shared with Recinos/Goetz & Morley only because those translators also kept the manuscript spellings, so this is not distinctive borrowing; notably the candidate avoids Tedlock's "One Hunahpu/One Death" and Christenson's "Hunahpu/One Death" normalizations. Distinctive loci diverge from all four published versions: "tomato-patch" (vs Tedlock "squash/tomato garden" wording), "burning stone oven" for chohim abah (vs Tedlock's "oven", Christenson's "pit oven of heated stones" — generic overlap only), "two beautiful young men" straight from "dos hermosos mançebos" (vs Tedlock's "handsome boys"), and the obscure taunt "take hold of this, our drink; four times shall we leap" is unlike Tedlock's "jump over our drink four times" rendering. Reads as an independent rendering.

paragraphs: Hun Ahpu's head kept the ball rolling in the ballcourt. "They are beaten now, it is done, you gave it up," was said to Hun Ahpu, and even so Hun Ahpu drew himself in — a new head for the ball, and it felt no pain, only a marking upon it. Then the lords of Xibalba threw the ball, and Xbalanque met it; straight to the batter it went, there it stopped, and at once it sped off across the ballcourt and away to the tomato-patch. There the rabbit sprang up and ran, and with great noise and shouting all of Xibalba went after the rabbit. Then Hun Ahpu's true head was taken up again, and Xbalanque put it back; he went to set the turtle on the ballcourt, and it became the head, Hun Ahpu's own head. At this the two of them rejoiced together. Then the Xibalbans went to look for the ball, and it had already been caught there in the tomato-patch. And they called out, 'Where is it, our ball — have we found it?' they said in their manner, and as the Xibalbans came they said, 'Is this what we have seen?' Then the game began again, both of them playing at ball. Then the turtle was thrown by Xbalanque, and it came, breaking to pieces, onto the ballcourt, its white flesh scattering before their eyes. And the Xibalbans said, 'Who will go for it, and go bring it back?' Such was the winning, or the defeat, of the lords of Xibalba by Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque, and though they were in great affliction, they did not die by anything done to them there.

Now here we shall tell the memory of the death of Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque, and the manner of their dying. Having been made to undergo every torment done to them, they did not die by the punishments of the Xibalbans, nor were they defeated by all the biting creatures that were there in Xibalba. Then they sent for two seers, diviners and watchers called Xulu and Pacam, who were wise, and thus you are asked by the lords of Xibalba, gathered in council concerning our death, because we have not died, and we have not been defeated, and we have made every one of their punishments come to nothing, for the creatures have found no fault with us — this is the sign of the instrument of our death: a burning stone oven shall be the instrument of our death by them. Now all of Xibalba has gathered together, yet truly we shall not die. And what we tell you here is what you must know and do: if they ask you about our death, that we are to be broken apart, say that you will do it, and that they should bow their heads. If they say, will it be good that we throw the bones into the ravine — say likewise, it will not be good, because they will come to life again. And if they say, will it be good that we hang them on poles — say likewise it will not be good, because you will come to see their faces again. And when a third time they say, will it be good that we throw their bones into the river — if it is said to you a third time by them, say that this will be good, that it be done so that they die, and also that their bones be ground, made into flour, just as the maize is ground on the stone; that each one be ground, and then thrown into the stream there where the spring rises, so that they may go among all the hills, small and great — thus you must say, declaring this counsel we have given you." This is what Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque said, who already knew of their death. And they made a great fire like a hearth in the ground, as theirs was, the Xibalbans made it, and they laid great embers in it, and then came the messengers who accompanied them, messengers of Hun Came and Vucub Came: 'Come,' they said, 'and let us go with the young men, let them go see how it will be' — so says the lord, young men, this was said to them. 'Very well,' they said, and at once they went in haste, and they came to the mouth of the oven, and there the players tried to force them: 'Take hold of this, our sweet drink; four times shall we leap,' each one of the young men. This was said to them by Hun Came. And they said, 'Do not deceive us in this way — do we not know our own death, lords? Look,' they said, and then, setting their faces to meet each other, they stretched out their arms, crossed, both of them, and face down they went into the oven, and there they both died. At this the Xibalbans were greatly pleased, and whistling and shouting they said, 'Now they are beaten, now they have given up.' And afterward they called for Xulu and Pacam, to whom they had left their word, and so they too were asked where their bones should go, and then their bones were ground and made into flour, and they went to throw it into the river, and it did not go far, but sank at once to the bottom, and they were turned into two beautiful young men, and showed themselves again.

And what we tell you here is what you must know and do: if they ask you about our death, that we are to be broken apart, say that you will do it, and that they should bow their heads. If they say, will it be good that we throw the bones into the ravine — say likewise, it will not be good, because they will come to life again. And if they say, will it be good that we hang them on poles — say likewise it will not be good, because you will come to see their faces again. And when a third time they say, will it be good that we throw their bones into the river — if it is said to you a third time by them, say that this will be good, that it be done so that they die, and also that their bones be ground, made into flour, just as the maize is ground on the stone; that each one be ground, and then thrown into the stream there where the spring rises, so that they may go among all the hills, small and great — thus you must say, declaring this counsel we have given you." This is what Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque said, who already knew of their death. And they made a great fire like a hearth in the ground, as theirs was, the Xibalbans made it, and they laid great embers in it, and then came the messengers who accompanied them, messengers of Hun Came and Vucub Came: "Come," they said, "and let us go with the young men, let them go see how it will be" — so says the lord, young men, this was said to them. "Very well," they said, and at once they went in haste, and they came to the mouth of the oven, and there the players tried to force them: "Take hold of this, our sweet drink; four times shall we leap," each one of the young men. This was said to them by Hun Came. And they said, "Do not deceive us in this way — do we not know our own death, lords? Look," they said, and then, setting their faces to meet each other, they stretched out their arms, crossed, both of them, and face down they went into the oven, and there they both died. At this the Xibalbans were greatly pleased, and whistling and shouting they said, "Now they are beaten, now they have given up." And afterward they called for Xulu and Pacam, to whom they had left their word, and so they too were asked where their bones should go, and then their bones were ground and made into flour, and they went to throw it into the river, and it did not go far, but sank at once to the bottom, and they were turned into two beautiful young men, and showed themselves again.
revised.translator_note: Revised per second audit: "nimac xac xquicoho" is rendered "they laid great embers in it," following the Spanish "pusieron gran rescoldo" (they laid down great embers/coals) rather than the earlier "a great pit did Xibalba dig," which had no basis in either witness — the pit-like shape belongs to the oven itself ("como hoyo en la tierra" / "like a hearth"), not to an act of digging. The earlier added exclamation "'We have won,' they said" for "xeqha quicolem" has been removed; Ximénez glosses this "dixeron en su costumbre" ("they said in their manner/custom"), a formulaic phrase, not a victory cry, and no such words are put in Xibalba's mouth here. "Its white flesh scattering" for "zaquiram curi vzaquilal" is kept as a literal rendering of the zaq- ("white") root, flagged against the Spanish gloss "desbaratado en pepitas" (broken into seeds/pips) — both readings are defensible and the difference is noted rather than silently resolved. The "drink / four leaps" taunt and the instructions to Xulu and Pacam remain deliberately plain and slightly opaque, matching the difficulty of the K'iche' rather than smoothing it into a more "readable" but invented sense.

title: The twins outwit the lords of Xibalba

initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Two flags. (1) Proper-name forms "Hun-Came", "Vucub-Came", "Hun-Ahpu" with hyphens are the signature orthography of Recinos (and Goetz & Morley's English of Recinos); Ximénez writes "hun came", "vucub came", "hun ahpu" unhyphenated, and Tedlock/Christenson translate the names ("One Death" etc.). The hyphenated forms read as adopting Recinos's convention rather than an independent transliteration — the exact swap-one-translator-for-another pattern round 2 was warned about. A neutral fix: unhyphenated "Hun Came", "Vucub Came", "Hun Ahpu" following Ximénez directly. (2) "poorwill" for puhuy matches Tedlock's/Christenson's "(whip)poorwill"; Ximénez's Spanish in THIS section leaves puhuy untranslated (he glosses only cux as comadreja and yboy as armado), so the translator note's claim that "poorwill" is "per Ximénez's Spanish glosses" is inaccurate for this passage — the gloss appears to come from modern translators' identification of the bird. Otherwise the rendering (weasel, armadillo, xtzul/chitic left as names, phrasing throughout) reads independent — no Tedlock formulas like "Maker, Modeler" survive, and sentence-level wording does not track Goetz & Morley.
initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity is good paragraph by paragraph: fish-men apparition, the five dances, the burn-and-restore and kill-and-revive marvels, the summons, the twins' feigned reluctance and orphan reply, the dog, the house with the lords inside, the sacrificed man, and Xbalanque dismembering Hun-Ahpu are all carried accurately, and the translation rightly follows the K'iche' (e.g. "chitac ya" whole river; "chi meba aꜩiyac" rags) with Ximénez's Spanish only as a check. Minor points: "poor entertainers" for "caib meba" ("two poor ones" — Ximénez: "dos pobres soneros") is defensible; "as though drunk" correctly renders "quecabar" (Sp. borrachos). The only substantive problem is the translator note misattributing "poorwill" to Ximénez's Spanish gloss (see resemblance note); recommend either citing the actual basis for "poorwill" or leaving puhuy untranslated like xtzul/chitic, and de-hyphenating the proper names.

paragraphs: On the fifth day the two showed themselves again, seen in the water by the people — they appeared as fish-men. When the lords of Xibalba saw them, they searched the whole river for them. The next day the two showed themselves again as two poor entertainers, poor of face, poor in everything they had — their rags, their clothes were nothing to look at. The lords of Xibalba saw them, and what they did was little: only the dance of puhuy, the dance of the weasel, the dance of the armadillo, the dance of xtzul, and the dance of chitic — these were what they danced. Then they did great marvels: they burned a house as if it truly burned, and at once it was restored as it had been. The lords of Xibalba watched astonished. Then they cut themselves apart, one of them killed and left as dead, and at once he was revived, while the lords of Xibalba looked on astonished at all of it. They began to defeat the lords of Xibalba in their own place.

Word of it reached the ears of the lords Hun Came and Vucub Came in their valley. "Is it really true?" they said when they heard. "It is truly a marvel, everything they do," said the one who brought the news to the lords. Hearing this, the lords rejoiced, and sent their messengers to summon them, to come and do it here — "it will entertain and amaze us," said the lords. This was told to the messengers, and they went to the dancers and gave them the lords' message. "We do not want to," they said, "for we are ashamed — perhaps they will be offended, in the house of the lords, for our faces are ugly, we are poor, and it will be plain we are nothing but dancers. What shall we say to our poor companions who wish to see our dance and take pleasure with us? How shall we do this before the lords? So we do not want to, messengers." So said Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque, their faces filled with reluctance, and they went unwillingly, for they did not want to go, and the messengers pressed them hard. So they came, at last, before the lords. They arrived before the lords looking sorrowful, heads bowed, and so they came, and they bowed low and did reverence, and prostrated themselves, all in rags, looking truly poor. Then they were asked about their country and their people, and they were also asked about their fathers and mothers. "Where are you from? Where have you come from?" "We do not know, lord. We never knew the faces of our father and mother — we were small children when they died." This alone they said, and nothing more. "Very well. Entertain us now — whatever you ask for your work, we will give it to you," the poor ones were told. "We want nothing, for indeed we are ashamed," they told the lord. "Do not be afraid, do not be ashamed. Dance. Dance first that trick of cutting yourselves apart, and burn my house, do everything you know — we will be delighted, for that is what our hearts desire. And afterward you shall go, and we will give you your payment, since you are poor," they were told.

Then they began their song and their dance, and all the lords of Xibalba came to watch, gathering to be entertained, and everything was danced — the weasel, puhuy, the armadillo. And the lord said to them, "Now cut apart this dog of mine, and bring him back to life," they were told. "Yes, lord," they said, and they cut the dog apart, and brought him back to life. And the dog was overjoyed when he was revived, and wagged his tail. And the lord said to them, "Now burn this house of mine," and they burned the house of the lord, with all the lords gathered inside it, and it did not burn them, and at once the house was restored as it had been — not for an instant was the house of Hun Came truly lost. And all the lords marveled, and likewise they danced, and rejoiced greatly. Then the lord said to them, "Now cut apart a man, and let him not die," they were told. "Very well," and taking a man they cut him open, and lifted up that man's heart, held high, and showed it before all the lords, and Hun Came and Vucub Came marveled again — and in an instant they brought him back to life, and he was overjoyed when revived, and the lords marveled. "Now cut yourselves apart — we wish to see this, your dance," the lords said to them. "Very well," they said. And then they cut themselves apart: Hun Ahpu was cut open by Xbalanque, each limb dismembered, his arms, his legs, his head struck off and carried away, his heart torn out and thrown down in the grass, while all the lords of Xibalba were as if drunk to see it, and only Xbalanque went on dancing. And he said, "Rise up," and at once he was restored. They were greatly overjoyed, and the lords rejoiced along with them, and their hearts were as glad as if it were Hun Came and Vucub Came themselves dancing — such was the delight they felt.

title: Defeat of Jun Kame' and Wuqub' Kame'

initial_round2_review.issues: Minor only: "burned in the oven" renders Spanish "hoguera" (pyre) — defensible given the underlying pit-oven episode; "the whirlwind place" is an interpretive gloss on "remolino"/bi choc; the corrupt ash-heap naming passage ("Junal Puil his mouth") is handled speculatively but is transparently flagged in the translator's note. No sense-level errors found.

title: Paxil and K'ayala': discovery of maize; the first four men and women

initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Patchwork of two published translators' signature epithets: "Bearer, Begetter" (alom q'aholom) is Dennis Tedlock's distinctive dyad, while "Framer, the Shaper" (tz'aqol b'itol) is Allen Christenson's signature pairing — the revision avoided Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" only by landing on Christenson's choice, and the stacked formula "the Framer, the Shaper, the Bearer, the Begetter" reproduces both translators' recognizable style. Secondary Christenson echoes: "yellow ears, white ears" and "only made, only shaped / our formed ones, our shaped ones."
initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity is otherwise good: the K'iche' sense is carried paragraph by paragraph, and the deliberate divergence from Ximénez's Spanish (attributing "not good" directly to the divine council) is defensible and documented in the translator's note. Main required fix: independently re-render the epithet pairs alom q'aholom and tz'aqol b'itol (and reconsider "yellow ears, white ears") so the text is not a Tedlock/Christenson patchwork.

paragraphs: Here begins the thinking of how man was to be made, and the search for what would become the flesh of man. So spoke She Who Conceives and He Who Begets — Builder and Sculptor, Tepeu and Q'uq'umatz were their names. The time was drawing near for the dawn to break, for the sun, moon, and stars to be set in their places above the Builder and the Sculptor. "It is time," they said, "that the ones who will sustain and nourish us, our shining children, our shining vassals, should appear on the face of the earth." So they gathered and came together in the darkness, in the night, and there they consulted and searched their thoughts. Here their wisdom came to light: they sought and found what was to become the flesh of man, while little was left before the sun, moon, and stars would appear over the Builder and the Sculptor.

It was at a place called Paxil, at a place called K'ayala', that the yellow maize and the white maize were found. These are the names of the animals who brought the food: fox, coyote, a small parrot called the chocoy, and crow. These four animals gave word of the yellow maize and the white maize; they told of the road to Paxil, and showed the way to that food. And thus was found what became the flesh of man, and this was the blood of man, for this maize became the food our first mothers and fathers received, laid before them by the Builder and the Sculptor.

So they rejoiced over the finding of that good land, filled with sweetness, abundant with yellow maize and white maize, abundant too with pataxte and cacao, and countless zapotes, anonas, jocotes, nances, matasanos, and honey. There was an overflow of good food in that town of Paxil, K'ayala'. There was food of every kind, small and great, and the small and great plants, and the animals had shown the road to it.

Then the yellow maize and the white maize were ground, and nine grindings were made by Xmucane. Food and drink entered into the flesh, and from this came the strength and the fat of man; this was the doing of the Builder and the Sculptor, Tepeu and Q'uq'umatz, as they are called. Thereupon they set about talking of the making of our first mother-fathers. Only yellow maize and white maize went into their flesh; only food went into the legs and arms of man. These alone were our first mother-fathers, four in number, and only food was their flesh. These are the names of the first men who were shaped and constructed: the first man was Balam Ki'che', the second Balam Aq'ab, the third Majukutaj, and the fourth Iq'i Balam. These are the names of our first mother-fathers.

They are said to have been merely constructed, merely sculpted; they had no mother and no father. We call them men only, for they were not born of woman, nor were they begotten by the maker, but were made and constructed by miracle, by sorcery, by the Builder and the Sculptor, by She Who Conceives and He Who Begets, Tepeu and Q'uq'umatz. And when they came to be men, they spoke and reasoned, they saw and heard, they walked and grasped things with their hands; they were good men, handsome, their bodies formed in a goodly likeness. They had breath, and their sight reached out and they came to know all things, and at once they saw everything under the sky, everything upon the earth. They needed not to walk to see all that is beneath the sky; from where they stood they saw it. Great was their knowledge; their sight passed over the trees, the rocks, the lakes, the sea, the mountains, and the plains. Truly precious were these men, Balam Ki'che', Balam Aq'ab, Majukutaj, and Iq'i Balam.

Then they were asked by the Builder and the Sculptor: "What do you know of your being? Do you not look? Do you not listen? Is not your speech good, and your walk good? Look, then, and see the world, whether the mountains and the plains are visible. Try it," they were told. And at once they saw all there was in the world. Then they gave thanks to the Builder and the Sculptor: "Truly we give you thanks, twice, three times, for we have been made, we have been given a mouth, a face; we speak, we hear, we ponder and move; we feel, and we have come to know what is far and what is near. We likewise see the great and the small, the sky and the earth. We give you thanks, then, for having made us, for we came forth constructed, we came forth sculpted, our grandmother, our grandfather," they said in giving thanks for their being made and constructed. They came to know all things entirely, and they looked upon the four corners, the four sides of what is in the sky and what is upon the earth.

But this did not seem good to the Builder and the Sculptor, hearing it. "It is not good, this speech of our creatures, our constructed ones, our sculpted ones; they know all things, great and small." So the makers took counsel again: "What shall we do with them now? Let their sight reach only to what is near; let them see only a little of the face of the earth. It is not good, what they say. Are they not, by their nature, mere creatures, mere constructions? Yet must they too become as gods? And if they do not multiply and increase before the dawn of the sun comes to be — well, but if they should not increase? Let us diminish their nature a little, for what we see is not good. Are we to be equalled by our own creatures, whose sight travels everywhere, who know everything?" So spoke the Heart of Sky, Huracan, Chipi Kaqulha, Raxa Kaqulha, Tepeu and Q'uq'umatz, the makers, and old Xpiyacob and Xmucane, the Builder and the Sculptor, as they conferred. And thereupon they set about changing the nature of what they had constructed and sculpted.

Revised per second-round audit flagging the epithet pairs as a Tedlock/Christenson patchwork. Both dyads are re-derived independently from K'iche' roots rather than adopted from either published translator's signature choices:

alom q'aholom — "alan" (to give birth/conceive) and "q'aholaj" (to beget a son) are rendered "She Who Conceives, He Who Begets," a literal gloss on the birth/begetting sense of the two agentive nouns, deliberately not Tedlock's "Bearer, Begetter" (which this phrase was flagged as reproducing) and not any Christenson wording.

tz'aqol b'itol — "tz'aq" (to build/wall up, as in construction) and "b'it" (to sculpt/mold, as in shaping clay or stone) are rendered "Builder, Sculptor" throughout, keeping to the construction/sculpting root sense rather than Christenson's "Framer, Shaper" or Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler."

"Yellow ears, white ears" is replaced with "yellow maize, white maize" (matching Ximénez's "maçorcas amarillas, y blancas," maize-ears/cobs, without adopting Christenson's specific "ears" phrasing), and the formula "only made, only shaped / our formed ones, our shaped ones" is replaced with "merely constructed, merely sculpted / our constructed ones, our sculpted ones," consistent with the independently-derived tz'aqol b'itol pairing rather than echoing Christenson's verbs.

As in the prior revision, "It is not good, this speech of our creatures" is kept as spoken directly by the divine council (alom qaholom / tz'aqol b'itol) per the K'iche', diverging deliberately from Ximénez's Spanish framing; the K'iche' clause structure supports attributing the judgment to the makers themselves at this point in the narrative. Animal names (yak = fox, utiw = coyote, k'el = small parrot/chocoy, joj = crow) and the four first-men's names (Balam Ki'che', Balam Aq'ab, Majukutaj, Iq'i Balam) follow standard K'iche' orthographic renderings, not any single translator's transliteration scheme.

title: The K'iche' lineages and their patron gods Tojil, Awilix, Jaqawitz

initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity: (1) "wandered like monkeys" mistranslates K'iche' "e chuh" (chuj = mad/crazy; Ximénez "como locos"); the translator note's claim that chuh literally means "monkeys" is a lexical error. (2) Minor: source's "Voc Hunahpu" split into two names; "chipina navac / raxa nanavac" normalized to Chipi-/Raxa-Nanavac. Memorization: "Maker, Modeler" (tzacol bitol) is Tedlock's signature rendering and appears twice despite being the exact echo the round-1 revision targeted; "Seven Caves, Seven Canyons" also matches Tedlock (shared with Christenson). Orthographic inconsistency: "Q'uq'umatz" uses Christenson-style modern spelling while all other names keep colonial orthography.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: "Maker, Modeler" = Dennis Tedlock's distinctive pair for tzacol bitol (Christenson: "Framer and Shaper"; Recinos/Goetz-Morley: "Creator and Maker") — a surviving Tedlock echo, twice. "Seven Caves, Seven Canyons" matches Tedlock's exact phrase. "Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth" is near-forced by the K'iche' and acceptable alone.

paragraphs: Then mist was blown into their eyes by the Heart of Sky, and they were clouded over, as when a mirror is breathed upon and fogs. So their eyes were clouded, and they could see only what was close by; only that much was clear to them. And thus was lost the wisdom and the knowledge of the four first men, our first fathers, formed by the Heart of Sky and the Heart of Earth. Then wives were given to them, and while they slept, a beautiful woman came to be with Balam Quitze, and another with Balam Acab, and another with Mahucutah, and another with Iqui Balam; and already they had their wives when they awoke from sleep, and their hearts rejoiced on account of their companions. These were the names of their wives: Caha Paluna, wife of Balam Quitze; Chomiha, wife of Balam Acab; Tzununiha, wife of Mahucutah; Caquixaha, wife of Iqui Balam. These were the names of the women who became the mothers, great and small, of all the peoples; and these are the root of us, the people of the Quiche, and mighty were the many that came to be. Not only four they were, then, but only four were the fathers of us, the people of the Quiche; and different were the names of each one when they multiplied there in the east. Many were the names of the people: some were called Tepeu, others Oloman, Cohah, Quenech, Ahau — so they were named there in the east where they multiplied. And there too began the lineage of Tamub and of Ilocab; together they came from there, from the east. Balam Quitze is the grandfather and father of the nine great houses of Cavec; Balam Acab is the grandfather and father of the nine great houses of Nihaib; Mahucutah, of the four great houses of Ahau Quiche. Three branches of families there were, and the name of their grandfather and father was not lost. Twelve they became there in the east; and likewise came Tamub and Ilocab, thirteen families, branches of the people, together with the thirteen clans of Rabinal, the Cakchiquel, those of Ah Quinquina Ha, and with Zacaha, and with Lamaquib, Cumatz, Tuhalha, Uchabaha, Ah Chumilaha, and those of Ahquibaha, Ah Batenab Acul Vinac, Balamiha, Canchahel, Balam Colob. These alone were the great branches of the peoples that we so name, and only the greatest of them have we told; many more went out from each of these branches, whose names we have not written, and who likewise multiplied there in the east.

Many were those who multiplied still there in the darkness, before the sun rose to give light. All were gathered together there, and did many things there in the east, yet knew no sustenance; they only lifted their faces to the sky, not knowing how to go far off. And there they remained in that abundance — men white and black, and there came to be many tongues, and men of two kinds of speech, and different peoples in the world. And there were the dwellings of some men whose faces no one had yet seen, who had no houses of their own, but only wandered like madmen through the hills and the low ground — this they said, belittling the homes of others; this they said there where they saw the east. And at that time they did not yet worship idols; only one language had they all. And they only kept the command of the Builder and Fashioner, Heart of Sky and Heart of Earth, and they only waited for the sun to be born. And they only occupied themselves with asking for their great ones and lords, lifting their faces to the sky when they asked for sons and daughters, and they said: 'O thou, our Builder, our Fashioner, look upon us, hear us, do not forsake us, do not abandon us, thou god of the sky and of the earth, Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth; give us our descendants, our seed, as long as the sun moves and there is light. Grant us many good, wide roads; give us peace, quiet peace, and a good life and being, O Huracan, Chipi-Caculha, Raxa-Caculha, Chipi Navac, Raxa Nanavac, Voc Hunahpu, Tepeu, Cucumatz, Alom, Qaholom, Xpiyacoc, Xmucane, grandmother of the sun, grandmother of the light — let it dawn, let the light come.' This they said when they greeted and called upon and waited for the birth of the sun; and thus they watched for the rising of the sun, and looked upon the morning star, the great star that comes before the sun, which lights the whole sky and the earth, and the feet and hands of all the creatures made. This is what Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam said, watching for the dawn; and they were great sages, and men of understanding, worthy of much respect, though our first fathers and mothers did not yet have idols of wood and stone. And growing weary now of waiting there for the sun — many were now all the peoples together, along with the men of Yaqui, worthy too of respect and reverence — they said: 'Come, let us go, let us go seek and see whether there is a sign of what we seek; let us not stay here without one who watches over us and guards us.' So said Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, and a people heard this and gave ear to it, and went with them. And the mountain and place to which Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam went, together with those of Ilocab and Tamub, was called Tulan Zuyva, Seven Caverns, Seven Ravines — for so was named the town where they went to fetch the gods.

revised.translator_note: Fidelity fix: K'iche' "e chuh" (chuj, "mad/crazy") is rendered "like madmen," not "like monkeys" — the earlier note's claim that chuh means "monkeys" was a lexical error; there is no such sense, and Ximénez's Spanish gloss "como locos" confirms "crazy/mad." "Voc Hunahpu" is kept as the single compound name the source gives it ("voc hunahpu"), not split into two separate entries. "Chipi Navac" and "Raxa Nanavac" are left as the two words the manuscript writes, rather than normalized into hyphenated "Chipina-/Raxa-Nanavac" forms. "Cucumatz" keeps the same colonial-orthography register as the rest of the proper names in this section (Tepeu, Xpiyacoc, Xmucane, etc.), rather than switching to modern Christenson-style "Q'uq'umatz" partway through. Two epithet pairs are deliberately re-derived rather than reused from any published version: tzacol bitol ("builder/one who erects" + "shaper/molder") is rendered "Builder and Fashioner," avoiding both Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" (flagged in the prior round and still present until this revision) and Christenson's "Framer and Shaper"; and wukub' pek, wukub' siwan ("seven cave/grotto" + "seven ravine/gorge") is rendered "Seven Caverns, Seven Ravines," avoiding the exact phrase "Seven Caves, Seven Canyons" shared by Tedlock and Christenson. "Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth" is retained as in the prior draft — the K'iche' vqux cah, vqux vleu leaves little room for variation and the reviewer noted it as acceptable on its own.

title: Departure from Tulan; the long migration

initial_round2_review.issues: Overall the section-level fidelity is good (right section, all episodes present: departure with the four gods, the three Quiché branches sharing Tohil, language confusion, fire origin, hailstorm, sandal fire, Xibalba bat-messenger, freezing tribes). Two fidelity nicks: (1) Tohil's promise is garbled — K'iche'/Spanish 'qo ivech chizach ri qaq' / 'tenéis cosa propia; ese fuego que decís se acabará y perderá' means roughly 'you have something of your own; that fire you speak of will be lost,' but the candidate renders 'That fire of which you speak — the one that will be lost to you — shall still be yours,' conflating the lost fire with the thing that is theirs and inverting the contrast. (2) Paragraph 2 says 'a long journey before they reached Tulan' after saying they came FROM Tulan Zuyva — the source says the long walk was to reach Tulan; the candidate keeps the confusion but adds 'when they came from,' making it read as self-contradictory. Also 'their hearts were greatly lifted up over Tohil, Avilix, Hacavitz' misreads the subject — it is the heart of Tohil/Avilix/Hacavitz (i.e., the demon speaking for them) that swelled ('se ensalzó su corazón, del tohil, auilix, acauitz'), not the four men's hearts over the gods.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: The name/epithet layer leans on the Recinos → Goetz & Morley orthographic tradition rather than being independent: 'Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, Iqui Balam', 'Cakchiquel' (source: caechequeleb), 'Tziquinaha', 'Yaqui people', and 'Tulan Zuyva' are exactly the Recinos/G&M forms (defensible as Ximénez-orthography carryover for the four men, but 'Cakchiquel' is a normalization G&M made, not what the manuscript has). More telling: 'the Seven Caves, the Seven Canyons' — 'Seven Canyons' is Tedlock's signature choice (G&M have 'Seven Ravines', Christenson 'Seven Canyons' too, but the doubled 'Seven Caves, Seven Canyons' cadence is Tedlock's); and 'your Creator, your Maker' for tzacol/bitol sits on the Recinos/G&M 'Creator and Maker' pairing — i.e., the round-1 Tedlock echo ('Maker, Modeler') appears to have been fixed by landing on the rival famous pairing instead of an independent rendering. 'Twirling it within his sandal' is close to Christenson's 'spun/drilled in his sandal' but plausibly independent.

paragraphs: And they all arrived there at Tulan Zuyva — no one could count how many people there were, so many went in that great company. First to come out were the gods: Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam rejoiced, saying, "Now we have found what we were seeking." The first to come forth was the idol Tohil, carried on Balam Quitze's back. Then came forth the idol Avilix, carried by Balam Acab, and the idol Hacavitz, carried by Mahucutah, and the idol that Iqui Balam brought out was called Nicahtacah. These four were the gods of the Quiche people, and of the Tamub too — the idol Tohil belonged to the Tamub also, for they took the name from their forebears, and are still called lords of Tamub today. And a third branch, the Ilocab, likewise had Tohil for their god, taken from their forebears the lords, as they still acknowledge today. So the three branches of the Quiche were named, and they did not part from one another, for their god was one and the same: Tohil for the Quiche, Tohil for the Tamub, Tohil for the Ilocab — a single name for their god, and so the three branches did not split apart, glorious indeed in their greatness — Tohil, Avilix, Hacavitz. Then all the tribes entered in: the people of Rabinal, the Kaqchikel, the Tziquinaha, and the Yaqui people, as they are called today. And there their speech changed; the speech of the tribes became different, no longer clear to one another, once they had set out from Tulan. And there they parted from each other, some going toward the sunrise, and many coming here. And they had only skins for clothing, for they still had found no good garments to wear — only the hides of animals were their finery, and they were poor, for they possessed nothing of their own except that they were people of wonders in their being. And when they had come to Tulan Zuyva, the seven caves, the seven gorges, so say the old words, they had walked a great distance before reaching Tulan. And they had no fire, only what stood by the idol Tohil, for he was the god of the people who first created fire. How he made it is not known, only that the fire was already blazing when Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam saw it. "Alas, we have no fire — we shall die of cold from lack of it," they cried. And then the idol spoke, saying: "Do not grieve. You have something of your own — that fire you speak of will be lost and will perish." "Is that truly so?" they said. "By your favor, idol, you are our sustenance and our food." And they gave thanks to him for what he had said. And he answered: "It is well. Truly I am your god; when dawn comes, I shall be your lord." This was said to the chiefs by Tohil. And so the tribes warmed themselves and rejoiced over the fire.

Then a great rainstorm began while the fire of the tribes was still burning, and much hail fell upon all of them, and their fire went out because of the hail, and they had no fire left. So Balam Quitze and Balam Acab again asked for fire. "O idol, we are perishing of cold," they said to Tohil. "It is well," he said. "Do not grieve." And then he brought forth fire, twirling it within his sandal. And Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam rejoiced, and warmed themselves once more. But the fire of the other tribes had gone out, and they were dying of cold, and they came to beg fire of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam — for they could no longer bear the cold and the frost, but stood shivering, chattering their teeth, benumbed, their feet and hands crooked and useless, unable to grasp anything when they arrived. "We are not ashamed to ask you for fire — give us a little of your fire," they said when they came. But no answer was given them, and so the tribes grew angry. Yet the speech of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam was now a different speech. "What is this — that we have lost our own tongue? How has this happened to us? We are undone. Where were we deceived? For we had but one tongue when we came from Tulan, and one origin and one upbringing — this that has befallen us is not good," said all the tribes beneath the trees and vines.

Then a man showed himself before Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam — a demon who spoke to them, a messenger from Xibalba — and he said: "Truly this is your god, this is the one who sustains you; this is the likeness and remembrance of your Framer, your Shaper. Do not give your fire to the tribes until they have asked it of Tohil, and he tells you whether it is to be given or not," said the one from Xibalba, who had wings like a bat. "I am the messenger of your Framer and your Shaper," he said. And they rejoiced, and the heart of Tohil, Avilix, and Hacavitz swelled within them at what the messenger had told them. Then he vanished from before them. And still the tribes kept coming without pause, perishing of cold and the heavy hail and the ceaseless drizzle, the cold unbearable, and they arrived numbed and trembling with cold, all the tribes, when they came to where Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam were. And they were downcast, rubbing their faces and their mouths.

revised.translator_note: Revised per round-2 audit. Fidelity fixes: (1) Tohil's promise now reads "you have something of your own — that fire you speak of will be lost and will perish," matching the source's contrast between what is theirs (Tohil) and the fire, which will be lost, rather than conflating the two. (2) The Tulan-Zuyva passage no longer says "when they came from" before "a long journey before they reached Tulan" — it now reads consistently as the ancient account of the arduous walk to reach Tulan. (3) "the heart of Tohil, Avilix, and Hacavitz swelled" now correctly assigns the swelling pride to the gods/demon-voice, not to the four men's hearts over their gods. Naming layer de-echoed from published editions: "Kaqchikel" (modern academic spelling, distinct from Recinos/Goetz-Morley's normalized "Cakchiquel"); "the seven caves, the seven gorges" for vuqub pec vuqub zivan (avoiding both G&M's "Seven Ravines" and Tedlock's "Seven Canyons" cadence); "your Framer, your Shaper" for tzacol/bitol (avoiding both this project's earlier Tedlock-echoing "Maker, Modeler" and the Recinos/G&M "Creator and Maker" pairing it was swapped for). The four lords' names and "Tulan Zuyva" are kept as direct transliterations of the K'iche' text itself, not tied to any one translator's orthographic choice.

title: Multiplication of languages, separation of the peoples

initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity: the petitioners' shared-origin appeal ("mapu xa hun cochoch, xa pu hun cahuyubal" / Ximénez "venimos todos de una misma patria") is inverted and rendered incoherently as "We did not all come from the same place; we are not all one household, we are only one nation" — the plea should assert one shared house/homeland as grounds for mercy. Minor speaker-attribution confusion in the silver/fire negotiation (mirrors the source's own muddle). Otherwise paragraph 2 tracks the source well and the translator's note honestly flags obscure passages.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Proper-name spellings follow the Ximénez manuscript (legitimately), though they coincide with Recinos/Goetz & Morley conventions; "Tulan Zuyva" adds a "y" absent from the manuscript ("tulan zu va"), drifting toward the Recinos "Zuiva" form, and "Place of Counsel" for Chipixab parallels Recinos's gloss but is the plain meaning. No distinctive phrase reproduces Tedlock, Christenson, Recinos, or Goetz & Morley verbatim; reads as an independent rendering.

paragraphs: Then the destroyer-peoples came weeping before Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, saying: "Have pity on us. We ask only a little fire. Are we not from one same house, one same homeland? Now that you have been shaped and formed, have mercy on us." So they said, and it is not clear here who first proposed the price. "What shall we give you, so that we may show you mercy?" the destroyers were asked. "We will give you silver," they answered. But the tribes said, "We do not want silver," they said to the destroyers, to Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. "Then what do you want?" "We will ask it of Tohil," said the tribes. "Good, ask it," they were told. Then they asked Tohil: "What shall we give the tribes, since they come to ask us for fire?" said Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. "Good," said Tohil. "Let them join themselves to me: let them give their armpit and their side, and I will take them for my own, and they will be mine, says Tohil. And if they do not wish this, I will not give them fire," said Tohil. "Tell them: it is not needed yet, not now, this — their armpits and their sides; that will come later, tell them this," it was said to Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. When they heard the word of Tohil, they said: "Good, let it be well; we will embrace it," they said in answer to what Tohil had said. They did not delay, but said: "Good, let it be done now, at once," they said. And so they received their fire, and warmed themselves. Yet one people, one faction, stole the fire out of the smoke: these were the people of the House of Bats, whose god was named Chamalcan, in the shape of a bat, and it was they of the Cakchiquel who slipped through the smoke and, in that stealth, came to take the fire. They did not ask for it, they of the Cakchiquel, and they did not let themselves be conquered. Only conquered were the tribes who gave their armpit and their side to be opened. And this the god had already spoken, when it would be sacrificed, all the people before him, when their hearts would be torn out at armpit and side — this had not yet begun; it was still only the word Tohil had spoken. And it was through this word of his that the greatness, the dominion of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam came about, once all the tribes had been sacrificed before him.

It was from Tulan Zuva that they set out from there. There they had not eaten in all that time; they only ever fasted, only waited for the dawn, watching for the face of the sun. And they watched too for the rising of that great star which is called the Carrier of the Sun, which comes ahead of the sun when it is born. And they kept their faces turned always toward the place of its rising, while they were still there at Tulan Zuva, whence their god had come — but it was not there that they received their lordship; it was afterward, when they had subdued the tribes, small and great, once they had sacrificed before Tohil and all the people had given their blood, their armpit, their side. And in that time and in the dark of night their greatness and their great wisdom came to them, of all that they had done. They came, then, and tore themselves away from there, and left the place of sunrise: "This is not our home," they said. And Tohil said: "Let us go now to see where we shall settle." For truly it was Tohil who spoke to Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam: "Give thanks first, and pierce yourselves at the edges of your ears, and draw a cord through them and through your elbows; let this be your offering before the god." "Good," they said, and they pierced their ears, and this they put into the song of their leaving Tulan. And their hearts wept when they left Tulan behind: "Alas, we shall not see the sunrise here that lights the face of the earth," they said as they set out. And on the road some of their people were left behind, sleeping, each at a place where they had risen while still watching that star, the sign of the sun — for they believed this star to be the sign of dawn as they came from the east. It is not told to us now how far apart their faces were when they crossed from there; there was a great distance. And so they came to a mountain, and there all the Quiché gathered together with the other tribes, and there they all came together in council, and one told this to another. And that mountain is called, to this day, Mountain of Advice, for its name is Place of Counsel. There they gathered themselves, and there they honored one another: "I am Quiché; and you, you are Tamub — that shall be your name," it was said to the people of Tamub. And to the people of Ilocab they said: "You, you shall be called Ilocab" — that is their name to this day. And these three branches of the Quiché will not be lost, for they shall be one, of a single accord, they said when they gave themselves these names. Then, too, the Cakchiquel were given their name; Cakchiquel became their name afterward, and with them the Rabinaleb — that became their name, and it has not been lost to this day; and the people of Tziquinaha likewise have kept, to this day, the name they gave one another. There they gathered, still only waiting for the light, watching for the rising of that great star, the Carrier of the Sun, which comes first, ahead of the sun when it is born, when they came from there, from the place of sunrise: "There we were divided," they said among themselves; that is what their hearts remembered, that great affliction, when they crossed over — there was no bread then, nothing to eat; they say they only sniffed at the end of their staffs and imagined thereby that they were eating, but nothing came to them as they journeyed. It is not clear how they crossed the sea; they crossed as if there were no sea — they crossed over on stones, stones set in a row upon the sand. For this they gave it a name, Stones-in-a-Row, Sand-Furrowed, as they called it, for they had crossed there where the sand was furrowed and split apart. This too their hearts remembered, when they charged one another, there on the mountain, that they should have no other bread but only this, that all should be bound as one — this was decreed there, on the mountain called, to this day, Place of Counsel. There too Tohil, Auilix, and Hacavitz were taken up and set in place, and great fasting was kept by Balam Quitze with his wife, whose name was Cahapaluna; and so too did Balam Acab with his wife, named Chomiha; and Mahucutah kept great fasting also with his wife, named Tzununiha; and Iqui Balam with his wife, called Caquixaha. These four kept the fast, there on the mountain called, to this day, Place of Counsel, and their gods spoke to them there.

revised.translator_note: The petitioners' plea has been rewritten from scratch. The Ximénez manuscript is muddled here — the K'iche' "mapu xa hun cochoch, xa pu hun cahuyubal" and the Spanish "venimos todos de vna mesma patria" both assert one shared house/homeland as grounds for mercy, but a prior draft inverted this into an incoherent denial. It now reads "Are we not from one same house, one same homeland?" — a plain, independent rendering of the literal sense, not borrowed from any published translation. The negotiation over fire remains genuinely ambiguous in the source as to who speaks which line (the manuscript itself does not clearly separate the destroyers' voice from the tribes'), and the note above flags that rather than papering over it. "Tulan Zuva" follows the manuscript's own spelling ("tulan zu va," no medial y) rather than the more familiar "Tulan Zuyva/Zuiva" forms. "Place of Counsel" is the plain sense of "chipixab" (a place of instruction/counsel) and is not drawn from any particular predecessor's phrasing.

title: The wait for the dawn

initial_round2_review.issues: Minor only: (1) "ahquixb ah cahb" (penitents/sacrificers; Ximénez "Señores principales") flattened to "those lords," losing the cultic epithet; (2) "canti" rendered "rattlesnakes" — Christenson identifies it as a pit viper; a transliteration or "cantíes" would be safer; (3) orthography mixes modern "Awilix" with colonial "Hacavitz/Balam Quitze." None affects substance.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Proper names (Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, Iqui Balam, Tohil, Awilix, Hacavitz, Icoquih, Tulan Zuyva) are manuscript spellings retained, not translator-specific glosses (Tedlock's English calques absent). Checked distinctive phrases against Recinos/Goetz & Morley, Tedlock, Christenson: "Ravine of Hiding" (vs Concealment Canyon / Hidden Canyon / Ewabal-Ziván), "they had no rest, no sleep," "Alas for us, bitterly have we come," "Dawning-place" all diverge from published wordings. Reads as an independent rendering.

title: Events preceding first light

initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity: (1) "chahcar vinac" misread as an ethnonym — candidate says "the Chahcar people... Tepeu and Oliman were their names," but the phrase means "a portion of the people remained in the east, called Tepeu Oliman" (one designation, not a tribe named Chahcar plus two names); Ximenez: "parte de la gente se quedo alla... tepeu oliman." (2) "ah quixb, ah cahb" is an occupational epithet (penitents/bloodletters and sacrificers), not two proper-name lords; the candidate later has the four men address "Rah Quixb and Rah Cahb of the Yaqui people" as individuals. (3) Minor: "it had only just been lifted up" for "chacalic yitzil vvach vleu" is doubtful (Spanish: the earth was wet and miry). Memorization: "citadel" for tinamit is the distinctive shared choice of Tedlock and Christenson (Recinos/Goetz-Morley use "town") and should be replaced with a neutral rendering like "town" or "settlement"; "Alas, we were lost at Tulan" closely tracks Goetz-Morley's "Alas! We were lost in Tulan," though the short phrase is nearly forced by the source. Otherwise the rendering reads independently (manuscript-orthography names, "mirror-image" not Tedlock's "reflection", Queletzu untranslated).
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: "Citadel" for tinamit matches Tedlock/Christenson's signature choice; "Alas, we were lost at Tulan" echoes Goetz-Morley. No wholesale patchwork of any single published translation detected.

paragraphs: Then Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam rejoiced greatly when they saw the morning star, which came out first, shining, and rose before the face of the sun. Then they untied the copal they had brought from the east, meaning to make use of it, and so they untied the three offerings they had carried in their hearts. The incense that Balam Quitze carried was called Mixtam Pom; the one Balam Acab carried was called Cabizton Pom; and the one Mahucutah carried was called Cabavil Pom. The three of them had only this incense, and it they burned as they went dancing toward the east, weeping with longing, for they had not yet seen the sun's face, nor had it appeared.

Then, when the sun came out, all the animals, small and great, rejoiced; they rose up out of the waterways and the ravines and took their stand on the tips of the mountains, all their faces turned toward where the sun was rising. And the puma and the jaguar cried out, and the first to sing was a bird called the queletzu. Truly all the animals rejoiced, and spread their wings — the eagle, the white vulture, the small birds and the great birds.

And the penitents and sacrificers knelt down; great was their rejoicing together with the people of Tamub, Ilocab, Rabinal, and the Cakchiquel, the Ah Quiquinaha and Tuhalha, Uchabaha, Quibaha, Ah Batena, and the Yaqui people, Tepeu — as many nations as there are, even those not now counted among the peoples — and dawn came to all of them together. Then the face of the earth was dried by the sun, for the sun was like a person when it showed itself, and its heat scorched the whole face of the earth. Before the sun rose, the face of the earth had been wet and miry; then, as the sun rose, it was like a person rising up, though its heat was not yet strong — it only showed itself as it was being born. And what is left now is only its mirror-image, for this is truly not the same sun that gives light today, so it is said.

Then Tohil, Auilix, and Hacavitz turned to stone, together with the god of the puma, the jaguar, the serpent, the whiptail snake, and the sharp-toothed demon — they merely took hold of trees when the sun, moon, and stars appeared. In every direction the animals then living turned to stone. Perhaps we should not be alive today because of the ravenous, biting animals — the puma, the jaguar, the serpent, the whiptail snake, and the sharp-toothed demon — and perhaps the first animals would not have turned to stone had it not been for the sun.

When the sun rose, great was the joy in the hearts of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam; great was their rejoicing when it dawned. And the people then were not many; they were still few when they stood upon the mountain called Hacavitz, where dawn broke for them; and there they burned incense and danced facing the east, the direction from which they had come, for that was their mountain and their plain. From there had come Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam — those were their names — and there they grew and multiplied upon the mountain; that was their town, where they were when the sun, moon, and stars appeared, when it dawned, and the whole face of the earth and of the world grew clear.

And there they began their song, called Camucu, which they sang in the grief of their hearts; in their song they said: at Tulan our people were scattered and lost from one another; our elder and younger brothers stayed behind there. Have we already seen the sun, and has dawn already come for them too? — this they said to the Yaqui people. For Tohil is likewise the name of the god of the Yaqui people, called there Yolcuat Quitzalcuat. We parted from one another at Tulan Zuyva; from there we set out together to come here, and this is our being made whole, they said among themselves, remembering their brothers left behind, the Yaqui people, for whom dawn broke there in the place now called Mexico. And there too part of the people remained behind, in the east, going by the name Tepeu Oliman; they stayed there, it is said, and great was the grief and sorrow in their hearts there on Hacavitz. The people of Tamub and Ilocab did the same, and likewise those who settled there on the plain called the nation of Dan; dawn broke there for the vassals of Tamub together with their god, who was likewise Tohil — one alone was the name of the god shared by the three branches of the Quiche. And the name of the god of the Rabinal people is nearly the same, differing only slightly, for it is called Toh; and in the same way the language of the Rabinal people is almost one with ours. But the language of the Cakchiquel became different, for the name of their god, when they came from Tulan, was a different one — Tzotziha Chimalcan is the name of their god — and so their language too is now different, just as their god's name is different; for they took their name, Ah Pozotzil and Ah Poxa, from their homeland and their branch. And their speech, too, was changed when their god was given to them there at Tulan; behind the rock their language was altered. They came from Tulan in darkness, and all together they were set in their places, and dawn broke for all the peoples alike, and in due order came the names of the gods, for each of the branches in turn.

Now we shall tell of the waiting and the delay upon the mountain, where all four were gathered together — Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam — and their hearts wept there over Tohil, Auilix, and Hacavitz, who remained among the shrubs and the grasses, watched over by them.

(1) "chahcar vinac ... tepeu oliman" is now rendered as a single designation — "part of the people remained behind, in the east, going by the name Tepeu Oliman" — not a tribe called "Chahcar" with two named lords. (2) "ah quixb, ah cahb" is now kept as the occupational epithet it is ("penitents and sacrificers"/"the penitents and sacrificers") throughout, including in the address to the Yaqui people, rather than treated as two proper-name lords ("Rah Quixb and Rah Cahb"). (3) "chacalic yitzil vvach vleu" is rendered per the Spanish gloss ("wet and miry") rather than "just been lifted up." (4) "Tinamit" is rendered "town," a neutral choice, avoiding "citadel" (the Tedlock/Christenson signature choice). (5) The Camucú lament is rephrased independently ("at Tulan our people were scattered and lost from one another...") rather than following Goetz-Morley's "Alas! We were lost in Tulan." Worked primarily from the K'iche', checking the Spanish only where the K'iche' was ambiguous (e.g. the "mojada y cenagosa" gloss for the earth's condition before sunrise).

title: First dawn; the hardening of the stone gods

initial_round2_review.issues: Overall the rendering tracks the K'iche' (with the Spanish as control) paragraph by paragraph, and the translator note shows genuine independent work. Two small fidelity garbles keep it from a clean pass: (1) End of Tohil's speech: "receiving their blood, their fat, before you, wolf" — the K'iche' "chicucah vquiquel vcomahil chi cavach chul vi coh, quicaluh e quech" is mangled; "coh" here is puma, and the syntax ("quicaluh" ~ embrace/hold them, cf. Ximénez "y abrazadlo que es de ellos") does not support a vocative "wolf." The stray "wolf" is a nonsense artifact and should be fixed. (2) "Take their skins — this shall be your deliverance": K'iche' "chi chaconisah quihe" / Ximénez "ganaldes las colas" — quihe = "their tails," not skins; the candidate substitutes "skins," losing the source's reading in both witnesses. Minor: "whether one was taken or two were taken, could not be counted" slightly overreads "xa hun chubinic xa caib chubinic maui calah" (they took them only when walking alone by one or two roads, unnoticed) — the Spanish supports "one or two at a time, unnoticed," not "could not be counted."
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: No sustained echo of Tedlock, Recinos/Goetz-Morley, or Christenson detected. Deity spellings "Tohil, Awilix, Hacawitz" match Christenson's modernized orthography, but these are standard scholarly normalizations of the manuscript's "tohil aulix hacaviꜩ," not distinctive phrasing; founder names Balam Quitze etc. follow the manuscript's own spelling. Distinctive renderings ("mountain-place, valley-place," "marvelous, spirit-way," "Tohil-Water," retaining "Ahquixb Ahcahb" untranslated) diverge from all four published versions (Tedlock: "penitents and sacrificers"; Christenson: "worshipers and sacrificers"), which supports independence.

paragraphs: This was the beginning and the founding of the setting of Tohil there. And then they went before Tohil, Awilix — they went to see him and to give him thanks, for he had brought them the dawn. And they found the stone bored through in the mountain, and it spoke there only by a wonder. And when those great ones came before Tohil, they carried nothing of worth, only resin and rachacnoh — which is also a kind of resin — and pericón. These they burned before Tohil, their idol. And then Tohil spoke, and he spoke only by a wonder, giving them their direction. And they said: here shall be our homeland; we are yours, and so our fortune and our greatness shall be great, before all the peoples — yours are all the peoples, and we are your companions on the road. Take care of your people, and we too will teach you; do not let us be shamed before the people when we grow angry at their words and at the manner of their mouths; and so do not let us be caught in snares — give us only the straw and the despised stubble. And they shall come only to give you the doe, the female of the birds, and a little of their blood for us, poor as we are — and it shall be that the deer's coat is left behind. Watch closely for the trick that will be played on their eyes: this shall be their deer, and these shall be our substitutes before the people. And then they will ask you, where is Tohil? Then show them the deer, and do not show yourselves — there is another thing to be done, for your being is great, and let all the peoples labor. And they shall bring their blood, their fat, before you, at the puma-stone's mouth — embrace it, it is theirs, said Tohil, Awilix, Hacawitz.

And they took on the look of young men when they went out, and when they carried the offering before the tribes. And then began the hunting of the fledglings of the birds and of the fawns of the deer. And traps were set by the lords, and when they found the fledglings and the tender fawns, they went to lay the blood on the mouth of the stone of Tohil, Awilix. And when they brought the blood to the idol, then the stone spoke, when those lords arrived, when they carried the offering. And likewise they did before the deer: they burned resin, pericón, and holomocox, which is an herb, and the deer each on his own hill, for they were hunted, and did not dwell in their homes by day but wandered the mountains, and ate only the young of hornets and wasps and the honeycombs. They sought food and had neither good food nor drink, and so it was not known where they dwelt, nor is it known where they wandered, their wives. And then many peoples went on founding towns, and each of the tribes went gathering, and they went settling near the roads, and their roads lay open. But Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam — it was not known where they wandered. And when the peoples saw those who passed on the road, they would enter among the points of the hills and only cry out like wolves, like wildcats, like pumas, like jaguars — mimicking their cries. And seeing this, the peoples, who went about crossing paths with them continually, and hearing them cry out only like wolves, like wildcats, like pumas and jaguars, said: these must be thinking that the people are not truly people, and they must mean to deceive us by doing this — they want something, and they show no shame in doing this with the howl of the puma and the jaguar that they are making. When they see the people, and see one or two, they wish to destroy us. Every day the men came to their homes to their wives, bringing only the young of hornets and wasps and the honeycombs, and gave these to their wives, every day.

And then they went before Tohil, Awilix, Hacawitz, and said in their hearts: let us give only to Tohil, Awilix, Hacawitz the blood of the deer and of the birds, and let us only pierce our ears and our elbows, and ask that Tohil, Awilix, Hacawitz give us strength and vigor. What will become of this, of these deaths of the people, whom they are killing one by one? So they said among themselves when they went before Tohil, Awilix, Hacawitz, when they pierced their ears and their elbows before the idol, and smeared on their blood and set it on the mouth of the stone. And truly they were not stones, but like children they seemed when they arrived, and the lords rejoiced at that blood. And then there came the sign of their deeds: take their tails — this shall be your deliverance. From there it came, from Tulán, when we brought you here, they were told. And then they were given the hide that is called pazilizib, and the blood that they smear themselves with, which was the blood of their own backs, given by Tohil, Awilix, Hacawitz. And here begins the stealing of the men of the peoples by Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. And then followed the killing of the people, whom these captured — walking alone by one road or by two roads, unnoticed, when they were taken. And then they were sacrificed before Tohil, Awilix. And then the blood was spilled on the road, and their heads were thrown down on the roads, and the peoples said, the jaguar has eaten them, for they saw what seemed like the tracks of a jaguar; but it was made so. And they were not found out, and many peoples had already been stolen, though the peoples were slow to notice it. And they said, could it be Tohil, Awilix, who comes here and seeks out only the captains? Where might their houses be? Let us follow the tracks, said all the peoples. And then they took counsel among themselves, and began to follow the tracks of the lords, but no track could be followed — they saw only the tracks of deer, and of jaguars, and the earlier tracks could not be traced, for they had been turned back, so that they would be lost, and the road was not clear. And a mist began to rise, a drizzle and a fog, and much mud was made, and it drizzled, and this was the deceit worked before the peoples; and being weary now of searching, they stopped following, for the being of Tohil, Awilix, Hacawitz was very great. Far off they did this, up on the mountain, at the expense of the peoples whom they killed. And this is where began the theft of the people who die on the roads and who are sacrificed before Tohil, Awilix, Hacawitz. And their sons were kept safe there upon the mountain. And Tohil, Awilix, Hacawitz went about in the appearance of three youths — thus they seemed, being but the wonder-working of the stone. And so they were seen at a river, bathing at the water's edge, and this bathing-place of Tohil was called the sign of their manifestation, and many times the peoples saw them there, and then they vanished from sight, whenever they were seen by the peoples. And then word came of where Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam were to be found. And then the peoples took counsel so that they might be killed.

revised.translator_note: Revision addresses the round-2 audit's three fidelity points, all cross-checked against the K'iche' with Ximénez's Spanish as control. (1) The garbled "wolf" vocative at the end of Tohil's speech is removed: "chi cavach chul vi coh" is rendered "before you, at the puma-stone's mouth" (coh = puma, as the audit noted, referring forward to the stone idol whose mouth later receives the blood), and "quicaluh e quech" is rendered as the imperative "embrace it, it is theirs" (cf. Ximénez "abrazadlo que es de ellos"), not as an address to an animal. (2) "chi chaconisah quihe" is now rendered "take their tails," following quihe = "their tails" and Ximénez's "ganaldes las colas" directly, replacing the earlier "skins," which had no support in either witness. (3) "xa hun chubinic xa caib chubinic maui calah" is now rendered "walking alone by one road or by two roads, unnoticed" — matching the Spanish "por vna o dos partes andaban... y nose manífestaban" — rather than the overreading "could not be counted." Independent renderings retained from the first pass ("mountain-place, valley-place" is not present in this section as extracted; "Tohil-Water" reflects "vꜩihel" bathing-place imagery rendered separately) and "Ahquixb Ahcahb" continues to be handled by context rather than a fixed gloss, since the term does not recur verbatim in this excerpt as extracted. Deity names (Tohil, Awilix, Hacawitz) and founder names (Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, Iqui Balam) keep standard manuscript-based spellings, which are orthographic normalizations, not borrowed phrasing, and were confirmed by the audit as showing no sustained resemblance to Tedlock, Recinos/Goetz-Morley, or Christenson.

title: Balam Ki'tze' and the first patriarchs

initial_round2_review.issues: Omissions: (1) "oxib cul" / "los tres paños" — the three cloths to be painted are dropped from the translation body ("paint the sign — the mark of what you are"), despite the translator's note discussing the phrase; (2) the maidens' errand omits the instruction/report to bring back a sign of having seen their faces ("traed señal de que aueís vísto sus caras"). Minor: garbled sentence "This was said, this was they were told"; "ah quixb ahcahb" rendered loosely as "lords"/"patriarchs" instead of penitents/sacrificers.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: No translator-specific echoes. Divine-name spellings (Awilix, Hakawitz) match neither Recinos/Goetz-Morley (Avilix, Hacavitz), Tedlock (Auilix, Hacauitz), nor Christenson (Hacavitz). Tedlock tells ("True Jaguar", "penitents and sacrificers", "Lust Woman/Wailing Woman") absent; Xtah/Xpuch follow the manuscript, not Recinos's Ixtah/Ixpuch. Phrasing reads as independent.

paragraphs: This was the first thing the tribes wished to take counsel on: how to defeat Tohil, Awilix, and Hakawitz. So the chiefs put it before the tribes, and all were called and summoned — not one clan, not two, held itself back; all of them gathered and were called together, and then they took counsel, asking one another: "What shall we do to defeat these newcomers of the K'iche', for our own people are dwindling? It is not clear how men are being lost, whether it is through some theft that has been committed, or whether this is some great wrath belonging to Tohil, Awilix, Hakawitz. Let this be our god as well — Tohil — for otherwise it will not be possible for us to defeat them, since surely we are the many, and this newcomer people of ours is few." This they said when they had all gathered. Then part of the tribes spoke, saying: "Has anyone seen where he bathes in the river every day? If this is indeed Tohil, Awilix, Hakawitz, we shall defeat them there first, and there the ruin of the great ones will begin." So spoke that half when it spoke. Then they said: "And what shall we use to defeat him?" the rest asked. "This is how we shall defeat him," they said, "for he shows himself as a young man when he appears at the river. Let two maidens go, ones who are truly lovely, ones who are truly desirable maidens, and let their longing go out to him." "Good," all of them said. "Let us seek two beautiful maidens," they said. Then they sought among their own daughters, and indeed they were fair young girls. And they instructed the maidens, saying to them: "Go, our daughters, and wash cloths at the river, and if you see three young men, undress before them, and if your bodies please them, tell them: 'we shall go there where you are.' If they say this to you, tell them yes, and when you are asked from where you have come and whose daughters you are, tell them: 'we are the daughters of the lords.' And say further: give us a sign of it, and bring back whatever sign is given you. And if they wish to know your bodies, give yourselves to them; and mark well — if you do not give yourselves, we will kill you. And if you bring back a sign, then our hearts will be content toward you, and we shall keep you. And if there is any sign, bring it." This they instructed the two maidens, one of whom was named Xtah, and the other Xpuch; and Xtah and Xpuch were sent to the river where Tohil, Awilix, Hakawitz bathed. This was what the tribes had devised.

Then the two maidens went off to make themselves ready and adorn themselves, and truly they were lovely when they went to the river, to the bathing place of Tohil, and shamelessly, indecently they washed themselves there. And the lords rejoiced over their two daughters whom they had sent. And on reaching the river they began to wash, and both undressed, each at her washing-stone, working, when Tohil, Awilix, and Hakawitz came, and they arrived at the river, and for a moment the three of them merely looked upon the two washing maidens. And the maidens then felt shame when Tohil arrived. But in no way did Tohil desire the two maidens. So then they were asked: "From where do you come?" the two maidens were asked. "What is it you seek, that you have come here to our water?" they were asked. And they answered: "We were sent here by the lords, and they told us: go and see the face of Tohil, and speak with him, and also bring back a sign that you have indeed seen his face — this is what was told to us." So the two maidens declared their errand. Now this was what the tribes wanted — that the maidens should lie with the naguals of Tohil, is what Tohil, Awilix, Hakawitz said among themselves. Then they said again to Xtah and Xpuch, for so the two maidens were named: "It is well; the sign of our word shall go with you. Wait a little, it will be given, to be carried to the lords." And so afterward the chiefs took counsel among themselves, and it was said to Balam Ki'tze', Balam Aqab, Majukutaj, and Iq'i Balam: "Paint, on three cloths, the sign of what you are, that it may go before the lords, before the tribes, to be carried by the same two washing-maidens. Give it to them" — this was said to Balam Ki'tze', Balam Aqab, Majukutaj, and Iq'i Balam. Now it was the turn of the penitents and offering-makers to take counsel — those who were Balam Ki'tze', Balam Aqab, Majukutaj, Iq'i Balam — and they were told: paint, on three cloths, the sign of your being, so that when it reaches the tribes it may be carried by the two maidens who go there washing, to give to them; and so it was said to Balam Ki'tze', Balam Aqab, Majukutaj.
