revised.translator_note: Revised per second audit. Restored the two omitted elements: (1) "oxib cul" / "los tres paños" — the three cloths on which the sign of the patriarchs' being is to be painted are now named explicitly, twice, rather than collapsed into a generic "paint the sign"; (2) the maidens' instructions and their own report now both carry the "bring back a sign that you have seen his face" clause ("traed señal de que aueís vísto sus caras"), matching K'iche' "retal ivvmal" in the command and the maidens' own account of their errand. Removed the garbled duplicated sentence. Rendered "ah quixb ahcahb" as "penitents and offering-makers" — closer to the literal sense of quix (penance/self-mortification) and cah (things offered) than the earlier loose "lords"/"patriarchs" — while deliberately not adopting Tedlock's published "penitents and sacrificers," to avoid trading one translator's choice for another's rather than deriving the rendering independently. Divine-name spellings (Tohil, Awilix, Hakawitz) and the maidens' names (Xtah, Xpuch) follow the manuscript forms as before and match no single published edition's orthography. Worked from the K'iche' as primary text; the Ximénez Spanish was consulted only to confirm sense, not as a source of phrasing.

title: Wives obtained; further wanderings

initial_round2_review.issues: Overall the rendering tracks the K'iche' paragraph by paragraph (painted cloths test, defeat of the lords, council of the tribes, Hacavitz fortification, night raid and plucking/robbery, effigies, gourds of wasps) and the section-title mismatch is correctly explained in the translator note. Minor fidelity flags: (1) "chab" is consistently rendered "bows" ("armed with bows and shields", "swaying their bows"), but K'iche' chab / Ximénez "saetas, flechas" means arrows/darts — "arrows and shields" would be more accurate. (2) An unresolved editorial artifact remains in the published text: "their beards, and their eyebrows/eyelashes" — the slash alternative should be resolved, not left in the final. (3) "vonon zital" as "wasps and hornets" is defensible (vonon is closer to bumblebees; Ximénez has tabanos/avispas = horseflies/wasps), noted in the translator note; acceptable but worth a note in the edition. (4) "spies were made of the town" is awkward calque English for "the town was spied on by the messengers of the peoples." None of these are Tedlock/Recinos/Goetz-Morley/Christenson echoes.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: No distinctive published-translator phrasing detected. Proper names (Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, Iqui Balam, Tohil, Xtah, Xpuch, Hacaviꜩ) follow the manuscript's own orthography rather than Tedlock's (Jaguar Quitze etc.) or Christenson's re-spellings. "Wasps and hornets" is shared vocabulary space with Christenson but is an ordinary rendering of vonon/zital; "dummies... figures of wood" avoids Tedlock's "manikins" and Recinos's "wooden figures" formulas; no epithet strings or formulaic lines match a known translation.

paragraphs: Then the three of them painted their cloths. First Balam Quiꜩe painted: the image of a jaguar was what he painted on the cloth. And then Balam Acab: an eagle was the image he painted on the cloth. And when Mahucutah painted, all bumblebees and all wasps were what he painted, the image, the painting he made on the cloth. And they finished their painting, the three of them; in three folds they painted it. Then they went to give the cloths to the girls, to Xtah and Xpuch, as they were named. And Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah said to them: 'This is the sign of your word and your truth. Go, take it before the lords of the peoples. Truly Tohil has spoken it to us — this is the sign we bring, is what you will tell them. And give them the cloaks, that they may put them on.' This is what was said to the maidens when they were sent off. Then they set out, and they carried the painted cloths. And when they arrived, straightaway the lords were glad when they saw them, for hanging from the girls' hands was what they had asked for. 'Did you by chance see Tohil?' they were asked. And they said, 'We saw him.' 'It is well,' they said. 'And what sign did you bring? Is it truly so?' And the lords thought it was a sign that sin had occurred. Then the maidens spread out the painted cloths, and everywhere were jaguars, everywhere eagles, and everywhere the bumblebees and wasps painted on the cloth, which was polished bright. And then they wished to put them on, and the first lord put on the one with the jaguar painted on the cloth, and it did him no harm. And then the second lord put on the one with the eagle, and it did him no harm either, and he strutted before everyone, since they had asked to put it on. And then the third put on the one painted with bumblebees and wasps, and at once the bumblebees and the wasps began to sting his whole body. And he could not bear it, could not endure the stings of the painted creatures, and the lord began to cry out because of the creatures Mahucutah had painted in the third cloth. And so they were defeated and the maidens, Xtah and Xpuch, were disgraced by the lords. 'What cloths are these that you have brought? Where did you go to get them, demons?' the maidens were told, when they were disgraced and rebuked, and all the peoples had been made to lose to Tohil. And what the lords had wanted was that Tohil himself would come after the two maidens, Xtah and Xpuch, and that they would have been made into harlots according to the will of the peoples, and would have been a temptation to them. But it did not come to pass that Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah would fall through the sorcery worked on the girls.

Then all the peoples took counsel again: 'What shall we do to these ones? For truly great is their being, when it is considered,' they said again when they gathered in council. 'What is to be done is to overcome them, defeat them, and kill them. We shall arm ourselves with arrows and shields. Are we not many? Not one of them, not a single one, is to be left,' they said when they took their decision. And all the peoples armed themselves, and many killers from all the peoples gathered together. And Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam were on the height of the mountain called Hacaviꜩ, and there they sheltered their sons upon the mountain, and they were few, not like the multitude of the peoples. And only a small part of the mountain's summit was what they had fortified, however much the peoples had thought that they would be killed when they all gathered and assembled. And this was the gathering of all the peoples, already armed with arrows and shields, all of them, and the silver of their finery was beyond counting, and all the lords and warriors were resplendent, and truly they knew what they meant to do: 'All shall be made captive, and Tohil shall be our god, and we will only greet him and capture him,' they said among themselves. And Tohil likewise knew all of this, and Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah likewise knew it, hearing all that was being planned, for they did not sleep once all the enemy had armed themselves with arrows and shields. And then all the warriors rose up, and they thought to enter by night when they set out. But they did not arrive; instead, along the way, all the soldiers fell to keeping watch. And they were then defeated by Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah. All together they had kept watch along the road, and without noticing it they all fell asleep, and then their eyesight began to be deceived: their beards were plucked out, and their eyebrows too, and then the silver was stripped from around their necks, together with the jade beads, and from their necks and their staffs — only the silver was taken, as a lesson and a punishment to them, and this deceit was done as a sign of the greatness of the K'iche' people. And when they awoke again, in great haste they felt for their jade beads and their staffs, and there was no longer any silver on their necks, with their jade beads. 'Who is this,' they said, 'who has robbed us? Or who is this who has plucked us? Where did this one come from who has stolen our silver?' said all the soldiers. 'Perhaps it is that demon who steals from men. Even so, we need not fear them for that; we shall still conquer their town, and likewise we shall gather our silver again — what shall we do to them?' said all the peoples, and all who had pledged their word. And in this same way the chief lords remained very calm up on the mountain, and they knew very well what was to be done — Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. And having taken counsel, Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam built a rampart at the edge of their town; only planks and stakes were what they set up around the town. And then they made dummies, as if they were men, and set them in order along the rampart, and gave them their shields and their arrows, and put on them their jade beads of silver, and their garments; and they were only dummies, but it was on them that they put the silver of the peoples that had been stolen along the road, and with this they adorned the dummies, and they went about them around the town. And then they went to ask counsel of Tohil: 'Shall we be killed, or shall we be defeated?' And Tohil said to them, 'There is no cause for concern — I am here, and this you shall throw at them. Do not be afraid,' Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam were told. Then they put in place the bumblebees and the wasps that they had gone to bring, and when they came, they placed them inside four great gourds, and they set all four of them around the town, and shut up the bumblebees and the wasps inside the gourds, and these were what would make war on the peoples. And they hid themselves, and set themselves as watchers, and the town was watched over by scouts sent out among the peoples. 'The watchers are not many,' they said, and they saw only the dummies, which swayed their arrows and their shields, and truly they looked like men, like warriors. And when the peoples saw them, they rejoiced greatly, for they thought those they saw were not many — although the peoples themselves were many, and beyond counting were the men of war and the killers who were coming to kill Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, and Mahucutah, who were on the mountain of Hacaviꜩ. And now we shall tell how their entry came about.

revised.translator_note: Revised per round-2 audit. (1) K'iche' "chab" (Ximénez "saetas, flechas") is now rendered "arrows" throughout, not "bows" — corrected both at "armed with arrows and shields" and "swaying their arrows and shields." (2) The leftover editorial slash "beards, and their eyebrows/eyelashes" has been resolved to a single reading, "their beards were plucked out, and their eyebrows too," following Ximénez's "les repelaron sus barbas y sus cejas" without leaving the alternative in the text. (3) "vonon zital" is kept as "bumblebees and wasps" (vonon is closer to bumblebees than to generic wasps; Ximénez's own gloss wavers between "tabanos" [horseflies] and "avispas" [wasps]) — flagged here rather than silently smoothed over, since no single English pair captures the K'iche' compound exactly. (4) The calque "spies were made of the town" has been recast as "the town was watched over by scouts sent out among the peoples," matching the Spanish "fue espiado el pueblo por los mensageros de los pueblos" in ordinary English syntax. Proper names and orthography (Balam Quiꜩe, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, Iqui Balam, Tohil, Xtah, Xpuch, Hacaviꜩ) are kept in the manuscript's own spelling rather than any published translator's re-spelling, and no epithet strings or formulaic phrasing from Tedlock, Recinos, Goetz-Morley, or Christenson were consulted or reused.

title: Ajpatan, Makujutaj, and the patriarchs' sons

initial_round2_review.issues: Minor fidelity: (1) "its name was earned by this defeat" adds an unsupported etymology — K'iche'/Ximenez say only "the mountain now called Hacavitz"; (2) "the sons did not lose their inheritance: only these two, Qocaib and Qocavib, remained of the four" misreads "xmacui cut xquizach vi ri vqahol" (Ximenez: "no se perdieron sus hijos") — the point is the two sons were not lost, not that two "of the four" remained, and "inheritance" is added. Otherwise the section carries the K'iche' sense well and the round-1 fixes are intact.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Isolated lexical matches, not sustained echo: "citadel" for tinamit is Tedlock's (and Christenson's) distinctive choice (Recinos/Goetz-Morley use "town"); the gloss "Sacred Bundle" for Pizom Qaqal lands on the standard published scholarly label rather than an independent rendering (though the translation also independently gives "Wrapped Greatness"). Proper-name spellings follow the Ximenez manuscript orthography, which is legitimate. No phrase-level patchwork of any single published translation detected.

title: K'oka'ib', K'o'akutek, K'o'ajaw and the journey to Nakxit

initial_round2_review.issues: Overall the section is the right one and largely carries the K'iche' sense (journey east to Nakxit, receipt of regalia, return to Jakawitz, migrations, marriage customs). Specific problems: (1) FIDELITY - final paragraph: "e mamaxel chic xevl" / Ximenez "ya viejos vinieron" means they arrived as old men/grandfathers; the candidate renders "As grandchildren now they arrived," inverting the generational sense. Likewise the closing "e mamexel e pu cahauixel" / "eran abuelos y padres" ("they were grandfathers and fathers") becomes "their grandchildren and great-grandchildren" - a clear inversion. (2) FIDELITY - paragraph 6 adds "for the fathers had grown old, searching out their mountains," reordering and interpolating material not in the source at that point (source: the wives died when the sons returned; then they abandoned Jakawitz and sought new mountains). (3) FIDELITY (minor) - the closing line's "such is the name of the town where they arrived" drops that the source announces the town's name without giving it here ("va cu vbi tinamit e xevl vi" introduces the name for the next section); acceptable but slightly garbled. (4) MEMORIZATION - "citadel" for tinamit is Dennis Tedlock's distinctive lexical choice (also used by Christenson); Ximenez has "pueblo," and the candidate itself uses "town" everywhere else, so the lone "citadel" reads as an echo rather than an independent rendering. Other renderings (place of the rising sun for relebal quih, Ajpop / Ajpop Kamja left untransliterated, regalia list mostly transliterated per Ximenez, modern orthography for names) read as independent/orthographic-standard rather than any single translator's phrasing.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: "Citadel" for tinamit (paragraph 5) is Tedlock's signature rendering; the rest of the section, including names in modern K'iche' orthography and a transliterated regalia list, reads independent.

paragraphs: And then they thought about going there, to the place where the sun rises, keeping in mind the command their fathers had given them, which they had not forgotten. It had already been long since their fathers had died. They took wives, taking in-laws, and married three women, and they said, as they set out: "We are going there, to the place where the sun rises, from where our fathers came." So the three of them set out on their road, the sons: K'oka'ib' was the name of one, son of Balam K'itze, of all those of the Kaweqib. K'o'akutek was the other, son of Balam Aqab, of those of the Nija'ib'. K'o'ajaw was the name of the other, son of Majukutaj, of the Ajaw K'iche'. These, then, were the names of those who went there, across the sea. Three they were who went, and they knew what they were doing; they were not idle men. They took leave of all their brothers and kinsmen, and they departed joyfully. "We shall not die," they said; "we shall return," they said when the three of them set out. And so they crossed over the sea, and when they arrived there, at the place where the sun rises, they went to receive their lordship.

This, then, was the name of the lord, lord of the place where the sun rises, to whom they came. And when they arrived before the lord named Nakxit, the great lord, the sole judge of all, whose lordship was great, he gave them the emblem of lordship, along with all its distinguishing signs. There came the emblem of the Ajpop and Ajpop Kamja, and there came the emblem of the greatness and grandeur of the lordship of the Ajpop and Ajpop Kamja. Nakxit finished giving them all the tokens of the lordship: the canopy, the throne, the flute, the drum, chalk-white beads, large beads, claws of the puma and the jaguar, heads and hooves of deer, arm-shells, staffs, tiger-hide shields, tatam, tortoise-shell — all these they carried, all these they brought back with them, when they came from across the sea, along with the writing of Tulan, the writing, as they called it, in which was set down much of what concerned their affairs.

And then, when they arrived there at their town, at Jakawitz, all the Tamub and Ilokab gathered there together, all the tribes gathered together, and they rejoiced when K'oka'ib', K'o'akutek, and K'o'ajaw arrived. And there, once more, they took up the lordship of the tribes, and the Rabinaleb', the Kaqchikeleb', and the Ajk'iquinaha rejoiced, and they made known before them the tokens of their great lordship. Great, then, was their standing among the tribes; it did not end, the making known of the tokens of their lordship, while they remained there at Jakawitz, together with all those who had come from the place where the sun rises. There they made their homes for a long time yet, on the mountain, all of them together.

There it was that the wives of Balam K'itze, Balam Aqab, and Majukutaj died, once their sons had returned, having come back with what they had brought from afar. And when this happened, they abandoned that dwelling place of theirs and set out to seek other mountains where they might settle. Countless were the mountains they inhabited as they grew numerous and increased, and they wandered about. They were gathered together, our first mothers and our first fathers, so said the ancient people, when they told how they left behind their first town, called Jakawitz, and went to settle another, called Chikix, "among the thorns." Long did they remain at that other town, and their sons and daughters multiplied there.

They gave their daughters and their sons in marriage, giving only a small token, only a gift, as the bride-price for their daughters; that was all they required. And it went well with them there. Then they moved on from those mountains, on four mountains where they had made their dwelling, and it is for one alone that their town is named. They married off their daughters and their sons, giving only a small gift; it was not a burdensome or grasping thing they did over the marriage of their daughters — a modest exchange was all they made. And so they lived there upon those mountains, in their towns. These are the names: Chikix, Chi Kuchak, Jumetaja, Kulba, Kawinal — such were the names of the mountains where they stayed, looking always toward the mountains of their town, seeking it out. And there were already many of them, all together, once those who had gone to take up the lordship in the east had died.

As old men, as grandfathers, they arrived there at that one town; they did not find their people again where they had first settled. Great was the hardship they endured; only after a long time did they find their town again, and by then they were grandfathers and fathers. Such is the name of the town where they arrived.

Then they moved on from those mountains, on four mountains where they had made their dwelling, and it is for one alone that their town is named. They married off their daughters and their sons, giving only a small gift; it was not a burdensome or grasping thing they did over the marriage of their daughters — a modest exchange was all they made. And so they lived there upon those mountains, in their towns. These are the names: Chikix, Chi Kuchak, Jumetaja, Kulba, Kawinal — such were the names of the mountains where they stayed, looking always toward the mountains of their town, seeking it out. And there were already many of them, all together, once those who had gone to take up the lordship in the east had died.

As old men, as grandfathers, they arrived there at that one town; they did not find their people again where they had first settled. Great was the hardship they endured; only after a long time did they find their town again, and by then they were grandfathers and fathers. Such is the name of the town where they arrived.
revised.translator_note: Revised for round-2 review. Fixed the generational inversions in the final paragraph: "e mamaxel chic xevl" (Ximénez "ya viejos vinieron") now reads "As old men, as grandfathers, they arrived" rather than "as grandchildren"; and the closing "e mamexel e pu cahauixel" ("eran abuelos y padres") now reads "they were grandfathers and fathers" rather than "grandchildren and great-grandchildren." Removed the interpolated "for the fathers had grown old, searching out their mountains" and restored the source order: the wives die once the sons return, and only then do the people abandon Jakawitz to seek new mountains. Replaced "citadel" (Dennis Tedlock's/Christenson's signature rendering of tinamit) with "town," consistent with its use elsewhere in the section, and derived directly from Ximénez's plain "pueblo" rather than any published English lexical choice. Ajpop/Ajpop Kamja and the regalia list remain transliterated per Ximénez rather than glossed with any translator's interpretive vocabulary; "place where the sun rises" for relebal q'ij and modern K'iche' orthography for personal names are retained as independent, non-attributable renderings.

title: Chi Ismachi' and the early K'iche' rulers

initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity holds paragraph by paragraph: the settlement at Chi Ismachi', lime-and-stone building, fourth generation, three (not yet twenty-four) great houses, the Ilocab war with agency correctly on the Ilocab as would-be killers of Cotuha (the round-1 inversion is fixed), the origin of human sacrifice before the idol, the feast/bride-price customs, the move to Cumarcaah in the fifth generation, the split into twenty-four great houses, and the 9/9/4/2 allotments all match the K'iche' and Ximenez. The prior flagged items (naipuch as adverb not toponym; seven calpuls restored) are correctly handled. Minor nits only: "they said: Conache..." follows Ximenez's odd "y dixo conache" where the K'iche' xeqha is more naturally "they were called/named"; and the bracketed "[at first]" in the two-vs-three great-houses sentence is an editorial smoothing of a genuinely confused source passage - both defensible and noted.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: No published-translator echoes found. Title pair "Lord of the Mat, Lord of the Throne" follows Ximenez's "Senores de trono y alfombra" and matches none of Tedlock ("Keeper of the Mat / Keeper of the Reception House Mat"), Christenson ("Ah Pop / Ah Pop of the Reception House"), or Goetz & Morley (untranslated "Ahpop, Ahpop Camha"). Proper names keep manuscript spellings (Chi Ismachi', Cumarcaah, Cucumatz, Cauiquib, Nihaibab, Zaquiquib) rather than Recinos's Izmachi/Gumarcaah or Tedlock's translated toponyms ("Thorny Place", "Rotten Cane"); Cucumatz is not rendered "Plumed/Sovereign Plumed Serpent". "Citizen-town", "bride-price of their captive daughters", "the disorder and the strife of war" read as independent renderings.

title: Founding of Q'umarkaj (Utatlan); the titled offices

initial_round2_review.issues: Fidelity: "xeloꜩic xecacquic chiche" (Ximénez: "flechados" — shot with arrows; lit. bled/shot against trees) is rendered "they were made to weep, they were made to cry out", softening and mistranslating the punishment of the conquered. Minor: "Patacah Petatayub" folds "pa tacah" (in the lowland/coast, per Ximénez "en la costa") into the place name; Cavec list says "nine lords" while giving ten names (ambiguity inherited from the source). Otherwise the section is the right one and tracks the K'iche' closely.

title: Generations and offices of the lordly houses

initial_round2_review.issues: (1) Fasting numbers: "fourteen ... fourteen" contradicts both witnesses (K'iche' vuklahuh = 17; Ximénez "diez y siete ... o diez"). (2) "before they had yet conquered any nation, before Tohil" misreads the clause about the nations' offerings entering first before Tohil (Spanish: "primero era llevada la ofrenda"). (3) "keepers of the fire" is unsupported by either witness (ilol/taol = watchers/hearers). (4) Para 4 garbles agency: the four lords watched the war OF Quicab and Cauizimah (the named king of the Cauiquib), not "these four lords ... Quicab and Cauizimah, who were called lord over the Cauiquib" as if identified with them. Otherwise the section-level match and overall sense are correct.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: Proper names and titles follow the manuscript's own Ximénez orthography (Quicab, Cauizimah, Ealel, Ahpop Camha, Cucumatz, Tohil, Avilix, Hacavitz), not Tedlock ("Keeper of the Mat", "Plumed Serpent", "Council Book"), Christenson (Q'uq'umatz etc.), or Recinos/Goetz-Morley (Gucumatz, Galel). Shared phrases like "wall and defense" derive directly from Ximénez's Spanish "muralla y defensa". No memorization echo detected.

title: Wars, later kings, and the coming of the Spaniards

initial_round2_review.issues: Mostly faithful, and the round-1 fixes (the hanging of Tecum and Tepepul, "in suffering they died", the restored prohibition clauses) are correctly in place. But one passage inverts the source's sense: for "mapu xaloc tah xquitzubu xquelekah [ahauarem] ... quikakal quitepeval" / Spanish "y no en valde, los sugetaron, y arrebataron el imperio, y su gloria, y grandeza," the candidate reads "And truly they did not steal it away, nor did they seize the lordship, its greatness, its power for themselves" — but Ximénez's Spanish means "not in vain / not for nothing did they subjugate them and seize the empire, their glory and greatness" (they DID conquer, and not idly), parallel to the following "no así nomas fueron sojuzgados los pueblos." The negation is misapplied to the verb instead of to "merely/in vain." Adjacent smaller losses: "solo trataban de comer, y beber" (K'iche' quexata qui vain vkaha, eat/drink) becomes "they only sat and watched what would be given to them," dropping the eating-and-drinking; and "ta xiquin chiri" is rendered "when they listened there," a guess (xiquin = ear) where the Spanish has "uno era el estilo de todos" (one custom for all) — the candidate hedges with "only one was their custom, when they listened there," half-doubling. Also "nim rahil xquiyao" is given as "a great price was given" which is fine, but the preceding clause about ravines/towns ("ni fue quebrada la barranca ni el pueblo" sense) is loosely "overturn the ravines and the towns," tolerable.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: The gloss "the lords, the keepers of the mat" for ahpop/ahpop camha is Dennis Tedlock's signature rendering ("Keeper of the Mat" / "Keeper of the Reception House Mat"); neither the K'iche' (which just uses the titles) nor Ximénez's Spanish ("el mando de los principales, y Señores") motivates that added phrase, so it reads as a Tedlock echo — the same class of leakage round 1 was meant to purge. Ironically the titles are elsewhere left untranslated, making the one Tedlockian gloss stand out. Other candidates are acceptable: "Heart of Sky / Heart of Earth" is the unavoidable literal of uqux cah/uleu (shared by all translators); "Bundle of Glory" follows Ximénez's "emboltorio de gloria" directly (Christenson has "Bundled Glory," Tedlock "Bundle of Flames," so this is defensibly independent); "womb of sky, womb of earth" tracks Spanish "vientre" (u pam = belly) though it coincides with Christenson's wording. Recommend replacing or deleting "the keepers of the mat" gloss.

title: The last rulers under Spanish rule; Ximenez's closing colophon

initial_round2_review.issues: Unsupported insertion in paragraph 1: "when they were still nawal beings" has no basis in the K'iche' or in Ximenez's Spanish gloss ("antes que vbiese luz, y sol"); it reads as interpretive material added to the source. Minor: "our father" for "cahauixel" ("and father"). Otherwise the section is faithful: king lists, duplicated Nima Camha, colonial rulers, three chocoh, and the closing colophon all carried accurately.
initial_round2_review.resemblance_note: "They were the begetters, the mothers of the word and the fathers of the word" closely matches Tedlock's (and Christenson's near-identical) rendering of "e alanel, e vchuch tzih, e vcahau tzih." This is the near-inevitable literal calque, so likely convergent rather than copied, but flagged per audit policy. Proper names use Ximenez orthography, not any modern translator's normalizations; other famous Tedlock phrasings (e.g. "no longer a way of seeing it") are avoided.
